cards.use_when: Workshopping or briefing a sponsored article draft for a product when your current creative is a flat product-plus-buy-button ad.
steps: Start from your standard ad: product claim, image, Buy button—recognize this as the baseline the source contrasts against.
Decide where the placement lives (e.g., a publication like The Wall Street Journal, or a BuzzFeed-style listicle) and write to that publication's editorial voice.
Draft the bulk (~70%) as content readers would want on its own merits—a story, how-to, or funny list—using the source's dog-food example of a viral 'dogs working out too hard' piece.
Insert the product mention into the content honestly and naturally (e.g., the product as a feature within a broader fun or useful piece), keeping the pitch portion to ~30% or less.
Add the promotional element—a deal, a link, a store mention—after the value has been delivered.
Test the resulting piece against the tear-out and shareability tests: would someone save it or send it to a friend?
Route advertorial readers to a conversion page (PDP or landing page) and measure reads-to-clicks-to-purchases separately from the article's engagement.
caveats: The walkthrough is a teaching exercise, not a documented ecommerce campaign result.
The source's 'Donnie the dog / Purina' scenario is hypothetical and does not imply a real brand relationship.
cards.source_name: Advertorials_ How To Write Them & Why They’re Awesome.docx

cards.title: Treat conversion rate as the primary growth lever when ad costs rise
cards.summary: Doubling conversion rate beats doubling traffic because CRO lifts ROI on every future dollar of ad spend and compounds.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to allocate budget and effort between paid traffic acquisition and landing page/checkout conversion work for your store.
steps: Recognize that ad platforms run on auctions: competitors bid for the same eyeballs, so CPMs and CPCs tend to rise over time. The source cites year-over-year increases of roughly 61% on Meta, 185% on TikTok, and 75% on Google CPMs (14% on search CPCs) as an example of that trend, not a forecast.

Think of two ways to double revenue: double traffic, or double conversion rate. The source argues conversion is superior because a higher-converting page multiplies the return on all traffic you send later, and the gain persists after the campaign ends.

Before buying more traffic, audit whether the page is fundamentally optimized: does the above-the-fold section state who you are, what you sell and the customer's benefit in under 5 seconds? Fix structural gaps first, then scale spend.
Also model the downstream effect: a conversion-efficiency gain expands your LTV to CAC ratio, which in the source's framing lets you outbid competitors in ads and reinvest in the business.
Keep spend scaling gated on measured conversion performance rather than launching more campaigns into an unoptimized page.
caveats: The specific platform cost increases are the source's illustrative figures and change over time; verify current data.
A conversion lift only compounds if the traffic quality and offer stay comparable; it is not a substitute for product-market fit.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Run one split test per week and let wins compound
cards.summary: Testing one element per week forces focus and produces a compounding record of what your audience responds to.
cards.use_when: Setting up a repeatable landing page or PDP testing cadence for your store instead of ad-hoc redesigns.
steps: Hold a weekly marketing meeting and commit to a single split test per week, as the source does. One test forces you to pick the hypothesis most likely to move results rather than spreading effort across many ideas.

Log every test's result, win or lose, in a shared document with the hypothesis, the variant, and the measured outcome. The source treats this dataset as the real asset, because winning insights transfer to ads, positioning, and product decisions.

When a test wins, immediately design the next test to double down on that same winning idea before moving to an unrelated element. The source describes an ecommerce client where moving price lower on the product page and adding trust elements above it produced a 32% conversion gain, and adding more trust elements above the price produced a cumulative 88% gain.
Over a year (52 tests) and multiple years, the compounding record makes each subsequent hypothesis better informed, so conversion improves as a process, not by luck.
Inspect the current testing tool's setup each time, since interfaces and statistical reporting change.
caveats: One test per week assumes enough traffic for statistical significance; the source notes a business with tens of thousands of visitors per month can sustain it, and that under about 1,000 visitors per week you likely cannot.
Sequential wins from doubling down on one theme are source-reported case results, not guaranteed outcomes.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Use an A/B calculator to set test duration on low-traffic stores
cards.summary: Low-traffic stores should calculate required sample size before testing, or make sequential changes measured with session recordings instead.
cards.use_when: Planning how many tests your store can realistically run per month given its traffic and current conversion rate.
steps: Enter your current traffic level and baseline conversion rate into an online A/B testing calculator before launching a test. The calculator returns how long the test must run and how many tests are realistically possible at your volume.
If you have fewer than roughly 1,000 visitors per week, the source says you realistically cannot run one statistically valid A/B test per week. Do not call a result a win on a sample that small.

For low-traffic stores in the range of about 10,000 to 20,000 visitors per month, the source's agency instead reviews objective behavioral data (the source mentions Microsoft Clarity session recordings and heatmaps) and makes changes based on observed friction, then measures what happens over time.

With this sequential approach, accept that you cannot attribute the change to a single element the way a 50/50 split would. Treat it as directional evidence and keep the change only if the metric holds after a full business cycle.
Re-run the calculator whenever traffic or conversion baseline shifts materially, since the required sample size changes.
caveats: Statistical significance thresholds and calculator interfaces vary by tool; verify the current tool's assumptions.
Sequential before/after changes are confounded by seasonality, promotions and traffic mix; the source explicitly frames them as an alternative to, not equivalent of, a true split test.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Test the above-the-fold section first — it is the highest-leverage area
cards.summary: The top of the page is the only section 100% of visitors see and roughly 60% never scroll past it, so headline and hero image tests generate the largest gains.
cards.use_when: Choosing which page element to test next on a landing page, PDP, or homepage when you can only run one experiment.
steps: Treat the above-the-fold area (headline and the image below it) as the default testing target, especially in early optimization stages. The source advises spending the vast majority of early effort there.

Test the headline first, then the hero image underneath it. The source's agency says nearly all of the biggest conversion jumps come from these two elements, with headline tests producing lifts in the 60–80% range and above-the-fold tests reported as high as 130% across both B2B and ecommerce clients.

Justify prioritization with two facts the source cites: 100% of visitors see the above-the-fold area, and statistically about 60% never scroll past it, so changes below the fold are only ever seen by a minority.
Keep one change per test so you can attribute the lift to the headline or the image rather than a combined redesign.
Once the above-the-fold is strong, move budget and test slots to lower sections such as trust elements or product-detail modules.
caveats: The 60% no-scroll figure and the percentage lifts are source-reported approximations and case examples, not universal benchmarks.
Some product categories need scroll depth for considered purchases; test whether adding above-the-fold information changes scroll behavior.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Write headlines that pass the 5-second who/what/benefit test
cards.summary: A headline must state who you are, what you do, and what's in it for the customer in under 5 seconds, with the benefit being the most important part.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the main headline and subheadline on a store homepage, landing page, or product page.
steps: Ask whether the headline clearly answers three questions: who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me. The third is the most important and the one most pages omit.
State the core benefit in concrete terms: does the offer save time, save money, reduce risk, or increase status? Make that legible within 5 seconds of landing.

Only after the benefit is nailed down, run variant tests on the headline itself, testing different phrasings of the value proposition or different framings of the end benefit. The source reports 60–80% conversion gains from headline tests alone.
Use the headline as the first place the Value Equation's dream outcome appears, and reinforce it in the body copy directly underneath.
Check that the subheadline and hero image do not contradict the headline's promise, since the three are seen together in the same 5-second window.
caveats: The 5-second rule and lift percentages come from the source's agency experience; treat as heuristic guides rather than measured thresholds.
Different awareness levels of traffic may need differently specific headlines; run variants rather than assuming one formulation.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Use the 'so that' chain to find the deepest customer benefit
cards.summary: Repeatedly asking 'so that…' drills past the functional feature to the end outcome the customer actually wants.
cards.use_when: Developing headline, hero, or ad copy for your store when the first benefit you write sounds generic or feature-based.
steps: Start with what your product functionally does, then ask 'so that…' and answer it.

Continue the chain until the answer reaches an outcome the customer would recognize as valuable in their own life. The source's worked example: 'Warm up your emails so that you land in the inbox so that you close more deals so that you generate more revenue.'
Put the deepest outcome in the above-the-fold headline, and keep the intermediate steps in the supporting body copy to make the logic credible.

Apply the same chain to physical goods: for a table, the functional answer is 'something to put things on,' but the deeper outcome is 'when guests walk into my home they feel immediately impressed,' which reframes the purchase around status.

For consumer products, spend more time translating what the status or lifestyle outcome means to the buyer and how painful the lack of it has been; the source notes B2B buyers are easier to reach because the outcome is usually money and time.
caveats: Pushing too far up the chain can produce abstract claims that lose specificity and credibility; balance the deepest benefit with a concrete product fact.
The status-based framing is the source's example, not a universal rule for every category.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Map the Value Equation to specific page elements
cards.summary: Hormozi's four-part value framework becomes page components: dream outcome in the headline, perceived likelihood under the CTA, time delay in copy and shipping, effort in 'done-for-you' wording.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing product page or landing page to find which value component is missing or weak.
steps: Dream Outcome: state the end goal explicitly in the main headline and subheadline above the fold. If the buyer wants to save time, make money, or lose weight, that outcome should be visible immediately.

Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (risk): place trust badges, guarantees, testimonials, case studies, free trials, no-credit-card terms or return policies directly below or around the CTA button. The source's example places free trial, fast setup, easy cancellation and API integrations under a SaaS CTA, and free 30-day returns, money-back guarantee, one-year warranty and free US shipping under an ecommerce add-to-cart button.

Time Delay: quantify how fast the buyer gets results or receives the product. Examples: a 'ships in 24 hours' line under the add-to-cart button, or 'get funded fast' on a mortgage CTA. The longer the perceived delay, the less valuable the offer reads.
Effort and Sacrifice: write copy that states what the customer will not have to do, such as 'we reach out to thousands of influencers so that you don't have to.'
Score your page against all four components and fix the weakest one first rather than rewriting everything at once.
caveats: The source's example lifts (e.g. a 30% conversion gain from adding guarantee badges, from A/B testing) are case-study results, not expected averages.
B2B pages often need less status framing because money and time outcomes are obvious; consumer pages may need more.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: De-risk the purchase with guarantees directly under the CTA
cards.summary: Placing trust badges, guarantees and return terms next to the buy button removes purchase uncertainty and, in the source's test, lifted conversion 30%.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a PDP or landing page where visitors hesitate or abandon near the add-to-cart or signup button.
steps: List the main uncertainties a buyer has at the moment of clicking buy: will it arrive, can I return it, is it guaranteed, does it work with my setup.

Place explicit assurances directly under or beside the CTA button rather than in a distant footer. Typical ecommerce set: free 30-day return, 100% money-back guarantee, one-year warranty, free shipping. Typical software set: free trial, fast setup, easy cancellation, integration logos.

If price is the objection, restructure the page so trust-building elements appear above the price, not after it. The source's ecommerce client saw a 32% conversion gain from lowering price position and adding trust above it, then a cumulative 88% gain after adding more trust elements above the price.
Run the badge set as a single A/B test against the page without badges; the source reports a 30% lift from adding guarantee badges under the add-to-cart button.
After a win, extend the same trust messaging into ad creative and email to keep the promise consistent across touchpoints.
caveats: Badges must reflect real policy; citing guarantees you don't honor creates refund and dispute problems.
Badge sets that work for physical goods may need different specifics for services or subscriptions; test your own set.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Quantify delivery and result timelines in copy and button labels
cards.summary: Reducing perceived time-to-result increases value; state shipping speed or result timelines in the copy and CTA, not just in policy pages.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, shipping messaging, or CTA labels for a store where fulfillment speed or time-to-outcome is a purchase driver.
steps: Find the time-related anxiety in your category — when will it arrive, how long until I see results — and answer it at the point of decision.
On ecommerce pages, place shipping speed under the add-to-cart button, e.g. 'ships in 24 hours', alongside secure-checkout reassurance.

On outcome-based products, quantify both amount and duration in the headline, as in the source's weight-loss example, 'lose 30 lbs in 90 days' — this states the dream outcome and the time delay together.
Use design as well as copy: a CTA button reading 'get funded fast' carries the time message without extra paragraph text, per the source's mortgage-lending example.
Test timeline messaging as its own variable, separate from price or image, so you can see how much of the lift comes from speed perception.
caveats: Do not promise timelines your logistics cannot meet; unmet speed claims drive returns and complaints.
The source notes that few companies quantify timelines properly, so this is often an untested gap rather than a proven winner for your store.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Write 'done-for-you' copy to reduce perceived effort and sacrifice
cards.summary: Stating explicitly what the customer will not have to do lowers the effort component of value, especially for services and complex products.
cards.use_when: Writing hero or feature copy for a managed service, subscription, or product that replaces manual work your customer dislikes.
steps: Run customer interviews to find the manual, repetitive or unpleasant tasks your customer associates with getting the outcome. The source's influencer-agency research found users frustrated by manually contacting large numbers of influencers.
Turn that finding into a headline that names the eliminated work: 'we reach out to thousands of influencers so that you don't have to.'
Extend the same logic to service elements: white-glove delivery, assembly, setup, onboarding, or migration performed for the buyer rather than by them.
Place the effort-reduction message high on the page, since it functions as part of the value proposition rather than a feature detail.
Pair the promise with evidence, such as volume numbers or process descriptions, so the claim reads as credible rather than dismissive.
caveats: The source's examples are its own clients; the conversion impact of effort-reduction copy varies by category.
Overpromising 'we do everything' can create operational and expectation problems; keep the claim within what you deliver.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Choose hero images that reinforce the value proposition
cards.summary: The hero image should visually demonstrate who you are and what you deliver; a weak or generic image is a common source of lost conversions.
cards.use_when: Selecting or testing the main image under the headline on a landing page, PDP, or homepage.
steps: Check whether the current hero image communicates the core value proposition on its own. The source's 'before' example was described as a boring image conveying nothing about the offer.
Identify what visual proof your product can show: outputs, customer usage, social proof at scale, or the end state the buyer wants.

Build the replacement image around that proof. For the influencer agency example, the agency assembled the client work produced with influencers into a collage or carousel to demonstrate social proof at scale, producing a reported 78% conversion gain from that image test alone.
Test the image as its own variable, separate from the headline, so you can attribute the result.
Once an image concept wins on the page, reuse the same concept in ad creative; the source reports a large click-through-rate increase after applying the carousel concept to ads.
caveats: Image tests can shift perceived audience or brand tone, so watch impact on lead quality, not just conversion count.
The 78% figure is one client case and depends on the original image being poor.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Treat CRO results as transferable customer research, not just a page metric
cards.summary: Every winning or losing test reveals what resonates with your audience and can be redeployed across ads, positioning, and product decisions.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to do with test results beyond keeping or reverting the variant on your store's pages.
steps: Log each test as a hypothesis about the customer, not just an element change: record what you believed would resonate and whether it did.

For winning tests, extract the underlying insight and inject it into other channels: ad creative angles, value proposition framing, product naming, UX changes, and feature ideas. The source's example carried the winning carousel image concept from the landing page into ads and saw a large click-through-rate increase.
For losing tests, treat the result as evidence to avoid that message in marketing rather than discarding the test.
Feed the insight back into the next landing page test so each weekly experiment builds on audience knowledge rather than starting fresh.
Use the accumulated record to make positioning decisions that span page, ads, and product messaging.
caveats: Transferring a landing-page insight to ads or product assumes similar audience and context; validate in the new channel rather than assuming the same lift.
Insights decay as audience and competitive context change; revisit them periodically.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Frame premium physical goods around status, not features
cards.summary: The dream outcome for a consumer product can be a felt status shift, which justifies a price far above the functional value of the materials.
cards.use_when: Positioning and pricing a premium or discretionary physical product in your store where competing on materials alone drives price comparisons.
steps: Identify the functional description of your product and then name the deeper outcome the buyer wants. For a table, the functional answer is 'a surface to put things on'; the status outcome is 'guests feel immediately impressed when they walk in.'

Translate the status outcome into risks and objections: if status is the goal, the risk is that the product fails to signal it, so show evidence that the style or trend is understood and valued (for example, demonstrating that the look is a recognized trend).

Reduce the friction around delivery and setup for heavy or complex goods: offer white-glove delivery, doorway fitting, on-site assembly, and near-immediate arrival so the buyer can use it for a specific occasion.
Tie all four value components to the status framing so the buyer is willing to pay for how much the status is worth to them, rather than for the wood or materials.
Because the source notes consumer buyers need more translation than B2B buyers, spend additional copy explaining the meaning of the status shift and the pain of lacking it.
caveats: The table example is the source's hypothetical illustration, not a tested campaign result.
Status framing can alienate buyers seeking value or durability; test against a functional framing for your audience.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Always test the headline before any other page element
cards.summary: Headline tests produce the largest and most reliable gains, so make the headline the first and most frequent test on every page.
cards.use_when: Deciding the first experiment to run on a new or underperforming store page.
steps: Start every optimization sequence with the headline, since it is seen by 100% of visitors and sits in the above-the-fold area the source treats as highest leverage.
Generate variants that express different value propositions or different phrasings of the same end benefit, rather than cosmetic edits like word order.
Verify each variant still answers who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me within 5 seconds before spending test budget on it.
Keep a running list of winning headline framings, because they transfer to ad copy, email subject lines and product descriptions.
Only after the headline has been optimized, move test slots to the hero image and then to lower-page elements.
caveats: The 60–80% lift figures come from the source's agency experience and vary with the original headline's weakness.
Low-traffic stores may need to run headline changes sequentially with over-time measurement rather than true split tests.
cards.source_name: Alex Hormozi's Advice on Landing Pages.docx

cards.title: Use product-quiz answers for recommendations and customer research
cards.summary: When building a store quiz that must select products and reveal buyer preferences.
cards.use_when: When building a store quiz that must select products and reveal buyer preferences.
steps: Define which SKU, size, format or bundle each question can change before adding the question.
Ask about intended use, current routine, preferences, compatibility and previous product frustrations. Skip demographic or health questions that do not affect a valid product choice.
Map answers to real recommendation rules and export answer distributions by traffic source.
Compare frequent needs with the assumed avatar; use the language in new ad hooks and identify gaps in the assortment.
caveats: Respondents represent the traffic sent to the quiz, not the entire market.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Place useful explanation screens between product-quiz questions
cards.summary: When shoppers abandon a quiz or cannot understand why a preference matters.
cards.use_when: When shoppers abandon a quiz or cannot understand why a preference matters.
steps: Test an explanation after roughly three to five questions, the source heuristic.
Branch the explanation on actual answers: explain why a selected use case needs a particular material, fit or format.
Use genuine customer evidence only; a percentage comparison needs an actual measured population.
Measure step abandonment and downstream purchases, not completion alone.
caveats: Three to five questions is a source heuristic, not an optimum.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Choose quiz input controls that fit product decisions
cards.summary: When a product quiz repeats many identical button screens.
cards.use_when: When a product quiz repeats many identical button screens.
steps: Use single choice for mutually exclusive formats, multi-select for preferences, and numeric input for a relevant size or consumption amount.
Avoid adding questions merely to lengthen the quiz. Each field must improve selection or useful research.
Keep keyboard and mobile interaction usable; map every control to a stable exported field.
Test a preference slider only if it is easier than buttons for this choice.
caveats: The source had not tested its proposed slider interaction.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Reflect product preferences in later quiz copy
cards.summary: When a recommendation quiz feels generic despite collecting useful answers.
cards.use_when: When a recommendation quiz feels generic despite collecting useful answers.
steps: Branch later copy on selected use, format and prior frustrations.
Show how a recommended product solves the named practical constraint; never claim every shopper needs the same SKU while implying individualized matching.
Limit branches to combinations the team can test and maintain.
Test incompatible and contradictory answer combinations before launch.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Reveal the product-match explanation before the buy box
cards.summary: When shoppers need to understand why a quiz recommends a particular SKU or bundle.
cards.use_when: When shoppers need to understand why a quiz recommends a particular SKU or bundle.
steps: Summarize the actual answers that determine the recommendation.
Show the matching SKU, size or bundle and explain the rule connecting it to those answers.
If calculating replenishment, show the consumption assumption and let the shopper correct it.
Follow with product details, price, relevant genuine reviews, delivery and returns, then a purchase CTA.
caveats: Do not simulate computation or invent medical outcomes, future-body projections or guaranteed result dates.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Use an occasion date to check product delivery suitability
cards.summary: When recommending products for gifts, travel, events or a move.
cards.use_when: When recommending products for gifts, travel, events or a move.
steps: Ask the occasion and needed-by date only if timing changes the recommendation.
Compare that date with actual stock, handling and delivery estimates.
Show suitable products and explain any delivery uncertainty before checkout.
Use genuine order deadlines where applicable; do not add resetting scarcity timers.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Use routine and consumption to recommend a starter configuration
cards.summary: When a store must choose a product format, starter kit or replenishment interval.
cards.use_when: When a store must choose a product format, starter kit or replenishment interval.
steps: Ask what the shopper already uses, how often, what failed previously and what routine is realistic.
Map those answers to a starter configuration or replenishment interval.
Respect exclusions and explicit dislikes in both the main recommendation and cross-sells.
Let the shopper adjust the suggested quantity or subscription before purchase.
caveats: Self-reported usage is an estimate.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Keep the quiz result page focused on a transparent product offer
cards.summary: When quiz completion is strong but product purchases are weak.
cards.use_when: When quiz completion is strong but product purchases are weak.
steps: Make the answer summary, recommended product and offered price consistent.
Remove unrelated outbound distractions while preserving access to delivery, returns, product details and support.
If offering to email results, explain what will be sent and capture marketing preferences separately.
Compare the full quiz-to-purchase journey with direct-to-PDP traffic; test one major change at a time.
caveats: The source uses a subscription-app example. Long quizzes and commitment steps are hypotheses, not guaranteed retail improvements.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Best 2026 Ecommerce Quiz Funnel Structure.docx

cards.title: Targeted social proof matched to buying objections
cards.summary: Collect the top buying objections through surveys and user tests, then hand-pick testimonials that neutralize each objection and place them at the point of action.
cards.use_when: Placing reviews and testimonials on a PDP or landing page, or when generic featured-in logos and star ratings aren't moving add-to-cart rates.
steps: Survey buyers and near-buyers with two questions: 'What stopped you from almost buying today?' and 'What motivated you to buy today?' Mine support tickets and chat logs for the same objections.
Rank the objections and pick a small number of testimonials (the source suggests three to four) that each speak directly to one of them, rather than displaying every review you have.
If you have only around 30 reviews, the source argues against displaying them as filler and prefers a hand-picked, objection-matched set.
Place the matching testimonial adjacent to the Add to Cart button, near bundle selectors, and above the fold where most visitors never scroll past.

Example pattern from the source's gas-mask brand: objections were 'will it protect me from chemicals' and 'will the mask fog up', so the chosen review explicitly covered eye and lung protection and fog-free visibility and sat beside the bundles and CTA.
caveats: Placement and review selection are described from the agency's client work, not proven universal rules; validate with your own test.
Featuring too few reviews can itself create doubt on high-consideration products, so match the volume to your category norms.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Let product imagery carry the value proposition
cards.summary: Because visitors skim text and process images far faster, build each PDP or landing page image set so the images alone communicate emotional, social and functional benefits.
cards.use_when: Replacing or briefing product photography, lifestyle imagery, and image galleries on a product page or landing page.
steps: Assume most visitors will not read body copy; the source's session-recording work shows users skimming text blocks and engaging with images. Treat the image set as the primary sales asset.

Build each image to carry one benefit: happy people using the product (emotional and social), the product in real use cases, ease of use, portability, group/social settings, and before-and-after transformation where honest.
Pair each image with short benefit text or icons so copy and image reinforce each other rather than repeating specs.
Write alt-text and captions to compress the benefit into a skimmable line for the visitors who do read.
Benchmark: check session recordings (the source uses Microsoft Clarity) to confirm where users stop reading and where image engagement spikes, then reorder or replace images accordingly.
caveats: The '60,000 times faster than text' figure is cited by the source as a common claim; treat it as directional rather than a measured outcome.
Before-and-after imagery must remain truthful for the category and region; many jurisdictions regulate health and beauty claims.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Above-the-fold formula: value prop, visual, CTA, social proof
cards.summary: The above-the-fold area is the only section guaranteed to be seen, so it must answer 'what's in it for me', reinforce with a visual, show one obvious CTA, and stack trust immediately.
cards.use_when: Redesigning the top of a homepage, PDP or paid landing page, or auditing a page where the hero is vague or has competing buttons.
steps: State who you are, what you do, and the tangible benefit to the visitor in five seconds or less, leading with the 'what's in it for me' (the source's example rewrote 'gas mask respirator and fire safety' to 'protection you can rely on to stay safe').
Add supporting body text that spells out selling points (seals to any face size, filters out toxins, fog-free visibility, comfortable) to reinforce the headline claim.
Use a single supporting visual that sells in three dimensions: emotional buy-in, social perception, and functional benefit; the source argues emotional buy-in matters most.
Provide exactly one obvious call-to-action button, benefit-oriented rather than 'shop now' or 'buy now', and color-contrast it so it stands out when the rest of the page is blurred.
Stack social proof in the hero (the source cites '400,000+ customers protected') so trust is established before the visitor scrolls.
caveats: The blur test and five-second rule are practical heuristics from the source's audits, not measured thresholds.
A single CTA suits one-goal landing pages; category pages with multiple intents may need more than one path.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Establish visual hierarchy with size and color contrast
cards.summary: Guide the eye down the page by making the headline 3-4x the body text, grouping content in sections, and reserving strong color contrast for the CTA.
cards.use_when: Fixing a page that looks chaotic, has a headline the same size as body copy, or where it is unclear what action to take.
steps: Set size contrast deliberately: the source suggests a desktop headline roughly 48-57 pixels against roughly 16-pixel body text, i.e. three to four times larger.
Remove all-caps, uniform bolding and excessive color, which the source identifies as the main causes of overwhelming pages.
Segment content into clear blocks so the eye flows top-to-bottom like a subway map, rather than scanning a wall of competing elements.
Use color to separate levels: distinct colors for headline, body and CTA. The cited example used a pink CTA and announcement bar and muted brown/gray text.
Check mobile separately: in the source's before example the logo and announcement bar dominated, so scale them down and let the headline and CTA lead.
Decide which one or two elements deserve priority (usually the CTA and announcement bar) and contrast them against everything else.
caveats: Pixel values are the source's suggested range for desktop; adjust for your typeface, device mix, and brand system.
Visual-hierarchy work is best A/B tested rather than assumed to lift conversion.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Smart pop-up timing instead of early interruption
cards.summary: Trigger pop-ups on behavior rather than on page load; exit intent, post-add-to-cart and scroll-depth triggers reach people who are already engaged.
cards.use_when: Deciding when an email-capture or discount pop-up should fire on a landing page, PDP or category page.
steps: Stop firing pop-ups in the first three to five seconds; the source argues visitors who don't yet understand the brand get friction and leave.
Use exit-intent for first-time visitors: fire when the cursor moves toward the close button, offer a discount or newsletter incentive, and capture the address for retargeting.
Use post-add-to-cart triggers to close hesitant buyers: fire an offer the moment an item is added but checkout hasn't started, when price doubt is most likely.

Use scroll-depth triggers at the point of drop-off: identify on heatmaps or session recordings where users lose interest (the source's example is 50% through a product description), then serve a help or discount offer there.
Accept fewer impressions: the source reports timing changes produced conversion increases up to 125% in their tests, because the pop-up reaches people ready to act.
caveats: The 125% figure comes from the source's agency tests; treat it as their result, not a forecast for your store.
Aggressive discount pop-ups can train customers to wait for a code and erode margin; segment first-time visitors from returning buyers.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Reduce choice to raise conversion and AOV
cards.summary: Cull navigation items and bundle options so fewer decisions are required; the source found fewer bundles increased both conversion rate and average order value.
cards.use_when: Simplifying a cluttered navigation, a product page with too many variants or pack sizes, or a bundle selector with five or more tiers.
steps: Cap primary navigation items below seven; the source reports diminishing returns above that and says fewer is better.
Use heatmaps to find navigation and on-page elements getting negligible clicks, then remove them. In the source's audit example, side elements received 0.21%, 0%, 0.08% and 0.92% of clicks.
Audit bundle counts: in their Wildman Drinking test, dropping from five options (1, 2, 3, 5, 10 packs) to three (1, 3, 5) produced a 53% lift in conversion rate and a 13.5% increase in AOV.
Diagnose before cutting: session recordings showed users picking the cheapest options or leaving entirely, which supported the too-many-options hypothesis.
Treat removal of clutter as a test: the cited Swatch-like audit combined removals with other changes and reported a 60% increase in monthly online orders, so isolate variables where you can.
caveats: These lifts come from the source's client tests and combine multiple page changes; attribute carefully.
Fewer options can hurt if your buyers genuinely need variety (sizes, flavors); check search and support data before cutting SKUs from the selector.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Structure bundles and use price anchoring to lift AOV
cards.summary: Bundle complementary products at a bulk discount, keep the original 'compare at' price visible as an anchor, and spell out dollar savings in the bundle headline.
cards.use_when: Designing bundle offers, subscription tiers, or add-on rows on a PDP to raise average order value.
steps: Bundle related items rather than selling a single SKU alone (the source's example bundles a two-step hair growth kit and shows the combined saving), and add complementary add-ons such as warranty or accessories to raise the order value.

Show a compare-at price next to the bundle price so the discount is visible; in the source's test they kept selling prices the same and raised the original compare-at prices, which increased perceived value without changing what customers paid.

Move savings out of body text and into the headline: the source tested '3 packs save $10 / 5 packs save $20' in the headline versus percentage savings in the small print and saw a 25% conversion increase and 28.57% revenue-per-user increase.
Make the math effortless: state dollar savings explicitly rather than asking shoppers to compute percentages themselves.
Review margin before discounting: raising a compare-at price must stay compliant with advertising and pricing rules in your market.
caveats: The 25% and 28.57% figures are single-test results from the source and are not benchmarks.
Inflating an 'original' price that was never charged can be illegal or platform-policy-violating; anchor against genuinely previous pricing.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Middle option bias to steer buyers to the target tier
cards.summary: Shape the savings ladder so the middle bundle looks like the safest, best-value choice, which moves buyers off the cheapest tier without pushing them to overcommit.
cards.use_when: Setting the tier structure and savings copy for a three-tier bundle or subscription offer.
steps: Start from your three most sensible tiers (the source's example used 1-pack, 3-pack, 5-pack) and check which tier people actually buy and why, using session recordings and order data.

Design the savings so the middle tier's incremental gain matches the top tier's incremental gain. In the source's test the 3-pack and the 5-pack each saved $20 over the previous tier, which made the 3-pack feel like a steal without requiring the larger commitment.
Keep the tiers honest: the source's audience bought the 3-pack for sharing with friends, so the middle tier matched real usage, not an arbitrary nudge.
Test the savings framing with an A/B test rather than assuming it lands; the cited version reported an 11.74% conversion increase and roughly 5% increases in AOV and revenue per visitor.
caveats: These are the source's test results in one store; the effect depends on price points, usage frequency and category.
Making the middle tier too attractive can cannibalize a higher-margin top tier, so check contribution margin per order, not just conversion.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Systematically reduce fear, uncertainty and doubt at action points
cards.summary: Place guarantees, security badges, shipping clarity and transparent pricing directly beneath critical actions such as the Add to Cart button.
cards.use_when: Auditing the cart, checkout and PDP action areas for reasons shoppers hesitate or abandon.
steps: Walk your funnel and ask what you would want to know before buying this product; list every unanswered question as a FUD to close.
Add a money-back guarantee and make the return policy explicit near the buy action so the risk of a bad purchase feels reversible.
Add security and payment badges to signal data safety, especially at payment entry.
State shipping timelines, costs and delivery expectations clearly rather than in fine print.
Show pricing upfront and remove hidden costs or surprises added later in checkout; the source cites surprise fees as a driver of drop-off.
Place all of these at the critical points of action: Add to Cart, above the fold, and checkout steps where hesitation peaks.
caveats: Badges and guarantees are trust signals, not proof of performance; none of these were given a measured conversion figure by the source.
A guarantee's terms must match what you can actually honor at your fulfilment and return volumes.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Humanize the brand to build know-like-trust
cards.summary: People buy from brands they know, like and trust, so add team stories, behind-the-scenes content and customer success videos, and write in a conversational voice.
cards.use_when: Building the About page, brand story modules on the homepage or PDP, and voice-and-tone guidance for product copy.
steps: Add team photos and founder stories that explain who is behind the brand, its mission and its origin.
Publish behind-the-scenes content showing how the brand started and how products are made, so buyers feel part of the journey.
Record customer success videos where real users explain why they like the product and how it fits their daily life; the source treats these as authenticity builders.
Write copy conversationally, as if speaking to a friend, rather than in corporate voice.
Accept that this is hard to measure directly; the source frames it as a longer-term trust investment rather than a testable CRO lever.
caveats: The source explicitly notes this tactic is much harder to track than an email pop-up trigger.
Humanizing content adds page weight and scroll depth; place it where it does not bury the buy path.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Make product content scannable with bullets, icons and subheadings
cards.summary: Since most visitors scan rather than read, convert dense description blocks into bullets, icons, subheadings and bolded highlights.
cards.use_when: Rewriting product descriptions, ingredient or spec sections, FAQ blocks and landing page body copy.
steps: Break large text blocks into bullet points and pair each with an icon where possible; the source says they have A/B tested this repeatedly with conversion increases.
Split long copy into clear subheadings and categories so a scanner can get a high-level overview and jump to what they need.
Bold or highlight the specific phrases you want remembered rather than bolding everything.
Keep each bullet to one benefit or specification (the source's example: protection, fog-free visibility, comfort) so it reads at a glance.
Reserve long-form narrative copy for pages where visitors are genuinely reading a full sales letter; elsewhere assume scanning.
caveats: The conversion gains are described qualitatively by the source without published figures.
Icons of unclear meaning can add confusion; label them with short text.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Run CRO tests with PXL prioritization and two-week minimums
cards.summary: Landing pages are never finished, so prioritize hypotheses by impact versus effort and run single-variable tests long enough to reach significance.
cards.use_when: Setting up an A/B testing roadmap for a store or deciding which page experiment to run next.
steps: Prioritize with the source's PXL framework: rank hypotheses so the highest-impact, lowest-effort tests run first.
Test one element at a time so you know which change drove the result; bundling many changes hides the cause of gains or losses.
Run each test for at least two weeks so it covers a full cycle, and confirm the result is statistically significant before acting.
Document every test, including losers, and record what you believe made it win or lose; the source says losing tests generated insights that seeded later wins.
Keep testing even when you are already above average: the source notes clients converting at 5-6% still test to squeeze more, and cites Amazon running over 12,000 experiments a year.
caveats: The two-week minimum is the source's rule of thumb; required duration depends on traffic volume and baseline conversion rate.
PXL is the source agency's own framework and is not a published standard.
cards.source_name: Brutally Honest Landing Page Advice from Alex Hormozi.docx

cards.title: Landing page composition for conversion
cards.summary: Strip navigation, footers and links from campaign landing pages and lead with benefit-driven copy to reduce exit paths and raise lead conversion.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a dedicated landing page for a paid campaign, email push or launch, where the goal is a single action rather than site browsing.
steps: Remove the site navigation bar and footer from the landing page. The page has one job; nav links only create exits. Keep only the elements that push toward the form or buy button.
Lead with benefit-driven copy, not feature lists. State the outcome the buyer gets, then support it with features further down.
Keep a visible primary CTA and make the page's single next step unambiguous — one offer, one action.
Strip other content that competes for attention: related posts, upsells, sidebars, social feeds.
After stripping, check that trust elements (proof, testimonials, guarantees) are still present so the colder, single-offer page doesn't lose credibility.
Once the page is live, split-test the stripped version against your standard site template to confirm lift with your own traffic rather than assuming.
caveats: The conversion numbers cited in this source (e.g. a 20% conversion rate, 10x average) are the presenter's own campaign results, not benchmarks you should expect.
Removing navigation can hurt pages whose job is exploration or SEO entry, not direct response.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Page load speed threshold: target under 2 seconds
cards.summary: The source advises keeping landing pages under 2 seconds load time, claiming conversion drops roughly 50% per additional second.
cards.use_when: Setting performance budgets for a landing page or diagnosing why a page converts poorly despite good copy and offer.
steps: Set a performance target of under 2 seconds for time to load on the landing page, and treat anything slower as a conversion problem to fix before writing more copy.
Audit the page with a speed tool and list the biggest offenders first: uncompressed images, unminified scripts, unnecessary third-party tags and fonts, render-blocking CSS.
Compress and properly size images, defer non-critical scripts, and remove tags you are not actively using for measurement or personalization.
Test on a throttled mobile connection, not just desktop on fast wifi — mobile visitors on slow networks are where the drop-off compounds.
Estimate the payoff before investing: if the source's rule of thumb holds, cutting load time from 4 seconds to 2 seconds is a large conversion gain, but validate with your own before/after data.
caveats: The '50% drop per added second' figure is the presenter's stated heuristic; treat it as directional, not a measured constant for your store.
Speed work competes with tracking and personalization scripts — you may need to trade off some tags.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: 45-second founder video on the landing page
cards.summary: Embedding a short founder video (around 45 seconds) is credited by the source with a 33% conversion increase on the page.
cards.use_when: Adding trust and human context to a landing page for a new brand, launch, or offer where visitors don't yet know who is behind the product.
steps: Record a roughly 45-second founder video: who you are, what problem the product solves, why you built it, and what the visitor should do next. Keep it tight — long videos rarely get watched on landing pages.
Place it high enough on the page that visitors see it before the form, but below the main headline and benefit copy so it supports rather than delays the offer.
Add a still thumbnail and avoid autoplay-with-sound; unexpected audio drives people off the page.
Keep the video file small and host it in a way that does not block the under-2-second load target — a heavy embed can erase the gain.
Pair it with a written summary for visitors who won't watch video.
A/B test the page with and without the video to measure the lift on your own traffic before making it permanent. The source's 33% figure is from one case, not a promised outcome.
caveats: Results are from the presenter's own campaign; your lift will depend on audience and product.
Video should not be used as a substitute for clear copy — visitors who don't watch still need the offer explained in text.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Video testimonials as landing page proof
cards.summary: Use embedded video testimonials on the landing page as social proof that reduces skepticism before the CTA.
cards.use_when: Placing proof elements on a landing page, product page or offer page where cold traffic needs reassurance before submitting a form or buying.
steps: Collect short testimonial videos from real customers — each one ideally naming the problem, the result, and something specific they got.
Place testimonials after the offer explanation and before or beside the primary CTA, where hesitation peaks.
Keep them short and skimmable in thumbnail form; let the visitor choose to play rather than autoplaying a wall of video.
Use specific, measurable customer statements where possible. Vague praise ('great product') does less work than 'cut my processing time in half'.
If you lack video, written testimonials in the same positions still serve the proof function.
Test proof placement and format against your current page rather than assuming video always wins — quality matters more than the format.
caveats: Source presents this as part of its own high-converting build; no independent benchmark is given.
Fabricated or unverifiable testimonials create compliance and trust risk; use real customers.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Track product-quiz or signup completion separately from purchases
cards.summary: Measure supporting store form completions without counting them as sales.
cards.use_when: When a campaign landing page collects quiz results or email signups.
steps: Fire a named form-completion event only after a successful submission.
Use a confirmation page or explicit success event and deduplicate repeat loads.
Track downstream purchase events separately and compare revenue by landing-page variant.
caveats: Form completion is a supporting outcome, not purchase conversion.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: A/B test landing page variants with PostHog traffic splitting
cards.summary: Split traffic across multiple landing page variants in PostHog and let the statistical winner emerge rather than guessing.
cards.use_when: Once a landing page is live and has enough traffic, deciding between competing headlines, layouts, offers or proof placements.
steps: Define one hypothesis per test — e.g. 'version B's benefit-led headline will beat version A's feature-led headline on form submissions'.
Build a genuinely different variant, not a color change, unless you are specifically testing color.
Split traffic between variants in PostHog so each visitor is bucketed consistently and sees the same version on return visits.
Let the test run to a pre-decided sample size or significance threshold before declaring a winner; stopping early on a lucky run produces false winners.
Check that your conversion event (e.g. Thank You page view) is firing correctly for both variants before trusting results.
Record what you learned and feed the winning element into the next test. Tests compound; one-offs don't.
caveats: Small stores with low traffic may take too long to reach significance — use qualitative methods like session recordings instead, or accept that you can't reliably A/B test every element.
Verify the current PostHog experiment interface before setting up, since it changes.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Use heatmaps and session recordings to find friction
cards.summary: Review heatmaps and session recordings to find where visitors hesitate, drop off or fail to interact before you change the page.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a landing page, PDP, cart or checkout that underperforms and you don't yet know why.
steps: Watch a batch of session recordings, prioritizing sessions from visitors who bounced without converting but showed intent (scrolled far, clicked CTA area).
Check heatmaps for the CTA and form: if clicks cluster around but not on the button, the button may look unclickable or be too small.
Look for scroll depth patterns — if most visitors never reach your testimonial or final CTA, move the important elements up.
Watch recordings on mobile specifically; rage-taps, zooming and horizontal scroll all point to responsiveness problems.
Write down each friction point as a specific hypothesis before changing anything, then decide which fix you'll test first.
Re-check recordings after the change to confirm the friction is gone rather than assuming the fix worked.
caveats: Recordings are qualitative; a few noisy sessions shouldn't drive a redesign — look for recurring patterns.
Some analytics tools require consent handling that can limit recording coverage.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Measure purchases separately from landing-page signups
cards.summary: Define purchase conversion as purchasing sessions divided by eligible sessions; track form completion separately.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Define purchase conversion as purchasing sessions divided by eligible sessions; track form completion separately.
Compare revenue and contribution margin per visitor by acquisition channel and page variant.
Validate event counts before judging the page. The source 20% figure concerns lead capture and is not a retail benchmark.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Judge design as binary trust, not beauty
cards.summary: Website aesthetics only need to clear a trust threshold; ugly pages still convert if the offer and proof are strong.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget and time to spend on visual design versus copy, proof and offer for a store or lead landing page.
steps: Assess the page against one question: does a first-time visitor trust this enough to keep reading, or does it look like a scam?
Note the source's claim that first impressions form in roughly 50 milliseconds — this is his stated figure, not a verified study you should quote as fact.
If the page clears the trust bar, redirect design time to copy, social proof, offer and speed instead of pixel-polish.
Use free design references (the presenter uses dribbble.com) to lift the baseline look when you lack a designer, then move on.
Apply the same test to product pages: a clean, credible PDP with strong photos and proof will usually beat a heavily designed page with weak proof or unclear offer.
caveats: The presenter still says good design increases conversion rate — it is simply not the primary lever. Do not use this as an excuse for a broken or dated-looking page.
Trust thresholds vary by category; a fashion store's aesthetic expectations differ from a B2B lead page.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Write less: control the 10% visitors actually read
cards.summary: Cut landing page copy so the headline and a few supporting lines carry the message; hide the rest for SEO.
cards.use_when: Editing a landing page or product page whose copy feels like a wall of text and where visitors bounce before reaching the CTA.
steps: Assume visitors read roughly 10% of your copy; the presenter's stated behavior is that people see the headline, subheadline, 2–3 bullets and maybe one more line.
Because you cannot control which 10% they read if everything is visible, deliberately choose what stays above the fold and in the main flow.
Strip any sentence that does not either establish credibility, state the outcome, or move the reader toward the form/CTA.

For pages you want to rank in Google, keep long-form text for SEO but place it inside accordions/dropdowns so the page stays visually short for readers while the words remain indexed. The presenter cites 1500+ words as a common SEO landing page target — treat as a heuristic, not a rule.
Rewrite remaining copy around benefits (time saved, money earned, pain avoided, peace of mind, status, freedom) rather than features or tech stack.
caveats: The 10% read figure and the 1500-word SEO target are presented as the speaker's working heuristics; verify with your own scroll and engagement data.
Concise copy still needs specificity — cutting words is not a license to drop the actual offer or proof.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Sell outcomes, let buyers rationalize with features
cards.summary: Lead with emotional benefits and keep features as supporting proof that buyers use to justify the decision afterward.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer block, hero copy or ad-to-page message for a store or service landing page.
steps: Identify the emotional benefit the buyer is really purchasing: saved time, more revenue, pain avoidance, peace of mind, status or freedom. The presenter uses a Ferrari as the analogy — nobody pays for leather seats, they pay for status and then justify it with build quality.
State the benefit in the headline or offer block, then use features (tools, process, materials, stack) further down as the rationalization layer.
Translate credibility assets into benefit language: 'top 1% of DJs out of 5,000' reads as peace of mind that the wedding won't be ruined, not a staffing stat.
Avoid leading with the tech or method you are proud of; the presenter notes builders love talking about their stack, but buyers don't care about it.
Test the same offer expressed as different benefit angles — the presenter says rotate and test promises rather than assuming one framing is right.
caveats: This is standard sales psychology asserted by the presenter, not an experiment he ran on benefit-vs-feature copy specifically.
Highly technical or regulated categories may require more feature detail up front for credibility.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Reduce distractions on dedicated product campaign pages
cards.summary: Prioritize one product purchase path on the campaign page.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Prioritize one product purchase path on the campaign page.
Remove unrelated promotional links, while retaining delivery, returns, support and required policy access.
Test navigation changes on dedicated campaign traffic; do not remove ordinary store navigation by default.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Place CTAs throughout the page and pin one on mobile
cards.summary: Distribute CTAs so the visitor can act the moment they're ready, and use a persistent bottom bar on mobile.
cards.use_when: Laying out CTAs on a landing page you're building or reviewing, especially after checking mobile rendering.
steps: Sprinkle CTAs down the page rather than relying on one button at the end, so a visitor who has read enough can act immediately.
Keep the desktop and mobile treatments different — the presenter explicitly calls this two devices, two rules.
On mobile, use a single CTA pinned to the bottom of the viewport so it stays visible while scrolling, and have it jump straight to the form.
Check the mobile version with browser developer tools: three dots → More tools → Developer tools → responsive/device mode, then switch between iPhone, tablet and desktop widths.
Have every CTA land on the form or call action — not on a section, accordion or secondary page.
caveats: The source gives no CTA density number; add as many as read naturally without breaking the page's flow.
Too many competing CTA labels can dilute the primary action — keep one action with consistent wording.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Use a short founder video to explain product credibility
cards.summary: Test a roughly 45-second founder introduction describing why the product exists and what the founder can substantiate.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Test a roughly 45-second founder introduction describing why the product exists and what the founder can substantiate.
Show genuine product evidence, explain who the product suits and end with the purchase action.
Measure purchase outcomes and page speed against a version without the video; the source service-lead result does not predict store lift.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Show examples of visually differentiated products
cards.summary: Show real examples of the relevant furniture, decor or custom product variant.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Show real examples of the relevant furniture, decor or custom product variant.
Match examples to the ad promise and shopper use case, with scale, materials and available variations clear.
Place examples near the product decision rather than burying them in a general gallery.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Turn FAQ into an objection-handling block
cards.summary: Use FAQs to answer whatever is actually stopping people from converting, sourced from real sales conversations.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting the FAQ section on a landing page or PDP, or when form submissions are low despite good traffic.
steps: Ask yourself what stops a visitor from filling out the form or buying: price, business model, unclear process, timing, guarantees.
Harvest objections directly from calls with prospects — the presenter says to explicitly ask whether anything felt ambiguous, and they will tell you.

Write the FAQ answers to dissolve those specific objections, not to fill space. The presenter calls the default 'I don't know what to put so I'll add text' approach useless for conversion (only useful if you're padding for SEO).
Update the FAQ as new objections repeat in sales calls, so each new batch of visitors gets the answers the last batch needed.
Keep FAQs discoverable but collapsed, consistent with the general 'less visible text' principle.
caveats: The source gives no measurable lift for FAQ changes; it's presented as a probable conversion contributor.
If FAQ text exists purely for SEO, keep it — that's the one exception the presenter allows.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Make the phone number a click-to-call on mobile
cards.summary: A tappable phone number captures high-intent visitors who want an answer now, not a form response later.
cards.use_when: Adding contact options to a mobile landing page where some visitors are in immediate-need mode rather than research mode.
steps: Place a clickable call action on the page — not just a displayed number — so a mobile visitor can be on the phone within seconds.

Apply the presenter's reasoning about intent: callers are in 'get it done now' mode, not planning mode, so a call may convert at a higher rate than a form. He states he is unsure of the exact comparative stat and is reasoning from psychology, and cites a Google-sourced claim he doesn't fully trust.
For attribution, buy distinct phone numbers per page or campaign so you can tell which page generated the call.
Use a VoIP number (the presenter mentions Twilio, or numbers bought through your CRM) so work calls are separated from personal and are callable from computer or app.
Route the call to a live human quickly — the source's speed-to-lead section targets connecting within about 10 seconds.
caveats: The presenter explicitly flags the 'phone converts higher' claim as his own speculation, not a stat he verified; test it in your own business.
Per-page phone numbers add cost and management overhead; weigh against the value of attribution.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Video testimonials: 30-second self-shot clips as primary proof
cards.summary: Ask clients to record short phone-video testimonials; the presenter credits nine of them with cutting cost per conversion from $200 to $30.
cards.use_when: Building the social proof section for a store or service page when written testimonials alone feel unconvincing.
steps: Reach out to real clients and ask for a genuine 30-second testimonial recorded on a phone — explicitly low production, no studio.
Aim for a set of several testimonials; the presenter used nine on his photo/video business.
Expect and accept that many visitors won't watch them — the presenter's argument is that the mere presence of video proof raises peace of mind.

Prioritize video over written testimonials. The presenter says he personally distrusts written testimonials, suspects AI-generated ones and stock photos, and treats video as the credibility anchor; written ones are better than nothing if video isn't available.
If using written reviews as a fallback, pair them with external review sources so they're not fully self-published.
caveats: The $200→$30 cost-per-conversion result is the presenter's own reported campaign result from a separate Google Ads account; it is an anecdote, not a promised outcome.
Filming testimonials requires client cooperation and time; expect it to take real effort, which the presenter acknowledges.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Present documented product-use outcomes
cards.summary: Use an authentic customer or product test with a measured before-and-after result where the category supports it.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Use an authentic customer or product test with a measured before-and-after result where the category supports it.
Explain the usage period, conditions and limitations.
Do not reuse agency revenue results as product proof or imply every buyer gets the same result.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Borrow authority with brand logos, review badges and trust stats
cards.summary: External credibility markers — logos, third-party review badges, and countable trust stats — raise trust with modest effort.
cards.use_when: Filling out the trust row of a landing page or PDP where the buyer has no prior relationship with the brand.
steps: Add logos of companies you've genuinely worked with (the presenter lists TD, Microsoft, McLaren and Samsung) to borrow their authority.
Add external review badges (e.g. Trustpilot) because the review process is outside your control, which increases perceived credibility.

Note the presenter's observation that a perfect 5.0 rating can read as suspicious — either no reviews or filtered — and that 4.7–4.9 often looks more believable. This is his opinion, not a tested finding.
Add 'trust stats' — years in business, number of events/projects completed, revenue generated, number of reviews — as concrete counters.
Place these markers where they'll be seen early, not only in the footer.
caveats: Only display logos and stats you can substantiate; the presenter's list is his own client history, not a generic example.
Trustpilot or equivalent badges require maintaining that profile — don't show a badge you can't back.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Make the product offer concrete and supportable
cards.summary: Name the product, intended benefit, contents and price.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Name the product, intended benefit, contents and price.
Use a quantified or time-bound benefit only where supported by product evidence.
Explain the actual guarantee and returns terms; test benefit framing without inventing guaranteed outcomes.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Mobile-first audit with browser device mode
cards.summary: Check every landing page at phone and tablet widths before launching, since the presenter claims most traffic is mobile.
cards.use_when: Running a pre-launch QA pass on a landing page or PDP layout.
steps: Open the page in a browser and enter developer tools: three dots → More tools → Developer tools → responsive/device toolbar.
Switch between iPhone, tablet and desktop presets, and also drag the responsive handle slowly to catch awkward breakpoints between standard sizes.
Check specifically that the sticky mobile CTA is visible and functional throughout the scroll, that the form is usable one-handed, and that content doesn't overflow.
The presenter cites device splits of roughly 64% mobile, 3% tablets and 33% desktop; treat these as his figures, not universal, and confirm your own analytics.
If a breakpoint looks broken, iterate on the layout until phone, tablet and desktop all render acceptably.
caveats: Device split percentages vary by industry; check your own analytics rather than adopting 64/3/33.
Browser developer tools interfaces change; the exact menu path may differ.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Fix page load speed with Lighthouse, not guesswork
cards.summary: Pull the Lighthouse report and hand it to an AI agent to fix the flagged performance issues, iterating until the score is high.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a slow landing page or PDP that may be losing conversions to load time.
steps: Run Lighthouse inside browser dev tools (three dots → More tools → Developer tools → Lighthouse) to get performance, SEO, accessibility and best-practices scores.

The presenter cites a study claiming 1-second loads convert around 3.05% and that every extra second roughly halves conversion — treat as a cited study, not your own data, but it justifies treating speed as a priority.
Identify the common culprits he names: images, videos and large graphics.
Copy the Lighthouse diagnostics and paste them into your AI coding agent with a prompt like 'here's the Lighthouse report, optimize for page load speed and for desktop, tablet and mobile'.
Re-run Lighthouse after changes (the presenter's example went from 90% to 95%) and repeat the copy-paste-fix loop until the score reaches the level you want.
caveats: The conversion-vs-load-time figures are cited from an unspecified online study; do not treat 3.05% or the halving per second as a guaranteed rule for your store.
Lighthouse scores measure technical performance and don't capture real user experience on slow networks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Build a reusable landing page skill to multiply pages
cards.summary: Package your page structure into a repeatable generator that produces city×service landing pages on demand.
cards.use_when: Scaling from one winning landing page to many local or service-variant pages for SEO or ads.
steps: Use the 'zipper' approach: one side is the city or region (e.g. Toronto, Vancouver, Manhattan, the Bronx), the other is the service (tree trimming, landscaping, snow removal).

Create a page for each meaningful city×service combination so the search result matches the query exactly — the presenter argues that searchers for 'tree trimming in Toronto' won't click a page about tree removal.
Make the headline and body specific to the same term the visitor searched, so ad or SERP → page → follow-up message → sales call are all aligned to the same keyword.
Encode the winning structure into a skill/workflow (the presenter uses a Claude Code skill named something like '/landing-page-generator') that takes service, city and traffic source as inputs.
Ramp publishing gradually — the presenter warns against generating hundreds or thousands of pages at once because Google may penalize it; start slow and increase over time.
Keep a homepage as the root, with landing pages branching off for each combination.
caveats: The presenter explicitly warns that mass-generating pages can get you penalized; his guidance is to ramp gradually with no specified safe rate.
The tool invoked here (Claude Code inside Anti-Gravity) is subject to interface changes — verify current setup before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Improve product landing pages through measured iteration
cards.summary: Start with a clear hypothesis about product understanding, offer or purchase friction.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: Start with a clear hypothesis about product understanding, offer or purchase friction.
Randomize comparable traffic between variants and measure purchases and revenue per visitor.
Plan adequate sample size and stopping criteria before testing; use findings for the next variant.
