The source tested many lead pages; neither its test count nor its 20% form rate is a store target.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Verify successful form events without treating them as orders
cards.summary: For a product quiz or email signup, record confirmed completion through a success event or confirmation page.
cards.use_when: When building or evaluating an ecommerce product campaign landing page.
steps: For a product quiz or email signup, record confirmed completion through a success event or confirmation page.
Deduplicate reloads and validate with test submissions.
Track purchases separately through order confirmation and a stable order identifier.
caveats: Merchant adaptation of the source principle; source service-funnel results are not store benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Use heatmaps and session recordings to find friction
cards.summary: Watch real visitors and see where they click to locate friction points, then fix the page based on what you observe.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a page with traffic but weak conversion, when you need qualitative clues before running new variants.
steps: Install a heatmap and session-recording tool — the presenter names PostHog, Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity as options, and notes they're free-tier friendly.
Watch a sample of recordings of actual visitors scrolling and clicking on your landing page or PDP.
Use heatmaps to see which areas attract attention and which CTAs get ignored; combine with the headline/10%-read rule to decide what to cut.
Look specifically for dead clicks, rage clicks and drop-off points near the form or CTA.
Turn findings into new variants to test rather than making a single untested change.
caveats: No method is given for how many recordings to sample before drawing a conclusion.
Heatmaps show attention and clicks, not why a visitor acted — pair with direct customer questions before making big changes.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Set Up Conversion Tracking Before Running Any Test
cards.summary: Define conversion as form submit or thank-you-page view, configure a primary metric, and whitelist domains so winners and losers are measurable.
cards.use_when: Planning a landing page or PDP A/B test and you need a reliable purchase/lead conversion metric before spending traffic on variants.
steps: Write the conversion math explicitly: conversions divided by page views equals conversion rate (e.g., 10 form fills / 100 visitors = 10%). Decide whether 'conversion' means a lead (form submit) or a purchase; for lead-gen landing pages the source uses form submission or arrival on a thank-you page.

Add a dedicated thank-you page that the form redirects to. Tracking arrival on that URL is the simpler of the two tracking options the source describes; tracking the raw form-submit event is the more complex alternative.

In PostHog (free tier), create an experiment, add a primary metric, and select the conversion event (in the demo, the event named 'quote submitted'). If the event is missing, submit the form once yourself so the event is registered, and check that an authorized URL is configured in Settings > Web Analytics.

Whitelist the root domain only — strip subpaths, drop the trailing '/', and note that 'http' without an 's' is normal. If running locally, confirm the port (localhost:3000 by default, but 3001/3002/3003 are possible) matches.
Launch the experiment only after the tracking code snippet has been added to both the control and test pages.
On any ecommerce test (PDP hero, bundle offer, checkout button copy), define the primary metric up front — add-to-cart or purchase — rather than optimizing a proxy that never touches revenue.
caveats: The source's workflow is built around lead-gen forms and thank-you pages; for ecommerce you must substitute purchase or add-to-cart events and verify they fire correctly.
PostHog's interface, wizard and naming may change — verify the current UI before following exact clicks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Run a 50/50 Split Test and Iterate Losers Out
cards.summary: Split traffic evenly between control and test pages, measure conversion rate, retire losers and promote winners as the new control in a continuous loop.
cards.use_when: Deciding which of two landing page, PDP or offer variants to keep, and how to keep improving after the first test.
steps: Create an experiment in PostHog with an even 50/50 traffic split between page A (control) and page B (test). The source says you can add more than two variants, but starts simple with two.
Optionally record a hypothesis (e.g., 'variant A will convert better') so future readers understand the intent.
Ask your build agent to insert the returned code snippets into both the control page and the test page — the labeling of which is 'control' is arbitrary.

Test routing in an incognito window: PostHog stores a cookie that pins you to one variant, so a normal browser will keep serving the same page. Incognito clears that cookie so repeated visits reveal both variants.
When a winner emerges, promote it to the new control and rotate the loser out, generating fresh variants to challenge it — a repeating cycle rather than a one-off test.
Apply the same loop to ecommerce-specific variants: two PDP hero treatments, two bundle price framings, or two checkout button labels, always resolving on the purchase metric.
caveats: There is no sample-size or duration guidance in the source; the presenter only says that 'if you do it enough times' results become statistically significant — treat that as a loose claim, not a benchmark, and consult a proper significance calculator.
Real-time dashboards can lag; the source warns data may take about 30 minutes to refresh, so refresh manually before reading results.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Use Session Recordings and Heat Maps to Find Friction
cards.summary: Review real visitor sessions and clicking heat maps to catch unexpected behavior that structured A/B tests miss.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a landing page or PDP underperforms — e.g., visitors clicking non-clickable elements, abandoning a form, or missing the CTA.
steps: Deploy the site live first; the source notes heat maps do not work on a localhost environment, so push to a real domain before capturing them.
In PostHog, add the deployed production URL as an authorized URL in Settings > Web Analytics, then create a new heat map, entering the URL and choosing 'screenshot' (or 'iframe') as the render mode.
Open the Activity/Sessions tab to watch individual visitor sessions in real time and identify actions you don't want — repeated misclicks, dead ends, form confusion.

Document each recurring anomaly, change the page to remove the cause, and re-check later that it no longer happens — treat this as qualitative input to generate test hypotheses, not as proof of causation.
For ecommerce, review sessions on high-traffic PDPs and the cart page to spot where shoppers stall or tap non-interactive price/size elements.

If you built the page yourself, remember the source's warning: creators find their own pages intuitive because of time invested, while first-time visitors may experience them as a maze — heat maps give the outsider's view.
caveats: The presenter states he personally finds A/B tests more valuable than session recordings; treat these as complements, with recordings best for spotting anomalies rather than proving a winner.
Session recording tools raise privacy/consent considerations that the source does not address — check applicable regulations before recording visitors.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Deploy From Localhost to a Live URL via GitHub and Vercel
cards.summary: Two-step free deployment pipeline (local code to GitHub, GitHub to Vercel) that makes the site publicly reachable so tracking, testing and heat maps work.
cards.use_when: You have a working landing page or store page on localhost and need it live so analytics, split tests, heat maps and real traffic can run.
steps: Understand why: a localhost:3000 site is rendered on your computer only; nobody else can visit it, and PostHog heat maps won't work until it is public.
Create a free GitHub account, create a new private repository (the source recommends private), and copy the provided setup command into your build agent with a request to upload the whole project.
Create a free Vercel account, connect it to GitHub, and import the repository as a new project.
In Vercel's import settings, set the application preset to Next.js and add the environment variable that reconnects PostHog.

Build the environment variable from your local .env file: the text before the equals sign becomes the Key, the text after it becomes the Value. This is required because .gitignore keeps secrets out of GitHub, so the connection would otherwise be missing in production.
Deploy (the source says roughly 60 seconds), view the live link, then optionally attach a custom domain bought through Vercel or imported from a provider like GoDaddy.
For an ecommerce store, this pipeline is the prerequisite for any live cart or checkout test — you cannot measure real buyer behavior on localhost.
caveats: Never commit API keys or secrets to a public repository; the source explicitly frames .gitignore and environment variables as the industry-standard way to keep keys safe.
Tool interfaces (GitHub, Vercel, PostHog) change over time — verify the current import and environment-variable screens.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Treat Landing Pages as Multi-Year Assets, Not One-Off Builds
cards.summary: The source argues a well-built landing page is an upfront investment that keeps converting for years, so optimize for durability.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in a dedicated landing page/PDP build versus a throwaway campaign page, or deciding whether to rebuild an existing page.
steps: Adopt the source's operating assumption: a page built once can convert for 5–7 years, so the build cost amortizes across that lifespan.
Because the page is long-lived, prioritize testable structure — clear tracking, a thank-you page, and a split-test setup — over short-term campaign hacks that can't be measured.
Keep iterating on the page over time (rotate losers, promote winners, review heat maps) instead of launching and forgetting it.
On the ecommerce side, apply this to core evergreen assets: the main PDP template, category landing pages, and the primary checkout flow, which persist longer than any single ad campaign.
When budget is tight, the source's logic implies spending on a durable, measurable page beats spreading spend across many disposable ones — but validate against your own traffic volume.
caveats: The 5–7 year lifespan is the presenter's personal experience, not a measured guarantee; page performance depends on traffic source, market and maintenance.
Durability claims assume ongoing optimization and measurement infrastructure, which the source treats as required, not optional.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Native image ads: structure and when to use them
cards.summary: How native-style image ads and advertorials break scroll patterns and lower buying defenses for cold traffic.
cards.use_when: Choosing the primary ad format for a cold-traffic acquisition campaign, or deciding whether a winning video angle should be rebuilt as a native image/advertorial.
steps: Build the core asset as a single image that reads like organic content rather than a branded product shot, so it interrupts the user's scroll pattern on Facebook rather than being skipped like a typical ad.

Pair the image with long-form copy that tells a story and introduces the product before asking for the click; the source positions the advertorial's job as creating an epiphany in the reader, not restating product features.

Reserve this format for problem-solving products that make sense to an older audience (roughly 35+, per the source) — the source says long-form native copy works best when the buyer will read a story before purchasing.
Skip it when the winning angle has not yet been established: the source treats the advertorial as an amplifier placed in front of a proven angle, not a tool for discovering which angle works.

Test the native concept alongside your existing video ads before assuming it replaces them; the source notes not every campaign needs an advertorial, but says it 'juiced up' results where the angle was already validated.
caveats: The source's $350k/30-day and $20 CPM figures are his own case results, not benchmarks you should expect.
Native ads concentrate on Facebook placements — the source leaves placements on automatic and says Facebook routes them there anyway.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Establish the winning angle before building the advertorial
cards.summary: Sequence: test 5+ angles in a CBO campaign first, then build an advertorial only for the statistical winner.
cards.use_when: Planning the order of work for a new product launch, or deciding whether to spend build time on an advertorial page.
steps: Run a CBO (Campaign Budget Optimization) campaign with roughly 5 different angles as separate creatives to find which message resonates; the source calls this his standard pre-advertorial test.
Wait for a clear winner rather than writing long-form copy speculatively — the source says none of the advertorial structure works without a proven angle underneath it.
Once an angle wins, build the advertorial as a dedicated page around that single angle, and scale it in a separate campaign rather than mixing it into the angle-testing campaign.
Keep the angle as the organizing principle for every section of the page: hook, common enemy, unique mechanism, proof, price anchor.

If your angle-testing shows no winner, change the angle hypothesis before investing in page build — the source explicitly warns that building the advertorial first and testing after usually produces the complaint that 'it doesn't work.'
caveats: The 5-angle count is the source's own default, not a validated optimum.
CBO structures and Meta's interface change; verify current campaign setup in Ads Manager before rebuilding this exact structure.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Angle-first audience selection for competitive niches
cards.summary: In saturated categories, win by picking an underserved avatar and speaking only to them rather than competing on the category's standard pain points.
cards.use_when: Product selection or campaign planning in a crowded niche (teeth whitening, supplements, personal care, etc.) where your CPMs are high and conversion is weak.
steps: List the obvious top desires and pain points buyers in the category have — then treat those as the crowded lane you should probably avoid, because every competitor's copy already speaks to them.
Instead, name a specific sub-avatar with a distinct, under-served problem (source example: parents of kids in braces with white-spot risk, instead of general adults wanting whiter teeth).

Reverse-engineer that avatar's pains and the way they talk about the problem, then write copy in that language; the source's favorite copywriter line, Dan Kennedy: 'When you try to speak to everyone, you end up speaking to nobody.'

Check whether anyone is running native image ads to that avatar — the source's product-hunting tactic is to find a brand scaling with video ads but not running native image ads, then run native to that audience yourself for less competition.
For non-competitive niches, the source says going after the category's top desires is fine; angle-first selection matters most where competitors are already spending heavily.
caveats: The source's stated avoid-list (teeth whitening, all supplements, anti-aging, weight loss, EMS/red light, sleep aids, etc.) is his personal risk tolerance, not a rule — he also says you can make money there if your angle is unique enough.
His brand was eventually hit by repeated DMCA claims from a competitor, which he attributes to the competitive niche, not the ad method.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Advertorial page structure (top to bottom)
cards.summary: The section-by-section skeleton of a converting advertorial: urgency hook, credibility figure, pain articulation, common enemy, mechanism, proof, price anchor, offer.
cards.use_when: Writing or assembling an advertorial/pre-lander page for a cold-traffic campaign where a winning angle already exists.
steps: Open with a headline that carries urgency and names the product (source used a limited-availability/urgency line at the top), followed immediately by a hero image or GIF that visually demonstrates the problem.
Use genuine customer evidence or a real qualified expert with accurate attribution to support a narrow, substantiated claim.
Articulate the avatar's specific daily problems in their own terms (rushing through brushing, food trapped in wires, gum inflammation, arguments over brushing) to show you understand them.
Introduce a common enemy: blame the tool or the standard method, not the buyer or their child (source's enemy was regular brushing and even electric toothbrushes).

Create the gap between the buyer's current state and desired outcome, then present the product as the bridge, listing concrete unique selling points (bristle counts, modes, battery life, design) so the buyer knows why not to buy a look-alike elsewhere.

Add proof (reviews, testimonials), a price anchor against the cost of the failure ($40 brush vs. $6,000 orthodontic repair), the offer, risk reversal/guarantee, and a final two-option close: buy now or risk the consequence.
caveats: Clearly identify the page as advertising; a disclosure does not make invented endorsements acceptable.
Build for mobile viewing and substantiate product comparisons and price anchors.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Feature-to-benefit translation with the So-That Method
cards.summary: Drill every feature and desire down through repeated 'so that' questions until you hit the emotional driver, then write from the customer's perspective.
cards.use_when: Writing product page copy, advertorial body copy, or ad hooks where the draft reads as a feature list rather than a reason to buy.
steps: Write the feature or surface desire plainly, then ask 'so that...?' and answer it, repeating until the answers stop changing (source example: grow revenue -> make more money -> retire your wife -> be happy).
Use the deepest answer as the emotional payoff for headlines and closing copy; the surface-level version is what competitors already say.
For every section of the page, ask 'what's in it for them?' and rewrite until the section answers that question rather than describing the product.
Translate product specs into that payoff explicitly — e.g., 'one charge lasts 90 days' becomes a convenience or safety benefit for the specific avatar, not a spec bullet.
Keep the drill-down specific to one avatar; the same feature yields a different ultimate driver for a different buyer, which is why the avatar should be fixed before you write.
caveats: The So-That Method is a copywriting drill, not a research substitute — the source pairs it with actual audience research to know which drivers are real.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Advertorial hook and headline patterns
cards.summary: Opening patterns that work in advertorials: urgency at the top, problem-qualifying headline, and leading with price when the angle supports it.
cards.use_when: Drafting the top 2-3 screens of an advertorial or pre-lander, or testing hook variations before scaling a page.
steps: Place a short urgency or scarcity line at the very top of the page (e.g., selling out faster than expected, lock in your order now) so the buyer sees scarcity before the story.

Write the headline to qualify the exact reader and problem: 'If you're [avatar] dealing with [specific symptoms], read this short article before trying anything else' — this filters the wrong traffic and confirms the right reader immediately.

In the source's winning version, lead with a financial positioning angle (the product saves you $6,000 in orthodontic repairs) rather than only improvement; he says if a credible money-saving frame exists, lean into it, and notes some of his other best advertorials also led with price early.

Test multiple hooks before committing: the source's top hook was found only after angle and hook testing, and he admits earlier guesses (coffee-stain angle) produced the highest CPMs and near-zero traction.

Match the hero image or GIF to the headline's claim — the source's best performer was a simple child smiling with yellow vs. white braces, which visually demonstrated the before/after the copy described.
caveats: Financial framing does not fit every product; the source says you can't always do it.
His specific winning hook is a single case result, not a guaranteed pattern.
Use urgency, savings and before/after claims only when supported by this merchant and product; source dental claims are not evidence.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Spam-testing creatives: high-volume minor variations
cards.summary: Generate many variations off a winning base asset — backgrounds, placements, text colors, image swaps — to find the best-performing version fast.
cards.use_when: You have one ad or image that works and want to squeeze more performance out of the same angle before moving on.
steps: Identify the base winner via the angle test first; spam testing is variation-hunting on a proven asset, not a discovery method.
Produce many near-duplicate images that differ in one or two visual variables: background color, where the product sits in frame, text color, which generated image is used.

Load the variations into the same campaign/ad set structure you used for the angle test — the source loaded batches of images (he mentions 10 images in a single ad set) into a broad-targeted CBO campaign.
Let the platform's delivery decide the winner rather than pre-selecting: he kept broad targeting, automatic placements, and no cost caps, relying on high-volume testing plus the algorithm.
Once a variant wins, iterate the same way again — create new variations of that winning image rather than writing a new angle.
Note the source's caution that the exact tools he used to generate images (kids/people) no longer work the same way; verify current generator capabilities and policies before building your asset set.
caveats: The source says he later realized he should have run multiple ad sets/variations rather than a single ad set, and that he mistakenly left 'shop now' CTA and creative-variation features on — he calls these mistakes, not recommended settings.
High-volume generation of images of people may breach current generator policies; verify before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: CBO creative testing setup and how he ran it
cards.summary: A concrete direct-response testing setup: broad targeting, automatic placements, no caps, one CBO campaign with 5 creatives, benefit-driven headlines.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new creative test campaign for an ecommerce product on Meta and deciding what to leave on default.
steps: Build a CBO campaign with broad targeting — no detailed interest stacking — and leave age, gender, and placements on automatic; the source says Facebook routes native-style images to Facebook placements on its own, so manual placement exclusions were unnecessary in his experience.
Skip cost caps and bid caps: he ran maximum spend with no caps, accepting the algorithm's delivery choices.
Load 5-8 creatives with benefit-driven headlines into the test, then let performance identify the statistical winner.
Once a winner is clear, spin up a separate campaign to scale it (in his case, the advertorial campaign), rather than continuing to test endlessly inside the discovery campaign.
Keep every metric visible at the ad-set level (CPM, CTR, CPC, add-to-cart cost, ROAS) so you can see whether a winner is winning on cost structure or on conversion quality, not just ROAS.
caveats: CBO, placements, and cap options change in Meta Ads Manager — verify the current interface before replicating.
The source's numbers (e.g., 7-cent cost per add-to-cart, 13x ROAS) are his own results on one product, not expected outcomes.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Using AI to draft the advertorial in HTML
cards.summary: Prompt structure for having Claude recreate a proven advertorial structure for your brand, outputting HTML so you can preview it as a real page.
cards.use_when: You have a validated angle and want a first full draft of the advertorial page for your own product without writing it from scratch.
steps: Attach your proven advertorial or structure document and instruct the model to recreate that structure for your brand — the source uploaded the structure PDF and asked for a rebuild.
Supply product context: paste your Amazon listing or product details, your brand name, your normal price, your sale price, and your current offer (e.g., buy one get one free plus free shipping).
State the winning angle explicitly and tell the model to focus the copy on that avatar (source example: stay-at-home moms).
Ask for the output in HTML format so you can see the recreated advertorial as it would look on a real site rather than as flat text.

Review the draft for angle-specific language: the source pointed out that lines like 'guilt about spending money on massage appointments just for themselves' come from genuinely knowing the avatar, so check whether the draft actually voices their concerns or drifts into generic copy.
Move the HTML into a page builder — the source used PageFly (which offered one free landing page) and also tested GemPages — then swap in your real product images, proof, and offer details.
caveats: The source says he can't build the avatar with AI — the avatar/angle must come from your own research and testing.
He notes the model sometimes fails to fetch an Amazon listing on the first attempt and later finds it anyway; verify pricing and product facts in the draft rather than trusting them.
AI-drafted claims still need your review for compliance with ad platform rules (see the disclaimer note on advertorials).
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Direct response design rules for the page
cards.summary: Five non-negotiable design elements: benefit headline, relevant hero, FUD reduction under the CTA, visually distinct CTA, benefit sub-headlines.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing a pre-lander, product page, or advertorial for conversion before sending paid traffic to it.
steps: Make the main headline answer 'who you are, what you do, what's in it for me' in benefit terms, not brand or feature terms.
Choose a hero image that directly relates to the headline's claim — the source's best performer visually showed the before/after problem the copy described rather than a generic product beauty shot.
Reduce fear, uncertainty, and doubt adjacent to the call to action: guarantees, security markers, refund terms, social proof placed beneath or beside the button.

Make the CTA button visually distinct from every other element on the page so it cannot be missed; the source notes he mistakenly used 'shop now' copy where 'learn more' was more appropriate, and treats that as his error.
Write benefit-driven sub-headlines that carry the deeper why — the source's phrase is 'the deeper why' — so each section reinforces a reason to keep reading, not just a label for the section.
caveats: The source's own page contained visible mistakes (double dollar signs, typos, wrong CTA label) that he says did not prevent it from converting once the copy was dialed in — so treat design rules as important but not as a substitute for a strong angle and copy.
FUD-reduction claims and guarantee wording must comply with platform and consumer-protection rules; verify before publishing.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Handling the 'why not just buy it on Amazon' objection
cards.summary: Use scarcity, exclusivity, and differentiation copy on the page to convert the portion of buyers who don't yet trust your brand.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer/proof section of an advertorial or product page where buyers can comparison-shop the same product on marketplaces.
steps: Name the objection explicitly in the copy — tell the reader they won't find this exact product in stores, on Amazon, or on eBay, and that look-alikes are cheap knockoffs.

Back the exclusivity claim with concrete differentiators (source example: nearly 2,000 silicone bristles, UV whitening, 3 cleaning modes, deep gum cleaning, 90-day charge, U-shaped design, waterproof), so the claim is not just assertion.
Add urgency and scarcity: limited units, running out of stock, 'click the button now to check if any are in stock.'
Reinforce with risk reversal near the CTA — the source used a 60-day money-back guarantee plus a warranty — and social proof markers (refunds, satisfaction guarantee, secure checkout).

Close with a two-option frame: pass on the offer today and risk the consequence, or act now while supplies last, so the reader's choice is between outcomes rather than between you and a marketplace listing.

Treat impulse context as a supporting argument, not a license to be sloppy: the source notes that Facebook is an impulse platform where people buy without comparison shopping, but the page still has to earn the click-through.
caveats: The source's out-of-stock/limited-supply framing was real for his store at the time; do not make scarcity claims that are not true, as that creates regulatory and platform risk.
Comparisons to named marketplaces should be accurate — false knockoff claims can create legal exposure.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Scaling an advertorial into a stacked product line
cards.summary: Once an advertorial-avatar combination works, extend the same structure to adjacent avatars and product variations rather than rebuilding from scratch.
cards.use_when: Planning the next product or offer after a first advertorial-driven offer is profitable, or extending a winning page to a new audience segment.
steps: Keep the structure fixed and swap the avatar: the source built a second advertorial targeting a different group (kids without braces who dislike brushing) using the same page skeleton.
Create multiple URL/page variations of the same advertorial to test angle refinements (source example: /braces vs. /teeth versions of one page), rather than rewriting the whole page for each test.
Stack complementary products into the same line once the first converts, so the advertorial becomes an entry point for a catalog rather than a one-off page.
Reuse the tested elements — urgency, common enemy, USP list, price anchor, guarantee — in the new version, changing only what the new avatar requires.
Track each variation separately so you know which avatar/page combination is scaling, instead of attributing blended results to the structure alone.
caveats: The source's stacked-line plan was in progress when his ad accounts were banned; this is intent and partial execution, not a documented completed result.
Account-level risks (competitor claims, policy violations) can interrupt a working structure regardless of page quality.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Page builder workflow for advertorials
cards.summary: Practical build path: generate the structure with AI as HTML, then assemble in a page builder with a free-tier option.
cards.use_when: Setting up the technical build of an advertorial or pre-lander page for a Shopify store.
steps: Get the advertorial drafted as HTML first so you can review structure and copy in a page-like layout before investing build time.
Choose a page builder: the source used PageFly and also tested GemPages, and preferred PageFly for beginners because it offered one free landing page at the time of recording.
Rebuild the HTML layout in the builder so you can manage images, sections, and edits without touching code later.
Keep the advertorial as a separate page from the product page so you can test page-level changes without altering the PDP.
Verify current free-tier limits, pricing, and Shopify app compatibility before committing, since app features and pricing change frequently.
caveats: Tool tiers and free offerings are time-sensitive — verify the current interface rather than assuming the free page still exists.
The source notes the advertorial should be built mobile-first since most traffic views it on a phone.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Common enemies and the gap framework
cards.summary: Create tension by naming a shared enemy (the wrong tool or method) and widening the gap between the buyer's current state and desired outcome before presenting the product.
cards.use_when: Writing the middle act of an advertorial or long-form sales page where the product introduction currently feels abrupt.
steps: Pick an enemy that is a method or tool, not the buyer or their family member — the source's enemy was regular brushing, including electric toothbrushes and flossing, which he framed as never fully cleaning around braces.
Show why the common remedies the buyer has already tried fail, so the reader feels understood rather than blamed.

Widen the gap between where the reader is and where they want to be: rattle off the issues, the money already spent, and the downstream consequences (source mentioned implications like a child's prom being affected in his longer copy).
Only then introduce the product as the bridge across that gap, immediately followed by USP specifics so the bridge is credible.
Keep the enemy consistent across the page so the reader's frustration has one clear target and the product has one clear job.
caveats: The gap framework is attributed to Russell Brunson in the source; it is a persuasion structure, not a measured conversion lever.
The source admits his advertorial version omitted some deeper consequences that appeared in his image ad copy, so consistency across assets is not automatic.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: What to keep from a winning advertorial when adapting it to a new brand
cards.summary: Transferable elements versus brand-specific ones when reusing a proven page structure.
cards.use_when: Repurposing a proven advertorial structure for a different product or store.
steps: Keep the skeleton: urgency line at top, hero image tied to the problem, credibility figure, pain articulation, common enemy, mechanism/USP list, proof, price anchor, offer, risk reversal, two-option close.
Keep the emotional logic of feature-to-benefit translation and the 'what's in it for them' check at every section.
Replace every brand-specific element: avatar research, the specific enemy, product USPs, pricing, offer, and proof.
Re-run the angle test for the new product before assuming the old structure will repeat; the source attributes results to the structure plus a proven angle, not the structure alone.
Expect the same angle-testing step to be necessary: he says he did not use structured research prompts or AI deep research early on and relied on guessing until the parent-with-braces angle emerged.
caveats: The source's claim that the structure works on 'just about any product' is limited to products that solve a problem and appeal to older buyers (35+), his own stated qualification.
Do not infer his specific metrics or angles will transfer to your category.
cards.source_name: Copy my $20k_day advertorial structure.docx

cards.title: Sequence an ecommerce advertorial around the next buyer objection
cards.summary: When cold traffic needs product education before reaching the purchase page.
cards.use_when: When cold traffic needs product education before reaching the purchase page.
steps: Map ad promise, hook, researched customer situation, alternatives, product mechanism, proof, objections, price and guarantee in that order as a starting structure.
Make each section answer the question raised by the preceding section.
Identify the page as advertising and carry the same angle from ad to page to product offer.
Test against the existing product-page journey using purchases, acquisition cost and contribution margin.
caveats: Source conversion and revenue figures are case claims, not benchmarks.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Align the cold-traffic ad with the advertorial hook
cards.summary: When ad clicks do not turn into engaged product-page visitors.
cards.use_when: When ad clicks do not turn into engaged product-page visitors.
steps: Choose one researched shopper problem and a supportable product benefit.
Let the ad introduce a specific question that the page answers promptly.
Match the audience, promise and tone in the opening headline; do not borrow the source example medical claims.
Test alternative hooks while holding the downstream offer stable.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Write a specific product-use story from customer research
cards.summary: When an advertorial describes abstract benefits instead of a recognizable buying situation.
cards.use_when: When an advertorial describes abstract benefits instead of a recognizable buying situation.
steps: Identify the practical moment that creates demand: the task, place, friction and desired outcome.
Use authentic customer language and observed details rather than invented personal testimony.
Show how the product changes that moment, then connect to the next objection.
If presenting a real customer story, preserve its actual limitations and permission.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Compare real alternatives before explaining product differentiation
cards.summary: When shoppers see the product as interchangeable with cheaper alternatives.
cards.use_when: When shoppers see the product as interchangeable with cheaper alternatives.
steps: List the alternatives customers actually consider, including keeping the current solution.
Compare relevant limitations using accurate features, total cost, compatibility or effort.
Explain the specific tradeoff the product addresses and acknowledge who may prefer another option.
Avoid unsupported competitor failures or claims that retail products replace professional treatment.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Explain a supported product mechanism before the offer
cards.summary: When the buyer needs to understand why product features address their problem.
cards.use_when: When the buyer needs to understand why product features address their problem.
steps: Identify a genuine, supportable cause of the practical product-use problem.
Connect each relevant feature to that problem with a clear explanation or demonstration.
Use specifications only when verified for the actual SKU; label uncertainty where evidence is limited.
Move to proof and the offer once the buyer can explain the connection.
caveats: The source medical root-cause and percentage examples are not reusable evidence. Do not invent an expert or proprietary scientific cause.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Match authentic product reviews to purchase objections
cards.summary: When shoppers need proof relevant to fit, use, value or reliability.
cards.use_when: When shoppers need proof relevant to fit, use, value or reliability.
steps: List the major buying objections and find genuine reviews addressing each.
Preserve the customer wording and actual result; do not write testimonial personas.
Use real usage timelines only where documented, without promising the same result to everyone.
Answer remaining delivery, compatibility and returns questions in the FAQ.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Reveal the price against a defensible product comparison
cards.summary: When the advertorial must explain value before the purchase CTA.
cards.use_when: When the advertorial must explain value before the purchase CTA.
steps: Use a genuine comparable product, bundle contents or total ownership cost as the anchor.
Show the actual price, quantity, recurring charges if any, and delivery costs clearly.
Use a compare-at price or stock deadline only when accurate.
Place a guarantee the merchant can honor beside the CTA with its relevant terms.
caveats: Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Close an advertorial with useful questions and genuine proof
cards.summary: When the bottom of the page leaves shoppers unsure about ordering.
cards.use_when: When the bottom of the page leaves shoppers unsure about ordering.
steps: Recap the product benefit, what is included, price and purchase action.
Answer real shipping, gifting, stock and returns questions.
Display authentic customer comments if available, or clearly label merchant-written answers as an FAQ.
Check that the CTA leads to the promised SKU and offer.
caveats: Do not fabricate comment threads, customer avatars or expert endorsements.
Merchant application of the source framework; not a source-demonstrated ecommerce result.
cards.source_name: Guide_ $100k_day with Advertorials.docx

cards.title: Advertorials Split Selling Pressure With the Ad
cards.summary: Use an advertorial as a second force in the funnel so the ad doesn't have to carry all the selling to purchase.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to send ad traffic to a plain product page or to an advertorial/landing page before checkout.
steps: Map the buying journey as a continuum from first ad impression to purchase; every funnel element exists to move the audience along it.
Recognize that a basic product page (benefits, product photos, trust elements) leaves all selling power sitting on the ad alone.
Add an advertorial so two forces push the prospect forward: the ad and the landing page.
Use the advertorial's editorial disguise to educate, handle objections, and intensify desire in a low-pressure, low-stakes environment where people engage as they would an article.
Write the copy well enough that by the bottom of the page the reader simply wants to buy.
caveats: Advertorials are framed by the source as amplifiers of already-winning messaging, not a fix for unvalidated offers or weak creative.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Validate Four Ad-Level Variables Before Building the Advertorial
cards.summary: Confirm avatar, desire, angle and unique mechanism at the ad level before investing in an advertorial landing page.
cards.use_when: Planning a new campaign or product launch and deciding whether it's safe to build an advertorial now.
steps: Test messaging on the ad level first to get confirmation of four variables: avatar, desire, angle, and unique mechanism.
Look for at least break-even conversion to a product page — the source cites break-even on roughly $1,000 of spend as sufficient confirmation, though any break-even signal works.
Build the advertorial once those four variables are proven, so the landing page amplifies messaging that already converts.
Extract each variable from a live winning ad: identify who the avatar is, the plainly stated problem/desire, and the named mechanism with its explanation.

Example structure from the source: avatar = retired senior men with sciatica; problem/desire = sciatica pain relief; mechanism = a physical-therapist-explained spinal decompression home device that stretches the spine and forces fluid back into bulging discs.
caveats: Source states this isn't an absolute rule, but in the overwhelming majority of cases launching an advertorial before testing any ads is unlikely to convert.
Break-even thresholds are the presenter's heuristic, not a universal benchmark.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Choose Advertorial Style by Product Type: Improvement vs Innovation
cards.summary: Match advertorial format to whether your product is a better version of a known product or a brand-new innovation.
cards.use_when: Selecting the advertorial angle and length for a product before writing any copy.
steps: Classify the product as an improvement product (a better version of something buyers already know) or an innovation/gadget (something the market hasn't seen or considered as a solution).
For improvement products, lead with personal stories of people who solved their problem after trying and failing with other products in the category.
For innovations, use a breaking-news or big-revelation frame (e.g. 'revolutionary device'), which lets you get straight into selling faster.
Then layer awareness level on top: consider the mindset of someone who just consumed your ad and pick an advertorial style that fits that awareness.
Don't copy a random advertorial from another product type — one advertorial style does not work for all products.
caveats: The source presents these style-fit observations as its own testing experience, not a controlled benchmark.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Match Advertorial Length to How Much Selling the Ad Already Did
cards.summary: Apply the selling-pressure continuum: less selling in the ad means a longer advertorial; more selling in the ad means a shorter, more direct one.
cards.use_when: Writing an advertorial lead length and deciding how soon to reveal the product, based on the current ad creative.
steps: Assess how much selling your ad creative does. Clickbait image ads that only sell the click (little or no body copy) do almost no selling.

If the ad does little selling, build a long advertorial with a long lead: remind the audience of the problem, agitate the pain, intensify desire, then introduce the product. In the source's example the reader scrolls roughly 50–60% of the page before realizing a product is being sold.

If the ad already sells heavily — long-form personal stories, 1,000–3,000-word sales letters, 1–2 minute UGC videos, or 4–5 minute VSLs — write a shorter advertorial with a shorter lead and cut to the product sooner.
Show the product early on the page (e.g. in the top image and the first few lines) when the ad has already done the persuading.
State the paradigm explicitly: less selling on the ad means more selling on the lander; more selling on the ad means less on the lander.
caveats: The presenter calls this 'not always true, but true the overwhelming majority of the time' — treat it as a heuristic, not a fixed rule.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Swipe Proven Advertorial Structures From Affiliate Hubs
cards.summary: Source advertorial structures from affiliate advertorial hubs, ideally from outside your own niche, to gain a structural edge.
cards.use_when: Looking for a proven advertorial layout to model before writing your own.
steps: Use affiliate advertorial hubs — pages aggregating many advertorials across niches — as a swipe library because they hold a high quantity and wide variety of advertorials.
Pick one that matches your product type; same-niche picks give extra confidence it already converts for a similar product.
Deliberately look outside your niche too: marketers in one niche often copy each other, so importing structures or avatar treatments from other niches can be genuinely differentiating.

Note the structure you intend to replicate (urgency banner, curiosity headline, author intro, problem, agitation, product reveal, mechanism, quality, social proof, price justification) so you can instruct the AI to mirror it.
caveats: Same-niche swipes are a confidence boost, not a requirement; the source explicitly says it doesn't always have to be in the niche.
Treat swiped structures as formats to adapt, not copy to publish verbatim.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Claude Advertorial Workflow: PDFs In, HTML Out
cards.summary: Feed Claude a full-page competitor advertorial PDF, an Amazon product-page PDF, and your four validated variables to get a structured advertorial in HTML.
cards.use_when: Producing a first-draft advertorial page for a Shopify store quickly, once the four ad-level variables are validated.
steps: Capture the competitor advertorial you want to swipe as a full-page PDF using a screen-capture extension (the source uses Ghost full-page capture).
Go to Amazon, find your exact product or a close equivalent, expand all highlights and feature sections, and capture that page as a PDF too.
Attach both PDFs to Claude and state the product you sell plus the goal: recreate the example advertorial's structure for your product.
Supply the four validated variables explicitly (avatar, desire, problem, unique mechanism) and instruct Claude to keep them consistent because they are proven winning ad messaging.
Ask for the advertorial output in pure HTML, exactly mirroring the example structure.
Note the source's own run took about 6 minutes 41 seconds, not the advertised 5 minutes.
caveats: Do not invent the four variables for a real campaign; the source does so only for demonstration and explicitly says you should use confirmed ones.
Claude's output still needs edits — headline tweaks, lead adjustments, mechanism phrasing, and real images.
Tool interfaces and available models change; verify the current capture extension and chat interface before relying on this exact flow.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Deploy Advertorial HTML on Shopify via PageFly Custom HTML Block
cards.summary: Paste Claude-generated advertorial HTML into a blank page builder page with hidden header and footer for instant Shopify deployment.
cards.use_when: Publishing a generated advertorial to a Shopify store and needing it to render as a standalone editorial page.
steps: Create a blank page using a page builder such as PageFly.
Add a custom HTML section/block to that page.
Upload/paste the full advertorial HTML from Claude into the custom HTML block.
Hide the theme's header and footer so the page reads as a standalone editorial rather than a store page.
Use the page builder's page list to keep track of all advertorial pages.
The source notes a native free Shopify route likely exists, but the page builder is preferred for header/footer control and page management.
caveats: PageFly specifics and any free Shopify alternative may change; verify the current app interface and block naming before building the workflow around it.
Input real product images and make final edits rather than shipping raw AI output.
cards.source_name: How I build $1k_day advertorials with Claude in 6 minutes and 41 seconds.docx

cards.title: Use a Quiz Funnel as a Dual-Purpose CRO and Research Asset
cards.summary: Quiz funnels simultaneously convert paid traffic into buyers and generate first-party customer data that ads and competitor research cannot provide.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build a quiz funnel for an ecommerce store's paid traffic, or justifying the investment when quiz completion rates look lower than a normal landing page.
steps: Treat the quiz as two assets in one: front-end conversion (personalized path to a purchase) and back-end data generation (pain points, age, awareness stage, failed solutions).
Direct ad traffic to the quiz instead of a static PDP or landing page when you lack reliable customer research.
Budget for the quiz even if front-end contribution margin is thin, because the data feeds better ads and messaging across all channels.
Expect to get paid to learn: buyers complete the quiz and purchase, while their answers become your research sample.
Collect email where possible, then segment by the specific answer/desire chosen so follow-up emails match that pain point.
Route respondents to pain-point-specific landing pages and offers to raise congruence between ad, quiz and offer.
caveats: The source's claim that quiz funnels 'print money' and drive $100k+ days is the presenter's experience with agency clients, not a guaranteed result.
Adding an email-capture step can lower front-end conversion — the source suggests this tradeoff may be acceptable for subscription models where front-end cash matters less.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: A/B Test the First Three Quiz Questions as the Hook
cards.summary: The first three quiz questions function like the hook of a video and dictate total funnel throughput, so they should be tested first.
cards.use_when: Launching or optimizing a quiz funnel and deciding which element to test first to increase completion and downstream purchases.
steps: Treat the first three questions as the bridge between intro and body — the 'hook' that determines whether users continue.
Test two versions of the first three questions and measure the percentage who complete them (e.g. version A: 70% completion vs version B: 85%).
Prioritize the version with the higher completion rate because more throughput means more customers, more data and more everything downstream.
Only after opening the funnel with strong early questions, work on optimizing later questions and nurture screens.
Keep the first three questions low-friction (age, main goal) rather than heavy or invasive to reduce early drop-off.
caveats: The source observed this across several clients but provides no universal threshold — treat the 70% vs 85% figures as illustrative client examples, not benchmarks.
Question order effects depend on quiz length and traffic temperature; retest if offer or audience changes.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Structure Quizzes to Nurture and Build Conviction Before the Offer
cards.summary: Intersperse educational screens, trajectory graphs and authority proof between data-gathering questions so users are sold before they see the final product offer.
cards.use_when: Writing or redesigning the mid-section of a quiz funnel to raise completion and conversion before the sales page.
steps: Ask a data-gathering question, then follow with a nurture screen that educates on the mechanism (e.g. how face yoga works).
Insert a visual trajectory graph showing expected results over time (e.g. timeline of hair regrowth from January to May) so customers get a realistic, visually represented outcome.
Layer in authoritative social proof at intervals: expert collaborations, named studies, before/after of the same person, and audience-size proof (e.g. '400,000 women in their 30s').
Frame study claims with specifics, such as 'based on a 12-week study of active users', to make the claim credible rather than vague.
Aim for roughly 15–25 questions (about 20 on average, ~5 minutes) so completers are high-intent prospects by the time they hit the offer.
Keep a simple direct-response sales page after the quiz — heavy social proof is often needed because quiz completers are close but not fully convinced.
caveats: The 15–25 question range and 5-minute completion is the presenter's recommendation, not a tested universal rule.
Trajectory graphs and study claims must be truthful to the actual product or they create refund and compliance risk.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Choose Whether to Gate the Quiz with Email Capture
cards.summary: Email capture inside the quiz boosts retargeting but can reduce front-end conversion; the right choice depends on your funnel KPIs and business model.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to require an email address mid-quiz for an ecommerce store, especially for subscription versus one-time-purchase offers.
steps: Add the email step if you want stronger retargeting and an owned list, and accept a possible drop in completion.
Skip the email gate if maximizing front-end conversion and cash matters more, but recognize you lose email retargeting.
For subscription models, the source suggests the tradeoff favors adding the email step since front-end ROAS matters less than retention economics.
Test both versions and compare conversion rate and downstream revenue per visitor, not just completion rate.
After email capture, route users to a simple sales page (e.g. 'resend instructions') that keeps the personalized context intact.
caveats: The source explicitly says the choice depends on your desired funnel metrics and KPIs — there is no single correct answer.
Any drop-off claim from adding email capture is a directional observation, not a measured benchmark in the text.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Generate Reports Every ~100 Quiz Submissions
cards.summary: Analyze aggregated quiz answers in roughly 100-submission batches to extract pain points, demographics and awareness stage while they are still actionable.
cards.use_when: Setting a cadence for mining quiz funnel data for product selection, ad angles and messaging decisions.
steps: Wait until you have about 100 submissions (not purchases) before generating a report — this should be achievable weekly at most ad spend levels.
Export the aggregated answers and feed them into an AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) to draw conclusions and produce a structured report.
Segment results by age brackets and pain-point selections to understand who you are attracting.
Determine awareness stage by asking what users have tried before: mostly 'nothing tried' signals top-of-funnel traffic; many failed prior solutions signals mid-to-bottom funnel.
Repeat the analysis a couple of times per month because results shift with ad changes and traffic mix.
Flag if your daily spend is very low (e.g. $7/day) — you will need more patience to reach 100 submissions.
caveats: Results are directional and change over time; a single report is a snapshot, not a permanent truth.
AI-generated reports still require human interpretation and should not be treated as precise research output.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Turn Quiz Pain-Point Frequency into Ad Angles
cards.summary: The most frequently selected quiz pain points become the hooks for new ad creatives, replacing blind competitor copying.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative for an ecommerce brand when you have quiz submission data and need new ad hooks.
steps: Aggregate pain-point answers and rank them by selection frequency (e.g. '70% selected chin fat' rather than generic skin tightening).
Write ad hooks that lead with the top-ranked specific pain point instead of a broad category.
Continuously generate a learning log from your ads (what won, what failed, and whether it was editing style or messaging) paralleling the quiz learnings.
Rework the highest-frequency pain point into ad angles and then test whether they outperform arbitrary or copied concepts.
Re-check pain-point rankings after each reporting cycle because they shift with creative and audience changes.
caveats: The source acknowledges you can still take inspiration from direct and indirect competitors to see what concepts resonate, but says that is only about 20% of the value — the rest comes from your own customer data.
A competitor's winning ad may be break-even or a loss for them; you don't have their data or ROAS requirements.
The 70% figure is a presenter's illustrative example, not a validated benchmark.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Match Marketing Frame to Quiz Psychographics
cards.summary: The 'frame' — whether you lead with doctor authority, raw social proof, or logical statements — should be selected based on the psychographic data collected in the quiz.
cards.use_when: Choosing which messaging frame to lead with in ads and landing pages after reviewing quiz respondent data.
steps: Define frames as distinct presentation lenses: expert/doctor authority, heavy raw proof (reviews, before/after), or logical/self-evident statements.
Review which quiz answers cluster around skepticism, aspiration, or rational objection and pick the frame that addresses the dominant cluster.
Test frames as a variable separately from angle so you can isolate whether the message or its presentation drives the result.
Apply the chosen frame consistently across ads, quiz nurture screens, and the post-quiz sales page for congruence.
Re-evaluate the frame whenever a new reporting cycle shows a shift in respondent psychographics.
caveats: The source treats frame as the biggest lever for scale but presents it as its own opinion and client experience, not an industry-validated finding.
Poor frame selection based on assumptions is identified as a common reason brands cannot scale — the quiz is the corrective, so frame choices should follow data.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Build the Quiz with AI to Avoid Founder Bias
cards.summary: Generate the quiz using AI with context about your product and audience so your own internal beliefs do not skew the questions.
cards.use_when: Drafting an initial quiz funnel structure before you have submission data, especially when the founder has strong assumptions about the audience.
steps: Provide AI with context: what you sell, who you are trying to target, and your hypotheses about the avatar.
Have AI draft the quiz questions and flow rather than building from your own biases alone.
Review the draft to ensure the first three questions are hook-appropriate and the body mixes data-gathering with nurture screens.
Keep the quiz flexible so it can be updated after reporting cycles reveal what respondents actually select.
Treat the AI draft as a starting point that the real customer data will refine, not a finished asset.
caveats: The source reasons that self-authored quizzes carry internal belief bias, but this recommendation is the presenter's method rather than tested fact.
AI drafts still require domain review for compliance and product accuracy.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Use Quiz Data to Refine Product-Market Fit
cards.summary: Brands often fail to scale because their message and offer do not match a specific avatar; quiz data lets you tweak messaging, problem and frame to raise resonance.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a scaling plateau in an ecommerce store and deciding whether the issue is the offer, the message, or the audience.
steps: Gather quiz data to establish who the avatar actually is versus who you assumed.
Adjust the problem statement, frame and messaging to reflect the exact pain points and language respondents used.
Then adjust the offer and funnel to match that refreshed positioning.
Iterate the cycle: new learnings → new angles and frames → updated creatives and funnel → stronger product-market fit.
Track whether increased resonance shows up in conversion and revenue-per-visitor, which the source treats as key scalability metrics.
caveats: The claim that PMF problems are the root cause of scaling failure is the presenter's opinion and should be treated as a hypothesis, not a universal law.
Results depend on traffic volume and data quality; a small sample can mislead.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Prioritize Customer Data Over Competitor Concept Copying
cards.summary: Stop copying competitor concepts and instead use your own customers, who hold the real answers, allocating only a minor share of effort to competitor inspiration.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative budgets and deciding whether to reverse-engineer competitor ads or invest in first-party research.
steps: Reverse-engineer competitor ads only to spot what ideas are warming up and what formats are resonating — treat it as about 20% of your creative effort.
Put the other roughly 80% into cracking your own frame: your message and how you present it.

Accept that you cannot know a competitor's margins: a high-engagement ad might be break-even or unprofitable for them (e.g. a brand needing 2.5x ROAS cannot assume a viral ad that merely breaks even is worth copying).
Use quiz and survey data to replace assumption-based reverse engineering of why people buy.
Evaluate every concept against your own unit economics rather than assuming a competitor is profitable.
caveats: The 20/80 split is the presenter's framing, not a measured benchmark.
Competitor inspiration can still be useful for format and trend awareness — it is the reliance on their data that the source discourages.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Track Awareness Stage and Demographics from Quiz Answers
cards.summary: Quiz questions about prior failed solutions reveal which funnel stages and age brackets you are attracting, tuning ad targeting and message accordingly.
cards.use_when: Interpreting quiz reports to decide whether to target top-of-funnel or mid-to-bottom-funnel customers with a given ad set or offer.
steps: Include a question about what users have tried before (e.g. products, treatments, routines).
Read the distribution: mostly 'haven't tried much' indicates top-of-funnel traffic; frequent mentions of prior failed solutions indicates mid-to-bottom funnel.
Cross-tab age selections to understand the demographic your ads are pulling in (e.g. 50% over 60, 20% between 40–50).
Use the awareness mix to decide whether to lead with education/nurture (top) or proof and differentiation (mid/bottom).
Compare the awareness mix against your intended avatar and adjust ad targeting or creative if the mismatch is significant.
caveats: These are directional inferences from a survey instrument, not precise cohort data.
The specific percentages cited are illustrative examples from one client, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Personalize Emails by Quiz-Selected Desire
cards.summary: Because quiz integration tags users by the specific pain point or desire they selected, you can send segmented, personalized emails impossible without a quiz.
cards.use_when: Setting up post-quiz email flows for an ecommerce store to increase relevance and repeat purchase.
steps: Integrate the quiz with your email platform so answer selections are stored as tags or custom fields.
Segment users by the specific pain point they picked (e.g. pain point #3 vs #1) and message each segment differently.
Route each segment to a landing page or offer matching that pain point to increase congruency between ad, quiz and offer.
Then personalize the sales process itself — showing the product in the context of the chosen need.
Recheck segment definitions periodically as pain-point popularity shifts in reporting cycles.
caveats: Personalization gains depend on the quiz really changing the path or message, not merely tag collection.
The source describes personalized email as a capability of effective quiz integration, not a guaranteed lift figure.
cards.source_name: How I scale past $100k_Day with Quiz Funnels.docx

cards.title: Match each campaign promise to the product landing page hero
cards.summary: Repeat the paid ad’s specific promise in the campaign page or PDP hero so shoppers immediately recognize they reached the right offer.
cards.use_when: Launching or diagnosing a paid Meta or Google campaign that sends traffic to a physical-product PDP, collection landing page, or advertorial-to-product journey.
steps: Export the live ad variations and identify the exact promise that earned the click, including qualifying details such as a stated saving, product benefit, use case, or bundle offer.

Make that promise the primary hero headline on the corresponding destination page rather than replacing it with a generic brand line. For example, an ad focused on a three-pack saving should arrive at a page that leads with that three-pack value.
Use the supporting line to explain how the product delivers the benefit: material, format, ingredient, construction, compatibility, or other genuine mechanism. Do not merely restate the headline.
Build separate landing-page hero variants when distinct ad angles target different needs or products; do not force all traffic through one vague message.
Audit the page whenever creative changes, especially after adding a new acquisition angle.
Place the purchase path and core reassurance in the first screen: product context, price or offer clarity, purchase CTA, and applicable shipping, warranty, or return information.
caveats: The source treats above-the-fold visibility as especially important and states that many visitors do not scroll, but its scrolling figures are heuristics rather than universal benchmarks.
Only make claims that the product, evidence, and local advertising rules support.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Build a physical-product hero around outcome, mechanism, proof, and reassurance
cards.summary: A product hero should pair a clear customer outcome with an honest explanation of how the item delivers it, a direct purchase action, relevant proof, and friction reducers.
cards.use_when: Designing the above-the-fold portion of a PDP or dedicated single-product campaign page for cold traffic.
steps: Write a benefit-led headline that identifies the shopper outcome or use-case instead of describing the company. Keep claims specific and supportable.

Use a subheadline to explain the mechanism: what the product is, how it works, why its materials or design matter, or what makes the bundle useful. The subheadline should add information rather than echo the headline.
Use an action-oriented purchase control such as “Choose your size,” “Build your bundle,” or “Add [product] to cart,” rather than a vague CTA.
Position genuine friction reducers close to the purchase action: shipping terms, return window, warranty, secure payment, compatibility guidance, or a legitimate guarantee.
Use product imagery or video that demonstrates the claimed use, outcome, scale, or contents—not decorative imagery that fails to clarify the offer.

Add relevant, authentic proof such as verified customer feedback, substantiated editorial coverage, or review ratings. If using publication logos, pair them with a real attributable statement when permission and context allow.
If multiple proof types appear, ensure each resolves a different concern rather than duplicating decorative badges.
caveats: The source’s preference for stacking two forms of social proof reflects its agency experience, not a guaranteed lift.
Do not imply endorsements, fabricate reviews, or present generic logos as evidence of product performance.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Remove navigation leaks from single-offer campaign pages
cards.summary: For paid traffic sent to one product or bundle offer, minimize header exits so the shopper’s next decision is to evaluate and buy that offer.
cards.use_when: Creating a dedicated paid-traffic landing page for a hero product, seasonal kit, limited collection, replenishment offer, or bundle.
steps: Define the one primary conversion event for the page, usually add to cart, bundle selection, or checkout initiation.
Remove the full storefront navigation from the dedicated campaign template so visitors cannot immediately divert to broad category, editorial, account, or blog pages.
Retain only controls needed to complete a confident purchase, such as a visible logo, cart access, customer support link where necessary, and the primary purchase CTA.
Make key product details, variant selection, price, offer terms, and reassurance accessible on the page so reduced navigation does not trap a shopper who needs decision information.
Check mobile carefully: ensure the minimized header does not crowd the CTA, obscure price, or push product context below the first screen.
Keep normal navigation on the broader storefront, category pages, and homepage when product discovery and comparison are the intended shopping behavior.
caveats: This is for dedicated, single-offer campaign pages, not a blanket recommendation to strip navigation from an ecommerce storefront.
If a product requires extensive comparison, compatibility research, or service documentation, provide those decision aids within the campaign path.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Use problem–agitate–solve to connect a product to a real shopper need
cards.summary: On cold-traffic product pages, name the shopper’s existing problem, briefly establish its consequence, and immediately show the product’s credible solution.
cards.use_when: Writing the first explanatory section below the hero of a PDP, advertorial-to-product page, or product-focused campaign landing page.
steps: Place the section directly after the initial offer and product overview, where a new visitor needs a reason the item matters.
Describe a recognizable customer problem in the customer’s language: an inconvenient routine, poor fit, storage issue, unreliable product experience, or other genuine pain point.
Agitate only enough to make the consequence concrete—lost time, wasted product, discomfort, repeat replacement, or frustrating setup—without resorting to fear tactics or unsupported harm claims.
Pivot immediately to the product’s specific solution and mechanism. Explain which feature, design choice, material, contents, or usage method addresses the problem.
Use visual demonstrations, concise benefit bullets, and authentic use cases to make the connection easy to scan.
Review every factual, comparative, and performance statement for substantiation before publishing; AI-generated draft language must not introduce invented statistics or claims.
caveats: The source positions PAS as useful for cold traffic; it may be unnecessary when shoppers already arrive with high product knowledge or strong purchase intent.
Avoid medical, diagnostic, or exaggerated root-cause claims unless they are properly supported and compliant.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Make product-page headings and CTA lead-ins understandable to skimmers
cards.summary: Assume many visitors scan rather than read, so each heading, image, and repeated CTA must communicate the product value without relying on dense body copy.
cards.use_when: Editing a long PDP or campaign page with vague section labels, low CTA engagement, or text-heavy feature explanations.
steps: Read every section heading without its body copy. Rewrite headings that do not communicate a customer benefit, proof point, product use, or reason to continue.
Replace internal labels and empty prompts such as “The details” or “Ready for your next step?” with useful statements such as “Keeps your carry-on organized without bulky compartments,” where true.
Break long paragraphs into short blocks and place the most important benefit or qualification first. The source flags long multi-line paragraphs as likely to bury important content.
Repeat the same primary purchase CTA after major decision sections—such as product benefits, demonstration, reviews, bundle choice, and guarantee—so a convinced shopper need not scroll back to buy.
Keep CTA labels tied to the purchase task: choose a variant, select a bundle, add to cart, or buy now.
Use the product images and headings to carry the core argument for scanners, while retaining accurate supporting detail for readers.
caveats: The source’s read-versus-scan split and claim that more buttons improve conversion are heuristics, not universal measurements.
Repeated CTAs should not bypass required choices such as size, shade, subscription frequency, or compatibility confirmation.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Close a long product landing page with a purchase recap
cards.summary: Treat the bottom of a product campaign page as a final decision block that restates the value, offer, and purchase reassurance before the shopper leaves.
cards.use_when: Building a long-form single-product, bundle, launch, or seasonal campaign page that ends weakly after reviews, FAQs, or product education.
steps: Create a visually distinct closing block rather than ending abruptly in footer navigation.
Restate the central customer outcome and summarize the two or three strongest reasons to choose the product or bundle.
Repeat the exact offer in clear commercial terms: selected product, quantity or bundle, price context where appropriate, and any genuine promotion conditions.
Add the same purchase control used above, allowing the shopper to select required variants or return to the configured add-to-cart module.
Place meaningful reassurance near the CTA: shipping timing, returns, warranty, payment options, or a truthful satisfaction guarantee.
Use a product image, concise demonstration asset, or customer proof that reinforces the final decision; do not add unrelated content merely to fill the page.
Check that any urgency is real and that promotion end dates, inventory statements, and savings claims are accurate.
caveats: The source presents this closing structure as a framework rather than an A/B-validated universal layout.
A short PDP may not need a separate closer if the sticky purchase module and core purchase information remain accessible.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Optimize the ecommerce homepage for product discovery using View Product Rate
cards.summary: Treat the homepage as a route into merchandise and monitor how effectively it moves visitors from brand context into actual product views.
