cards.use_when: Auditing a store homepage when traffic is arriving but category and PDP sessions, add-to-carts, or revenue are weak.
steps: Measure View Product Rate: the share of homepage visitors who proceed to a product page. Use it alongside downstream add-to-cart and purchase metrics so higher product views do not conceal worse-quality traffic.
Make the homepage headline state the shopper-facing benefit or merchandising promise rather than leaving the value proposition buried in supporting copy.

Choose lead imagery that supports the intended emotional outcome and product category. For a pet brand positioned around happier pets, use imagery that communicates that promise rather than imagery that suggests the opposite.
Make top discovery choices visual. Test category tiles, icons, or product images beside category labels instead of relying only on text dropdowns.
Limit top-level menu choices enough to keep navigation legible; the source suggests seven or fewer as a practical heuristic, not a fixed rule.
Test visual navigation by device and category. The source reports a 15% conversion lift in one pet-client image-navigation test, which is a case example rather than an expected outcome.
caveats: View Product Rate is a discovery metric, not a substitute for revenue, conversion rate, or contribution-margin analysis.
Menu item count and visual-navigation results vary by catalog breadth and customer shopping intent.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Put purchase-critical PDP information in a scannable first screen
cards.summary: Make the product gallery, identity, rating, options, add-to-cart path, and key reassurance easy to find before shoppers must scroll.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a PDP above the fold, especially on mobile, where shoppers struggle to understand the product or reach the add-to-cart control.
steps: Expose the product gallery with visible thumbnails or another clear gallery control rather than relying only on subtle carousel dots; shoppers should be able to see that more product views exist.
Keep product identity and credible review information prominent near the gallery. Test the precise ordering for your category, but do not bury either below long descriptive copy.
Surface the information needed to make a purchase decision: price, variant or quantity selection, availability where relevant, and the Add to Cart control.
Keep purchase reassurance close to the button, such as legitimate free-shipping thresholds, return policy, warranty, secure checkout, or delivery expectations.
Translate dense feature copy into short benefit-led bullets, supported by icons or imagery, while preserving links to full specifications and care instructions for detail-oriented buyers.
Review both desktop and mobile layouts. On mobile, verify that gallery controls, option selectors, price, and the cart action are not separated by excessive scrolling.
caveats: The source has strong hierarchy preferences derived from its framework; exact ordering of title, rating, and purchase controls should be validated with your own users and analytics.
Do not hide legally required pricing, subscription conditions, or material/product disclosures in the name of a cleaner first screen.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: State bundle savings so shoppers never need to calculate them
cards.summary: Put the exact monetary saving in each bundle option so customers can immediately compare quantity choices and see the reason to trade up.
cards.use_when: Merchandising multipacks, buy-more-save-more offers, starter kits, replenishment quantities, or volume discounts on a PDP or campaign page.
steps: Calculate each option’s total price, per-unit price where helpful, and exact saving versus purchasing the same units individually.
Name the saving directly in the bundle label, such as “3-pack — save $20,” rather than showing only a reduced total that requires mental arithmetic.
Display options side by side or in a clear vertical comparison that makes the increasing value obvious. Include quantity, total price, savings, and any recurring-purchase terms.
Make the saving legible on mobile; do not rely on faint, small, or below-the-fold discount text.
Ensure the shopper can tell which option is selected and that the cart accurately reflects the selected quantity and saving.

A/B test explicit-savings labels against your existing presentation, monitoring not only conversion but also bundle mix, average order value, margin, returns, and subscription cancellation if applicable.
caveats: The source says it has tested this approach but supplies no lift figure; treat it as an experiment rather than a guaranteed conversion tactic.
Savings must be calculated against a legitimate reference price and shown in accordance with applicable pricing and promotional rules.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Convert dense product information into visual benefit modules
cards.summary: Turn long specification blocks into image-led, icon-supported benefit modules that help scanners understand why a feature matters.
cards.use_when: Reworking a PDP, collection landing page, or product campaign page dominated by paragraphs about materials, specifications, ingredients, construction, or features.
steps: Locate text-heavy blocks that require a shopper to read several sentences before learning the product benefit.
For each feature, write the customer-facing consequence first. For example, present a construction detail as the durability, cleaning, packing, comfort, or performance benefit it credibly enables.
Build a compact module with a relevant product visual, an icon or visual cue where useful, a concise benefit headline, and one short supporting explanation.
Use imagery that demonstrates the feature in use, material detail, scale, or before-and-after setup where authentic; avoid decorative visuals that add no product understanding.
Repeat this format across key value propositions so the page develops a consistent scan path.
Retain accessible full specifications, dimensions, ingredients, compatibility, safety details, and care information for shoppers who need them before purchase.
caveats: The source’s preference for scannable visual presentation is based on a scanning heuristic, not proof that all audiences avoid detailed copy.
Do not convert factual requirements into vague benefits; regulated disclosures and material details must remain complete and accurate.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Audit proof and best-practice elements for decision impact
cards.summary: Testimonials, badges, guarantees, and media logos help only when they answer a real shopper question and reinforce the product’s actual value proposition.
cards.use_when: A PDP or campaign page has reviews, trust badges, and press logos but still feels generic or produces weak add-to-cart and purchase performance.
steps: Inventory every proof and reassurance element on the page: reviews, ratings, user photos, press logos, claims, badges, shipping messages, guarantees, and FAQs.
For each element, state the customer doubt it is meant to resolve: performance, fit, quality, delivery risk, return risk, legitimacy, or value. Rework or remove elements with no clear job.
Select authentic customer reviews that describe the same outcome or use case promised by the headline, rather than using generic praise that could apply to anything.
If using press or retailer logos, include an authorized, attributable quote or specific context when available instead of a bare “as seen in” strip.
Replace filler headings and decorative trust components with product-specific proof, demonstration, or clear policy language.
Prioritize improvements that make existing elements more meaningful before adding another generic badge or logo row.
caveats: This is the presenter’s audit principle, not an empirical rule that every proof element must visibly change conversion.
Never alter reviews to manufacture outcomes, imply unsupported endorsements, or use guarantees that the business will not honor.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Above-the-fold hero formula for landing pages
cards.summary: A six-element hero section (benefit headline, USP sub-headline, two social proofs, CTA, risk reducers, complementary image) that captures the majority of visitors who never scroll.
cards.use_when: Building or redesigning the topmost section of a product, offer or lead-capture landing page for paid traffic.
steps: Treat the above-the-fold area (visible without scrolling) as the make-or-break section: the source states a large share of users never scroll past it, so put 80–90% of early effort here.
Write one benefit-driven headline that answers 'why should I care?' and ties to the customer's dream outcome. Avoid stating who you are, what you do, jargon or vague phrasing.
Add a sub-headline that carries your USP — who you are and why you differ from competitors.
Include at least two forms of social proof above the fold (reviews, testimonials, featured-in) to build credibility and give a reason to scroll.
Place a clear, action-oriented CTA button that stands out visually.
Directly beneath the CTA, place FUD reducers (free trial, money-back guarantee, easy returns, warranty) to defuse online-purchase anxiety.
Add one image or video that complements the messaging and subtly communicates the offer.

Run A/B tests on the headline and on the FUD block separately — the source reports these two elements alone produced large lifts for agency clients, but treat those figures as case examples, not guaranteed results.
caveats: Conversion lifts cited (e.g., 80% from headline alone, 40–60% from FUD testing) are the source's agency case-study examples, not universal benchmarks.
Apply to landing pages for a specific offer; top-of-funnel ad scaling belongs elsewhere.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Emotion-first copy and imagery using PAS
cards.summary: Use imagery and the Problem-Agitate-Solve framework to trigger the emotional decision first, then support it with logical proof.
cards.use_when: Writing landing page copy or selecting hero/PDP imagery for cold traffic that doesn't yet know your brand.
steps: Decide what emotion the visitor arrives with — frustration at a problem or desire for an end-state improvement — and make that the emotional anchor of the page.
Lead with imagery: choose photos/video of real people experiencing the outcome (e.g., a happy customer using the product) because visual processing is much faster than reading text.
Structure a section with Problem-Agitate-Solve: name the problem in the visitor's own terms, amplify the pain it causes, then present your offer as the clear way out.
Layer logical reinforcement after the emotional hook — value props, guarantees, specs, comparisons — so the visitor can rationalize a decision already made emotionally.

For a product page, test replacing generic product-only shots with lifestyle images showing the outcome state; the source reports a tanning brand saw conversion lift after revamping its hero to feature a happy person using the product.
For a service or course, test a PAS section quoting the visitor's actual described struggles — the source reports a 282% lift after adding such a section, treating it as a case example.
caveats: The source's numeric lifts come from agency client cases and are illustrative, not guarantees.
Emotional imagery must match the target buyer — a mismatch (e.g., imagery aimed at the wrong persona) can hurt trust.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Long landing pages convert when every section earns its place
cards.summary: Page length isn't the conversion problem — unhelpful, padded sections and hidden content are; treat the page like a digital salesperson.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many sections a paid-traffic landing page should have and what content to compress or cut.
steps: Accept that cold traffic generally won't convert straight from the ad — the ad gets the click; the page must do the selling.
Build the page like a salesperson: multiple value props, multiple social proof sections, multiple objection-handling sections, and clear reasons you're the best fit.
Audit each section with one question: does it move the visitor closer to converting? If not, cut or rewrite it.

Never hide critical content (especially reviews) in carousels, accordions, drop-downs or tabs — the source's rule is 'what is hidden will not get seen', and such elements get low engagement, especially on mobile.
On mobile, expose reviews inline rather than in a swipe carousel so visitors are forced to consume them.
Test page length as an experiment rather than assuming shorter is better; the source argues there is no fixed optimal length.
caveats: 'Long pages are fine' only holds if sections add value — padding for length's sake still hurts.
Length guidance is the source's opinionated stance; it directly contradicts common 'shorter is better' advice, so validate with your own traffic.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Write for scanners: descriptive, benefit-driven section headlines
cards.summary: Assume visitors read only headlines and bullet points, so make every heading communicate the benefit on its own.
cards.use_when: Restructuring landing page or PDP copy so skimmers understand the offer without reading body text.
steps: Assume people read roughly 20% of content and scan the rest; design for the scanner first.
Replace generic section headers ('How it Works', 'Our Services', 'What Makes Us Unique') with full benefit statements that communicate the point themselves (e.g., 'What makes us different is X').
Use headings and sub-headings, bullet points for main value props, and bold text emphasized especially in headlines.
Run the headline-only test: read only the headlines top to bottom — is the full value proposition still clear and persuasive?
Write as a reader, not a writer: identify the one thing someone must know at a glance and put it front and center.
Ensure the reading flow is clear — body text kept in close proximity to its headline so scanned headlines and supporting detail stay connected.
caveats: Benefit-driven headlines must remain specific and honest; overclaiming in headlines can increase bounce or distrust.
This is copywriting craft guidance; results depend on traffic quality and offer strength.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Make social proof verifiable to overcome skeptics
cards.summary: Add quotes to 'featured on' logos and use reviews with real names, photos and platform sources so credibility can actually be checked.
cards.use_when: Auditing or upgrading the social proof on a landing page or PDP, especially for cold paid traffic.
steps: Identify weak-but-common proof: bare 'featured on' logo bars, anonymous reviews, and repeated/duplicated logos. Remove repeats — repeated logos erode trust.

For each featured-on logo, add a short quote or snippet from the actual publication or appearance to add a layer of credibility. The source's agency client reportedly saw a 38% lift from this one change.
For reviews, require a real name, a photo of the reviewer, and the source platform (Google, Trustpilot, etc.) so a visitor can independently verify it.
Prefer verifiable third-party review sources over testimonials that could easily be fabricated.
Place at least two forms of proof above the fold, and expose reviews inline rather than hidden in carousels.
Test proof variants — logo-only vs. logo-with-quote, anonymous vs. named review — as separate experiments.
caveats: The 38% lift is a client case example, not a benchmark.
Consumer skepticism toward standard proof formats is described as a current marketplace trend; re-evaluate as behavior changes.
Only use real, verifiable reviews and quotes — fabricating proof defeats the purpose and creates legal/reputational risk.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Use visual hierarchy and reduce choice to drive the CTA
cards.summary: Guide the eye from headline to sub-headline to CTA with size, weight, color and proximity, and remove competing elements that cause analysis paralysis.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a landing page or product page layout when the CTA is getting lost or the page feels cluttered.
steps: Define the priority order of elements: headline first, sub-headline second, CTA third, everything else after.
Use font size, weight and color to create clear distinction: headline bold and prominent, sub-headline subdued, CTA button large and contrasting.
Keep the CTA in close proximity to the headline and value copy so the eye flows naturally top to bottom.
Cut or demote competing elements — too many buttons, links, texts and colors cause analysis paralysis, and the source's mantra is 'less is more' (too much choice equals no choice).
Audit for clashing colors and elements of equal visual weight competing for attention; fix by reducing contrast conflicts and establishing one clear focal point.
Test the restructured hierarchy against the original; the source reports a 64% conversion lift from a hierarchy redesign for one client.
caveats: The 64% lift is an agency case example, not a promise.
'Less is more' must not conflict with the long-page principle — sections can be many, but each must have a clear single focus.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Follow Jakob's Law: familiar layouts beat creative reinvention
cards.summary: Users expect landing pages to look and function like other sites they use, so standard structures (one headline, close body copy, top social proof, CTA) convert better than clever deviation.
cards.use_when: Choosing a landing page layout, template or redesign direction, especially when balancing brand creativity against conversion goals.
steps: Apply Jakob's Law: because users spend most of their time on other sites, they expect your page to follow familiar patterns — deviating from standard structure forces them to relearn navigation and hurts conversion.

Adopt the source's baseline structure: one clear headline, body text in close proximity to the headline, social proof near the top, CTA button directly underneath, FUD reducers beneath the CTA, and an image or video.
Avoid the minimalist trap of headline-only pages with no body text and no CTA — minimalism that removes clarity removes action.
Avoid multi-headline hero sections, oversized social proof that overpowers the headline, and body copy that sits far from the headline.
Before shipping a novel layout, ask whether the creativity comes at the cost of clarity; if yes, revert to a standard pattern.
When the layout is unconventional, run an A/B test against a familiar-layout control rather than assuming the creative version wins.
caveats: Jakob's Law is a UX heuristic, not a conversion guarantee; some strong brands convert well with differentiated design.
This contradicts advice to stand out visually — the source frames it as a trade-off favoring clarity over creativity when conversions are the goal.
cards.source_name: I Studied 1000 Landing Pages, Here's What Works in 2025.docx

cards.title: Reduce Cognitive Friction Across the Entire Buying Journey
cards.summary: Frame every page decision as lowering the mental effort a shopper spends to decide and buy.
cards.use_when: Auditing a landing page, collection page, PDP or cart to find why traffic isn't converting.
steps: Define cognitive friction as the brain power or mental effort a visitor must spend to shop and decide; aim for cognitive ease instead.

Recognize a cognitive threshold: when a page exceeds how much a person can process at once, navigation feels confusing, information feels excessive and choices overwhelm, so people leave without buying.

Look for cognitive ease on five levels the source uses: streamlined navigation, crystal-clear benefit articulation, scannable text, easy product selection, and images that reinforce your value proposition.

Apply the checklist as a repeatable sequence before publishing any new page: remove elements, then add images/icons, then fix messaging, then fix visual hierarchy, then simplify product selection and cart feedback.
Treat removing elements as the starting move, not adding more CRO widgets; the source argues clutter from stacked upsells and cross-sells can hurt rather than help conversion.
caveats: The five-step checklist is the presenter's own framework, not a validated universal method; treat each step as a hypothesis to test on your store.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Cut Navigation to Seven Items and Move Secondary Links Out
cards.summary: Apply the source's seven-item navbar heuristic and remove non-buying links to reduce paradox-of-choice abandonment.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a store's top navigation menu or deciding where About, Blog and FAQ links belong.
steps: Adopt the source's rule of thumb: never show more than seven items in the top navigation; beyond that the source says returns diminish and conversions suffer.
Install a session-recording tool such as Microsoft Clarity to see which navigation items people actually click, then remove items showing close to 0% of clicks.
Cut the Home link from the nav — the presenter states it's universally known that the logo returns you to the homepage, so the link is redundant.
Move About, Contact, Blog and FAQ either out of the nav entirely or into a much smaller sub-menu or footer, since they are not critical to the buying action.
If you carry many products or collections, use a nested menu that limits how many items are displayed at once instead of flattening everything into the bar.
Expose the Shop menu directly rather than hiding it behind a dropdown or a redundant click; the source treats an extra click to reach shopping as wasted effort.
caveats: The seven-item rule is an explicit rule of thumb from the presenter's experience, not a tested threshold; the click-data step is what makes it defensible for your store.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Test Reducing Bundle Tiers from Five to Three
cards.summary: A bundle-count reduction test that the source says raised both conversion rate and average order value.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many bundle or package tiers to show on a product page or offer page.
steps: Watch session recordings on your bundle page for signs of overwhelm: shoppers picking the cheapest option or exiting instead of choosing a bundle.
Form the hypothesis that too many bundle options create analysis paralysis, per the paradox of choice — too much choice equals no choice.
A/B test cutting the number of bundle tiers, e.g. from five options down to three, keeping the test simple and measuring conversion rate and AOV together.
Expect that fewer, clearer tiers may push buyers toward higher-priced multi-packs rather than only raising site-wide conversion, since AOV is part of the outcome the source observed.
Read the source's Wild Men Drinking result as an example, not a benchmark: 53% conversion lift and 13.5% AOV lift from the bundle-count change.
caveats: These lifts are one client case study with its own context; do not promise similar numbers or apply a fixed tier count without testing on your own traffic.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: State Exact Dollar Savings in the Bundle Headline
cards.summary: Replace percentage discounts with the precise dollar amount saved to remove math from the buying decision.
cards.use_when: Writing bundle and tier copy on a PDP or offer page where shoppers must compare options.
steps: Apply the source's 'don't make them do math' rule: never require a visitor to calculate the difference between tiers.

Show the exact dollar amount saved in the headline itself (e.g. 'Save $20') instead of a percentage buried in small sub-headline text — the source contrasts this with a client whose savings appeared only as a small percentage.
Combine the dollar saving with a visual of the bundle so the shopper sees what they get, since images are processed far faster than text.
Test the wording directly: the source reports Wild Men Drinking saw a 25% conversion increase and 28.5% revenue-per-visitor increase from moving the exact dollar saving into the headline.
Treat that result as a single A/B test example and validate on your own audience before rolling out.
caveats: The 25%/28.5% figures are one client example; no universal effect size should be assumed.
The source also criticizes a coffee brand (Javvy) for not showing dollar savings on its bundles — an opinion about a specific site, not a controlled test.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Show Bundle and Variant Images to Cut Comparison Effort
cards.summary: Attach an image to each bundle tier and variant so shoppers recognize differences without reading.
cards.use_when: Designing bundle selection blocks or product variant pickers on a PDP.
steps: Identify bundle or variant options that are currently described in text alone; the source argues the brain processes images roughly 60,000 times faster than text.
Add an image of each bundle (e.g. the three-pack and the four-pack) so the visual difference is immediate and the shopper does not have to mentally reconstruct the package.
Follow the pattern the source praises at Yeti: change the image when the shopper changes color or size so the visual updates with the selection.
Test this addition as a discrete experiment — the source reports a 32% conversion lift for Wild Men Drinking after adding images to bundles that previously had none.
Keep images relevant to the buying decision; the source criticizes galleries that only show more angles of the same product as wasting prime page real estate.
caveats: The 32% lift is a single case study; it is an example of the technique, not a guaranteed outcome.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Replace Text Navigation with Icons and Story-Style Visual Menus
cards.summary: Use image or icon navigation, including a stories-style menu, to speed category comprehension and lift clicks.
cards.use_when: Reworking a collection or category navigation bar that visitors skip or ignore.
steps: Audit your current nav for fully text-based menus — the source argues a text-only bar gives shoppers no reason to click deeper or any visual cue of what the product looks like.
Replace category text entries with images or icons that show the actual product, letting shoppers visualize their purchase and reducing the effort to decide where to go.
Consider the source's 'social media icon' pattern: lay all navigation items out in the open like stories-style icons, which removes a click and gives a fast visual snapshot of all product lines.
Keep the seven-item ceiling in mind when adding visual nav elements so the visual treatment does not become its own clutter.

Test the change as one experiment tied to conversion rate and revenue per visitor, not to clicks alone; the source cites Parcel Safety at +60.7% conversion and +92% revenue per visitor, and a pet client at +72% conversion and +82% revenue per visitor.
caveats: Both sets of metrics are single client A/B tests cited by the presenter; use them as examples of what the test looked like, not as expected results.
Verify the current interface of any analytics or testing tool you use, as tool UIs change.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Convert Product Photos into Benefit Infographics
cards.summary: Combine product imagery with scannable value props so the most-clicked page element also sells.
cards.use_when: Improving the product image gallery or hero image on a PDP or landing page.
steps: Check heatmap data for your product pages; the source says product images are consistently among the most-clicked elements, so they carry disproportionate influence on the decision.
Stop filling the gallery with near-identical angles of the same product — the source treats this as a waste of the page's most valuable real estate.
Transform key images into infographics: take the product photo and add scannable value propositions, benefit sections, social proof, and how-the-product-works callouts onto the image itself.
Keep each graphic scannable rather than turning the image into a dense block of copy, since the goal is reducing, not adding, cognitive load.
Test the infographic treatment as its own variant — the source reports a 32% conversion increase for Wild Men Drinking after this change.
caveats: The 32% figure is one case study; effect will vary with product category and audience.
Do not sacrifice accurate product depiction for marketing overlays; the source's emphasis is on pairing photos with value props, not discarding real imagery.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Break Long Page Copy into Icons, Bullets and Subheads
cards.summary: Chunk descriptive text into scannable visual units to stop losing visitors to walls of copy.
cards.use_when: Editing long product descriptions, landing page sections or feature explanations that visitors scroll past.
steps: Identify large blocks of paragraph text on PDPs and landing pages; the source argues nobody reads them and they raise cognitive friction.
Chunk that content into scannable icons, bullet points and sub-headlines so each benefit is digestible at a glance.
Pair each chunked point with a visual where possible, reinforcing the idea that images are processed faster than text.

As one reference point, the source reports Wild Men Drinking gained 25% conversion and 34% revenue per visitor after converting large text blocks into scannable icons, and Fiddler's Green saw a 158% boost in store orders after rebuilding a text-heavy landing page with compelling icons and digestible content.
Run this as a controlled variant so you can attribute the change rather than assuming chunking alone caused the lift.
caveats: Both reported results are case-study examples from the presenter's agency work, not benchmarks.
Icons should clarify the benefit; purely decorative icons add clutter without reducing effort.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Write Headlines as the Only Thing a Scanner Reads
cards.summary: Assume visitors read only your headlines and make each one answer 'why should I care?'
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting headlines on a landing page, PDP or paid-traffic destination.
steps: Operate on the scanning framework: the source states people read roughly 20% of page content and scan the other 80%, so write as if the headline is the only text anyone reads.
Avoid the three headline failures the source calls out: vague or jargon-filled copy, statements of who you are and what you do, and generic phrasing with no benefit.
Put yourself in the shopper's position and identify the single hard-hitting benefit that would make them buy, then lead the headline with that end benefit.
Quantify value where you honestly can: the source contrasts 'trusted by happy customers' with 'trusted by 700,000 happy customers' as the stronger pattern.
Apply it across every section headline, not only the hero, so a scanner who reads only headlines still has an incentive to purchase.

Validate with an A/B test on your own traffic; the source cites Parcel Safety at +80% and Carolina at +157% conversion after benefit-oriented headline rewrites, which are examples rather than expected lifts.
caveats: Only use quantified proof points you can substantiate; do not invent customer counts.
The 20% read / 80% scan split is the presenter's framing, not a cited study.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Build Visual Hierarchy Instead of Emphasizing Everything
cards.summary: Rank page elements and vary size, weight and color so only what matters stands out.
cards.use_when: Designing or fixing an above-the-fold hero or PDP where competing elements fight for attention.
steps: Understand visual hierarchy as the deliberate flow from most important to least important element, controlled through font, size, color, weight and spacing.
Diagnose the failure mode the source describes: pages where everything screams in different colors and font sizes end up emphasizing nothing.
Decide explicitly which element should stand out most (typically the benefit headline) and which should stand out second (the CTA button), then give those the strongest size, weight and contrast.
Deliberately subdue everything else: body text gets less weight, supporting badges sit on a neutral bar that does not compete with the CTA, and decorative elements stay visually quiet.
Check the flow top to bottom so a visitor's eye moves from headline to supporting proof to the primary action without ambiguity.
Test it — the source reports Parcel Safety's above-the-fold redesign produced a 64% conversion lift and 72% revenue-per-visitor increase, though that is a single example.
caveats: The Parcel Safety figures are a single agency case study, not a general benchmark.
Hierarchy should support your genuine priority; if everything is truly important, the page needs fewer elements rather than more styling tricks.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Use Badges to Guide Product Choice on Collections and Variants
cards.summary: Add Best Seller, Most Popular or benefit badges to steer shoppers toward confident and higher-value picks.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a collection grid or designing a bundle/variant selector on a PDP.
steps: On collection pages, badge products as New, Most Popular or — most importantly per the source — Best Seller, because shoppers naturally gravitate to what others are buying.

On variant and bundle selectors, add a contextual badge to the option you want chosen; the source points to an 'Faster Results' badge on a pricier bundle option as a way to give that option relevance and incentive.
Use a Most Popular tag to nudge shoppers toward a higher-priced bundle; the source treats this as a legitimate subconscious cue that raises AOV.
Keep badges honest and few — the point is reduced decision effort, so a page where most items carry badges defeats the mechanism.
Measure both selection distribution and AOV when testing badge placement, since badges can shift mix without changing total conversion.
caveats: The source's badge examples are observational (I Restore Laser, Perfect Snacks), not tested lifts; treat badge placement as a hypothesis.
Using 'Most Popular' when it isn't true is a deceptive practice — only badge claims you can support.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Replace Page-Reloading Cart Confirmation with a Slide-Out Drawer
cards.summary: Give immediate add-to-cart feedback and put upsells inside a non-disruptive cart drawer with a progress bar.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the add-to-cart interaction and cart experience on a product or collection page.
steps: Stop using full-page reloads just to confirm an item was added; the source calls this disruptive and a source of cognitive friction.
Implement a sliding cart drawer that confirms the addition immediately without leaving the page, preserving the shopper's browsing context.

Use the drawer's space for a small, focused set of upsells or cross-sells rather than piling on every CRO widget — the source shows an overstuffed cart where everything competes at once and argues it likely hurts conversion.
Add a progress bar at the top of the cart indicating what the shopper must do to unlock a higher discount, following the pattern the source highlights at Perfect Snacks.
Keep the cart to basics: higher-tiered options, the items in the cart, minor upsells/cross-sells, and a simple next step.
caveats: The source's critique of a cluttered cart is an opinion based on client observations, not a measured test.
Discount-threshold progress bars affect margin; model the offer before adopting it broadly.
cards.source_name: Increase Your Conversion Rate INSTANTLY With This CRO Concept [Ecommerce 2025].docx

cards.title: Sell the transformation, not the feature
cards.summary: Reframe a product's features as the customer's post-purchase identity or capability to make an offer emotionally compelling.
cards.use_when: Writing the hero headline, offer promise, or bundle positioning on a PDP or landing page, and deciding what the offer actually promises beyond the object.
steps: Identify the core feature or ingredient (the source's 'Fireflower' — a power-up the customer has to know how to use).
Translate it into who the customer becomes or what they can suddenly do ('Super Mario shooting fireballs').
Make the offer itself about the transformation: name the outcome, the identity shift, or the before/after state, not the spec sheet.
Test the framing against the feature-led version; if the feature version only speaks to people who already understand the category, lead with the transformation and let the feature serve as proof.
Keep the feature available lower on the page as substantiation for skeptics.
caveats: The Mario analogy is a teaching device from the source, not a measured result. Treat transformation-led framing as a hypothesis to test on your own traffic.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Turn the offer into an event, not a listing
cards.summary: Package a launch or promotion so it reads as a happening people want to join, leaning on the crowd-attracts-a-crowd effect.
cards.use_when: Planning a product drop, limited-time promotion, or launch campaign and deciding how to structure the offer rather than just discounting.
steps: Decide what makes this a moment: a deadline, a countdown, a limited quantity, a live reveal, or a collective milestone.
Add visible social proof of participation (counts of buyers, waitlist size, community activity) so the offer communicates that others are already in.
Structure the offer so joining is time-bound or capacity-bound; an event with no edges reads as a permanent listing.
Coordinate the landing page, email, and ad creative to hit the same moment so all channels reinforce one event rather than several separate promotions.
Measure participation rates and repeat visit behavior during the window, not only same-day revenue, to see whether the event mechanic itself is working.
caveats: Scarcity and deadline mechanics must be honest; fabricated urgency erodes trust and repeat purchase.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Use a dramatic demonstration to bypass skepticism
cards.summary: Build a visual, often exaggerated demonstration that proves product efficacy viscerally rather than through claims.
cards.use_when: Creating the main visual or video asset for a PDP, ad, or landing page where the product's benefit is hard to believe or hard to see.
steps: Find the single most viscerally provable outcome your product delivers (the source's examples: Otis cutting an elevator cable to prove the brake, a sword cutting a bullet, popping fat-cell balloons on air).
Design the demonstration so the proof is visible in one glance without reading; assume the viewer will not read a caption.
Exaggerate the staging or scale to make the mechanism obvious, but keep the demonstrated mechanism truthful to what the product actually does.
Place the demonstration above the fold or as the primary ad creative so it does the persuading before copy is read.
Pair it with a short explanation of what the viewer just saw so the demonstration converts into understanding, not just spectacle.
caveats: The source describes demonstrations as dramatic and often exaggerated; exaggeration in staging is different from false claims about efficacy, which create legal and trust risk.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Stack unquestionable third-party proof into the offer
cards.summary: Use concentrated outside validation — expert consensus, practitioner endorsements, or influencer adoption — to make claims hard to dispute.
cards.use_when: Building the proof section of a landing page or offer when your own claims are not credible enough to carry the sale alone.
steps: List who your buyer already trusts: credentialed experts, practitioners in the field, or creators they follow.
Recruit or cite validation at a scale that reads as consensus rather than a single testimonial (the source cites examples like thousands of doctors endorsing a position).
Have validators demonstrate or use the product, not just lend a name, so the proof also functions as a demonstration.
Place proof next to the specific claim it supports rather than in a generic testimonial block.
Note that the source treats influencer validation as a form of proof; if using creators, align the claim they verify with the claim that drives purchase.
caveats: Do not fabricate credentials, counts, or endorsements; use only real, verifiable validators. Regulatory rules on health and medical claims apply.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Attach the product to an existing daily behavior
cards.summary: Increase retention and habit formation by designing the product into a routine the customer already performs.
cards.use_when: Designing subscription or replenishment offers, onboarding messaging, or usage instructions meant to drive repeat purchase.
steps: Identify a behavior the target customer already does every day without thinking (the source's examples: morning coffee, a daily supplement).
Position the product as an addition to that existing behavior rather than a new behavior the customer must remember.
Give explicit pairing instructions at the point of first use and in post-purchase email ('add it to your morning coffee', 'take it with your existing routine').
Reinforce the pairing in packaging, reminders, and subscription cadence so the reorder matches the routine's frequency.
Track repeat purchase and subscription retention after introducing the pairing, comparing cohorts who received the pairing instruction against those who did not.
caveats: The source presents behavior change as a marketing hijack; whether a specific pairing increases retention in your store is untested until you measure it.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Sell the aspirational outcome behind the product
cards.summary: Show the glamorous end-state the product delivers — the source's 'movie star smile' — rather than the product mechanism.
cards.use_when: Choosing hero imagery and headline for a PDP or landing page for a product with a visible or status-linked outcome.
steps: Define the outcome your buyer is really purchasing: the visible result, the status, the moment they picture.
Lead with that image or scenario rather than the mechanism (the source's contrast: the film on your teeth vs. the movie star smile).
Keep the mechanism and ingredients on the page for the buyers who need proof before purchase, but do not lead with them.
Check whether hero creative shows the outcome or the object; switch to outcome-led if the current asset only shows the product.
Segment messaging if your audience contains both outcome-driven and mechanism-driven buyers, and route each to the appropriate lead.
caveats: Aspirational framing can overpromise; ensure advertised outcomes are achievable and compliant, especially in health and beauty.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Position the brand as rebellion against the category leader
cards.summary: Give buyers a way to signal independence or superiority by choosing you over the dominant incumbent.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand positioning, ad angle, or landing-page narrative for a challenger brand in a category dominated by a large competitor.
steps: Name the incumbent or category convention your buyer resents or feels constrained by (the source's example: wearing barefoot shoes to rebel against Nike).
Frame the purchase as a stance or identity choice, not just a spec comparison, so the buyer gets social meaning from choosing you.
Put the rebel position into the creative and the offer copy, then keep the product claims accurate underneath it.
Build community and content around the stance so customers can display it publicly (reviews, user content, community).
Confirm the positioning is distinct from competitors' so you are not just paying to reinforce the incumbents' frame.
caveats: The source's 'Torches of Freedom' example is a historical manipulation case; using rebellion positioning ethically means the customer's stance is genuine, not manufactured around a harmful behavior.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Match the offer to the market's awareness stage
cards.summary: Diagnose whether the market is clueless, curious, or saturated, then lead the offer with education, interception, or a unique mechanism accordingly.
cards.use_when: Deciding what the top of a PDP or landing page should say before you write it — problem education, a contrarian intercept, or a differentiated mechanism.
steps: Classify the audience: clueless (does not know the problem or category), curious (knows the problem, has tried solutions), or saturated (knows everything and sees the category as commoditized).
For clueless markets, open with the problem the buyer already cares about (the source's example: digestive issues before probiotics) and educate before introducing the product.
For curious markets, intercept existing knowledge with a contrarian or sharper claim (the source's example: 'your doctor says throw your probiotics in the trash' because of insufficient strains).
For saturated markets, lead with a strong unique mechanism or a personality-driven brand, since feature comparison no longer differentiates.
Re-check the classification when entering new channels or geographies, since awareness differs by audience.
caveats: These three stages are the source's heuristic framework, not a measured segmentation model; the diagnosis should be validated with customer research and traffic behavior.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Lead with the problem in a clueless market
cards.summary: Educate an unaware audience on the problem before presenting the product, so the solution has something to attach to.
cards.use_when: Writing the top of a landing page or ad for a new category, new mechanism, or product whose problem is not yet understood by most traffic.
steps: Identify the symptom or problem the buyer already feels, even if they do not know its cause or category name.
Open the page or ad with that problem, using familiar language, before any product mention.
Introduce the mechanism or category only after the problem is framed, so the product arrives as an explanation rather than an unfamiliar object.
Use proof and demonstration to make the new mechanism believable rather than asking the buyer to accept it on assertion.
Measure scroll depth, time on page, and add-to-cart from cold traffic; if the problem framing is not landing, the audience may already be past the clueless stage.
caveats: Problem-first education costs page space and reader patience; for aware audiences it slows down conversion, so confirm the stage before adopting it.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Intercept a curious market with a contrarian claim
cards.summary: For audiences who already know the category, enter the conversation with a sharper or contradictory claim that reopens the decision.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks or page headlines for a category where buyers have already tried competing products and believe they know the options.
steps: Assume the buyer already knows the problem and the standard solution categories; do not spend the top of the page re-explaining them.
Enter with a claim that challenges their current belief or current product (the source's example: supposedly throw out your probiotics because they lack enough strains).
Immediately substantiate the contrarian claim with the specific difference your product has — this is where the unique mechanism earns its place.
Keep the tone as interception, not insult; the goal is to make them re-evaluate, not to attack the buyer's past choices.
Test the contrarian hook against a plain benefit hook on the same traffic to see whether challenge or reassurance converts better for your audience.
caveats: Contrarian claims invite scrutiny and can invite regulatory attention in health categories; every claim needs support you can show.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Use a unique mechanism to break through a saturated market
cards.summary: In a commoditized category, differentiate on a specific mechanism or personality rather than on features or price.
cards.use_when: Competing in a category where every product claims the same benefits and comparison shopping has flattened the field.
steps: Accept that in saturation the category claims are exhausted; adding a louder version of the same claim will not differentiate.
Identify a specific mechanism — an ingredient, process, technology, or delivery format — that explains why your product performs differently.
Name the mechanism and give it a clear explanation so it becomes the reason to choose you rather than a generic feature bullet.
Alternatively, build the differentiation on personality and brand voice when the product itself is mechanically similar to rivals.
Support the mechanism with proof and demonstration; an unproven mechanism in a saturated market reads as another claim.
Track whether traffic responds to mechanism-led messaging versus price-led messaging to confirm the market is actually saturated.
caveats: The framework says saturation calls for a unique mechanism or personality; if competitors are still unknown to your traffic, that is a different stage and this approach may be premature.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Make the offer about the buyer, not the product
cards.summary: Shift the entire framing of the offer from what the product is to what it does for the buyer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a draft offer or landing page and finding that most copy describes the product rather than the buyer's outcome.
steps: Audit the page for first-person product language ('our formula', 'our technology') versus buyer-centered language ('what you'll feel', 'what changes for you').
Rewrite the offer promise so the buyer is the subject of the sentence and the transformation is the object.
Check that each section answers a buyer question (will this work for me, how do I know, what changes) rather than listing what the company did.
Keep mechanism and specification content, but demote it to a supporting role beneath the buyer-centered promise.
Compare the rewritten offer against the original with a holdout or A/B test before rolling it out across channels.
caveats: Buyer-centered framing is the source's recommended default for category-defining campaigns, not a universal rule; technical or B2B buyers may need specification-led copy first.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Sell the transformation, not the feature (Mario Marketing)
cards.summary: Frame product copy around who the customer becomes after purchase, not the product's features or your excitement about it.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP headlines, hero copy, ad creative or a landing page where you are tempted to lead with specs and features.
steps: Draw the customer before and after: small Mario versus Mario with the fireflower. The fireflower is your product; the fireballs are the customer's new capability.
Write the benefit as a status or identity change the customer wants (movie star smile, flying like Mike, energy to last the workday), not a spec list.

Claude Hopkins' Pepsodent ad did not explain the formula — it promised the movie star smile behind the film on your teeth. Copy that structure: name the desired end state, then show the product is the mechanism.
Kill copy that talks only about why you are excited about your product. Rewrite each line answering 'what is in it for them?'
caveats: The source presents this as a recurring pattern across historic campaigns, not a tested conversion benchmark.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Build a do-it-yourself demonstration into the page
cards.summary: Create a visual or physical demonstration the prospect can perform or watch so belief bypasses logical skepticism.
cards.use_when: Designing PDP media, landing page sections or ad creative for a product whose efficacy is doubted or invisible.
steps: Find a demonstration anyone can do themselves and put it in the copy or page: Pepsodent had readers run their tongue over their teeth to feel the 'film'.
Or stage a dramatic visual proof event: Otis stood on an elevator while an assistant cut the ropes ('all safe here, gentlemen').
Use real proof rather than a claim: Dr Oz popped balloons to represent fat cells; the water-filter demo showed someone drinking the dirty water.
For modern ecommerce, shoot a short video that shows the product visibly doing the hard thing (a sword cutting a bullet, a steak sliced) and use it in ads and PDP media where platforms allow.
caveats: The Otis result (from 3 elevators in year one to about 2,000 over the following decade) is a historical example, not a forecast.
Exaggerated demonstrations can cross into false claims — check ad platform rules and substantiation requirements before publishing.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Turn your campaign into an event
cards.summary: Staging ads as events draws crowds and press coverage you could not buy directly.
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch, brand activation or PR push for a store that needs attention beyond paid ads.
steps: Design the launch as a public event people can attend or watch live, as Bernays did with the Easter Parade float and Otis did at the Crystal Palace.
Give the press a reason to cover it: a novel visual, a named spokesperson, and a quotable line (Otis's 'all safe here', Bernays's 'torches of freedom').
Exploit the crowd instinct — 'nothing attracts a crowd like a crowd' — by filming the event and reusing that footage as ads and social content.
For ecommerce, this can be a livestream drop, a stunt video, or a launch moment with influencers, not only a physical event.
caveats: The source treats event-based attention as powerful but gives no quantified lift; treat results as case-specific.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Match the message to the market's awareness stage
cards.summary: Lead with the problem when the market is unaware, and with the mechanism or personality when the category is saturated.
cards.use_when: Choosing the hook for a landing page or ad when deciding whether to open on the problem, the solution, or a unique mechanism.
steps: If the market is clueless (e.g., nobody brushed teeth daily in the 1920s), start with the problem they already care about before introducing the product category.
If the market is saturated and commoditized, a strong unique mechanism or distinct personality is needed to break through.
When competitors are attacking the category leader's claims ('doctor says throw your probiotics in the trash because they lack strains'), the opening must answer that objection with your mechanism.
In practice: write the first three seconds of the ad or the hero line to match awareness stage, then adjust after seeing hook-level engagement data.
caveats: The source describes awareness stages qualitatively; it does not give numeric thresholds for clueless versus saturated markets.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Position the purchase as rebellion or superiority
cards.summary: Giving customers a mainstream norm to reject lets them buy as a statement of identity rather than need.
cards.use_when: Building brand positioning, community angle or ad creative for products in categories where functional differentiation is weak.
steps: Identify the incumbent norm or establishment the customer already resents (work shoes, big cars, IBM, Nike).
Frame the purchase as joining the rebels: Volkswagen's 'think small' made driving a Beetle the hipster statement against big 1960s cars; Apple's 1984 Super Bowl ad positioned Mac against IBM.
Allow the customer to feel in on something exclusive — Snapchat deliberately made the app hard for older users so young users could teach each other the secret.

In ecommerce, apply this to product choice and creative: pick the enemy, name what your customer is rejecting, and make the product the badge of that choice. Verify claims about competitors are accurate and legally safe.
caveats: The source's examples (Lucky Strike, political ads) include manipulative and harmful cases; attribution of effectiveness is the source's, not an endorsement.
Aspect-specific rebellion positioning can date quickly once the rebel look becomes mainstream.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Use people of prominence as unquestionable proof
cards.summary: When a known figure visibly uses a product, audiences infer it is acceptable and desirable.
cards.use_when: Selecting influencers, testimonials or expert endorsements for a PDP, landing page or ad campaign.
steps: Recruit a figure the target customer already admires and show them using the product in a real context (Steve Prefontaine wearing Nike, socialites smoking on the parade float).
Treat this as a form of unquestionable proof: the source says people automatically assume something is okay and want to copy it when someone of prominence does it.
For ecommerce, this can be a serious athlete, a credentialed expert, or a visible community leader — match the figure's authority to the belief you need to install.
Make the endorsement visible in the product media, not buried in text.
caveats: Disclose paid or material connections as required by advertising rules in your market.

Lucky Strike's gala campaign shows prominence can move fashion and sales without the audience consciously connecting it to the brand — the source treats this as powerful but it also means attribution is hard to measure.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Manufacture consensus with expert letters and press pickup
cards.summary: Publishing agreement from many experts, then getting media to repeat it, converts an opinion into an accepted fact.
cards.use_when: Seeking third-party credibility for a supplement, food, health or wellness product claim.
steps: Have a credible source write to many peers proposing the claim (Beech-Nut's doctor sent 5,000 letters proposing bacon as part of a hearty breakfast; about 4,500 reportedly agreed).
Rather than running it as a direct ad, give the result to newspapers so the headline carries it: 'doctors agree a hearty breakfast containing bacon is the best way to store energy.'
In ecommerce, gather expert or professional endorsements and place them where buyers evaluate claims, then pursue editorial coverage that repeats the finding.
Distinguish this from paid testimonials — the mechanism is borrowed credibility from a trusted third party.
caveats: Reputable health claims require substantiation and compliant wording; the bacon campaign is a historical persuasion example, not a compliance model.
The source does not provide conversion data for this tactic.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Anchor a new consumption habit to an existing daily behavior
cards.summary: Selling an addition to a routine the customer already has spreads faster than selling a new routine.
cards.use_when: Designing replenishment, subscription or bundle offers around daily rituals like coffee or breakfast.
steps: Find the daily behavior already happening (morning coffee, breakfast) and make your product an additive to it rather than a replacement ritual — Bulletproof Coffee added butter and MCT oil to existing coffee.
Connect the product to meals or routines in the copy so it feels like part of the day (Sunkist tied orange juice to meals for nutrient absorption).
Offer a low-friction entry device or bundle to start the habit — Sunkist mailed a cheap juicer for proofs of purchase.
Because customers talk about what they do daily, a daily-use product generates ongoing word of mouth: the source cites The Miracle Morning selling steadily because readers journal every day.
caveats: Habit-change campaigns were run over years (Pepsodent's ran for decades); expect long timelines, not immediate conversion lifts.
Subscription or auto-ship framing must be transparent — the source criticizes scam auto-billing sites that trapped customers.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Ride a rising cultural trend to sell a new category
cards.summary: Attaching a product to an existing social movement or trend gives it momentum and meaning it lacks alone.
cards.use_when: Launching a new category or product line where there is no existing demand to convert.
steps: Identify the live cultural current (women's rights marches, the running boom, the anti-alcohol trend the source observes now).
Attach the product to that current with language that reframes consumption as participation (cigarettes as 'torches of freedom').
Borrow existing celebrity or community momentum instead of building awareness from scratch — Nike rode Prefontaine and the running boom, then Jordan.
In ecommerce, look for the trend your category can join (sober-curious socializing, barefoot-style training) and align product messaging and creative with it rather than fighting it.
caveats: The source's flagship example, marketing cigarettes to women, is a harmful case; the mechanism is neutral, the use is not.
Trends reverse — the source notes smoking later became unfashionable again.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Use sound bites and verbal kill shots to brand and differentiate
cards.summary: Short repeatable phrases stick in memory and can define competitors, not just your product.
cards.use_when: Writing taglines, ad hooks, founder talking points or competitive comparison copy.
steps: Compress your message into a phrase that can be repeated verbatim by customers and press — 'yes we can', 'think small', 'like Mike'.
Use a consistent branded label for a competitor weakness where it is factual and fair, the way political verbal kill shots branded opponents in one phrase.
Repeat the same simple message across ads rather than varying it; the source credits Trump's effectiveness to consistent repetition and self-branding.
For ecommerce, build one core sound bite for the brand and test it across ad hooks and landing page headlines for recall.
caveats: The source attributes the kill-shot analysis to blogger Scott Adams; it is commentary, not a measured marketing result.
Defamatory or false competitor labels carry legal risk — keep comparisons factual and substantiated.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Create ASMR-style sensory video and remix it with product
cards.summary: Oddly satisfying sound-and-visual videos attract huge watch time; integrating the product into that format borrows the attention.
cards.use_when: Producing TikTok or Reels ad creative for a physical product that needs low-cost attention.
steps: Find a satisfying, high-retention format — the source cites glass bottles of marbles rolling down concrete stairs, racking up around 10 million views.
Recreate the video and integrate your product into the sequence so the satisfying mechanic is attached to your item.
Use it as a top-of-funnel hook, then connect to product benefit before the viewer drops off.
Test several satisfying formats and keep the ones that hold viewers, since the format itself — not the product — is what gets the initial attention.
caveats: The 10 million view figure is an example from the source's observation, not a benchmark you should expect.
The source says only that they remixed this format for their brand; it does not report the resulting performance.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Use visceral prop demonstrations to make an invisible mechanism visible
cards.summary: Physical props that dramatize a mechanism make the claim memorable and believable long after the ad runs.
cards.use_when: Creating explainer or demo content for a mechanism that cannot be seen or directly shown (fat loss, filtration, absorption).
steps: Take the invisible mechanism and make it a physical object on camera — Dr Oz popped balloons to represent fat cells; a filter demo drank visibly dirty water.
Accept dramatic exaggeration of scale for the demonstration: the source notes technically-minded people object that the balloons are not realistic, but the visceral image is what sticks.
Follow the format with proof that you personally use the product — the presenter's willingness to drink the filtered water is the proof, not the technical explanation.
For ecommerce, build a repeatable demo prop or sequence for your mechanism and use it consistently in video ads and PDP media.
caveats: The Garcinia cambogia example the source uses is an unethical scam that produced fraudulent auto-billing; do not copy the fraud, only the demonstration mechanics.
Health and wellness demonstrations may trigger regulatory scrutiny — check claim substantiation rules for your category.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Win repeat orders by engineering a sensory signature
cards.summary: A distinctive sensory cue customers associate with efficacy keeps them repurchasing instead of switching to copycat ads.
cards.use_when: Designing product experience and differentiation for consumables like oral care, supplements or beverages.
steps: Identify or engineer a sensory signature customers can feel (Pepsodent's minty tingle after brushing) and keep it consistent.
Understand that imitation ads alone do not win repeat orders — competitors copied Pepsodent's claims but customers who did not feel the tingle returned to Pepsodent.
Protect the signature against copycats; the source notes Pepsodent's advantage lasted roughly a decade until competitors replicated the tingle.
In ecommerce, make the sensory or experiential cue explicit in retention communications so subscribers notice and trust it.
caveats: The decade-long exclusivity and repeat-order advantage are historical examples; do not read them as guaranteed retention benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: The 'Human Hijacks' Checklist for Ad Creative and Landing Hooks
cards.summary: Seven recurring psychological levers (make it about them, event, demonstration, proof, daily behavior, dream, rebel) that creators like Clemens use to make product messaging stop the scroll.
cards.use_when: You're writing the hook, headline or first seconds of a video ad, advertorial or landing page and need a menu of angles to test.
steps: List the seven hijacks: (1) Make it about them — lead with the customer's benefit, not your product. (2) Make it an event — 'nothing attracts a crowd like a crowd'. (3) Powerful demonstration — PT Barnum's elephant, the axe, the sword through the bullet, the dirty-water demo; show dramatic, near-shocking proof instead of stating a feature. (4) Unquestionable proof — doctors, named experts, influencers, someone willing to literally stand in the elevator being cut. (5) Change a daily behavior — bolt your product onto something they already do (in their coffee, at breakfast) or create a new daily ritual. (6) Sell the dream — the outcome in vivid, specific personal terms. (7) Help them be a rebel or feel superior — give them the badge and the tool to stick it to 'the man'.
Source argues each of these can change a company's trajectory on its own, so generate several angle variants and test rather than picking one.
caveats: Demonstration and proof claims must be truthful for your product; Clemens describes tactics like deliberately baiting a video with ASMR before revealing the product, which carries real brand-trust and platform-policy risk if overdone.
'Rebel' and 'superiority' framings require care in regulated or mainstream categories.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Hijack Existing High-View Attention Formats (the ASMR Remix)
cards.summary: Find a proven high-view organic format, replicate its opening, then swap in your product at the payoff moment.
cards.use_when: You need a cheap, high-retention video hook for paid social and want to borrow a format that already has proven viewership.
steps: Scan TikTok/Reels/Shorts for oddly-satisfying formats with very large view counts (Clemens cites glass bottles full of marbles rolling down concrete stairs, which he says routinely hit ~10 million views).
Identify the exact sensory/hook mechanics — here, the sound of glass rolling, the clink on each stair, then the crack and the marble cascade.
Shoot the same opening so it reads as that format, then 'hijack' the video at the natural payoff moment (the smash) and reveal your product.
Clemens' team reported far higher watch-through doing this than starting on the product, and they describe the technique candidly as 'a complete bait and switch'.
caveats: Clemens himself calls it a bait and switch — using someone else's format can damage trust, invite negative comments and risk platform or IP complaints.
The retention benefit is the presenter's reported experience, not a guaranteed benchmark.
Verify current ad-platform policies on misleading creatives.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Lead With a Problem the Market Already Cares About When the Category Is Unknown
cards.summary: If buyers don't know your product category, open on a pain they already feel and educate them into the category from there.
cards.use_when: You're launching a product in a category buyers have never heard of, so a benefit statement does nothing.
steps: In Clemens' 'Clueless' market stage, he argues you must create the marketing wave yourself: the audience knows nothing about the product.

Open on the familiar symptom instead. For probiotics he started with digestive issues and bathroom irregularity — things people already cared about — and only then explained the microbiome and the product as the aid.

Build a 'bigger villain' into the story so the uncomfortable symptom has an external cause. In the probiotic case: hidden sugars and artificial sweeteners in foods labelled healthy, plus alleged suppressed studies (a paid livestock-sugar experiment where cows died; aspartame tested on animals with claimed falsified tumour reports).

Position your product as the simple daily fix to that villain. His Keybiotics presentation reportedly reached 100M+ views in roughly four months and birthed the biggest probiotic brand of the time — treat that as an illustrative case, not a promise.
caveats: Villain narratives must be factually defensible; Clemens is repeating claims about food and sweetener companies, so don't restate them as your own without verification.
Reaching that volume required major organic and celebrity amplification that can't be planned.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Diagnose Your Market Stage Before Writing Copy: Clueless, Curious, Saturated
cards.summary: The message that works depends on whether the market has never heard of the product, has heard of it, or is fully saturated.
cards.use_when: You're setting copy strategy for a product launch, relaunch or ad refresh and need to know which kind of hook is viable.
steps: Clueless stage (nobody knows the category): You must create the marketing wave. Lead with the related pain or symptom the audience already feels, not the category term. Clemens' 2013-14 probiotic ads opened on digestive health.

Curious stage (audience knows the term but not the detail): You can 'jump right' in and use a counter-intuitive hook that presumes knowledge. His 2018 headline: 'Doctor says throw your probiotics in the trash' — it only works because the reader already believes probiotics are good, then the page explains most probiotics lack the right strains and that prebiotics matter.

Saturated stage (category commoditised): Clemens says the probiotic market is here now and he is not launching new probiotics; at conferences he tells would-be entrants 'good luck'. Breakthrough still happens, but requires a strong campaign rather than category education.
caveats: These three stages are Clemens' own heuristic from his Twitter thread, not a measured formula; validate against your own search and survey data.
The stage can be different for your sub-niche than for the whole category.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Read Your Market Stage Off Branded Search Trends
cards.summary: Category-level search curves show when education campaigns are creating demand and when the market matures.
cards.use_when: You want evidence of whether your category is clueless, curious or saturated before committing to messaging or spend.
steps: Track the category search term (e.g. 'probiotics') over years, not months, and overlay your brand and spokesperson terms.

Clemens notes the category trend visibly spiked after their education-led campaign, dropped the day they were kicked off Google, then recovered with the next brand — and spiked again when Dr. Gundry campaigns ran, with 'Gundry' searches rising on days campaigns were strongest.

If your brand or spokesperson term tracks the campaign bursts, your education is creating the category wave; if the category curve is flat or above your brand's, buyer knowledge already exists and you can use 'curious'-stage hooks.

Historical analogue: he points to cigarette search-interest spiking after the Easter Day parade and VW Beetle after 'Think Small' — attribution caveat aside, the pattern is demand created by campaigns.
caveats: Search interest is a proxy for attention, not sales; cross-check with revenue and new-customer data.
Attribution between campaign and trend cannot be proven from the curve alone.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Pick the Awareness Stage, Then Choose the Headline Type
cards.summary: Match your headline to what the reader already knows: symptom-first for unaware buyers, contrarian category-claim for aware buyers.
cards.use_when: You're choosing between a problem-led and a contrarian headline on a PDP, advertorial or landing page.
steps: For unaware audiences: use a symptom or consequence headline that presumes nothing about your category, then teach. Clemens used 'digestive health' framing in early probiotic ads.

For aware audiences: use a pattern-interrupt that contradicts a belief they already hold — 'throw your probiotics in the trash' — and deliver the counter-explanation on the page (not enough strains, prebiotics matter, etc.).
The contrarian headline only converts if the reader has a prior belief to disrupt; on a clueless audience it reads as nonsense.
Keep the proof and dream elements of the seven hijacks after the headline: the page still needs demonstration, believable proof and a vivid outcome.
caveats: Clemens' examples are his own campaigns; timing and performance aren't transferable as benchmarks.
Contrarian claims may be scrutinised by ad platforms and regulators — keep them defensible.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: Turn the Buying Ritual Into a Daily Habit Hook
cards.summary: Attach your product to a behaviour the customer already performs each day, or give them a new daily ritual, so repeat use and retention follow.
cards.use_when: You're designing the offer, bundle or PDP benefit copy for a consumable or supplement and want repeat purchase built into the message.
steps: Identify an existing daily moment you can bolt onto — Clemens cites Bulletproof-style 'add this to your coffee', or swapping a light breakfast for a hearty one.
Alternatively create the ritual: for probiotics the strategy was to encourage taking something every day, which also builds the replenishment/subscription habit.
Write the PDP and ad copy around that moment ('add it to your morning coffee', 'take it with breakfast') rather than around the product alone.
Support the habit with a fulfilment and replenishment design that matches the daily cadence — subscribe-and-save intervals, reminders, pack sizes that fit the ritual.
caveats: Daily-use positioning raises regulatory and substantiation requirements for supplement-type claims.
Habit framing works best for products genuinely consumed daily; forcing it on occasional-use products can feel dishonest.
cards.source_name: Psychological Tricks I Used To Sell $1 Billion in Products Online - Craig Clemens.docx

cards.title: GA4 Purchase Journey Funnel Audit and Benchmarks
