For each bundle, state exactly what is included and the monetary saving versus eligible individual items. Do the calculation for the shopper rather than making them compare prices mentally.
Place relevant trust support near the selection and CTA: authentic reviews, delivery or returns information, genuine guarantees, compatibility guidance, and payment details where applicable.

Avoid a full-page refresh solely to confirm an add-to-cart action. The source considers this disruptive to conversion. Instead, use a clear current-platform-supported confirmation such as an updating cart drawer or unobtrusive cart state.
Use the cart drawer or cart surface to offer genuinely complementary cross-sells and upsells, not unrelated products. Preserve a fast, obvious route to checkout.
Measure add-to-cart rate, cart-to-checkout progression, average order value, and purchase conversion after changes; a larger cart is not valuable if checkout completion falls.
caveats: The source describes repeated A/B-testing experience but does not provide universal result figures; validate the flow on your own storefront and devices.
Verify current theme and platform behavior before implementing asynchronous cart or drawer logic.
cards.source_name: The Only Landing Page Guide You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Structure a Complete Ecommerce Landing Page Around Decisions
cards.summary: Organize campaign and product landing pages so each section resolves the next shopper uncertainty: relevance, product choice, proof, differentiation, use, risk, and purchase.
cards.use_when: Planning a long-form product landing page, bundle campaign, or collection page that must educate and sell without becoming a generic lead-generation page.
steps: Start with a hero matched to awareness: communicate the relevant benefit, introduce the product, expose product or bundle selection for high-intent traffic, and add immediate trust cues.
Follow with the most important decision support: problem-and-solution education for lower-awareness traffic, or social proof and product comparison for solution-aware visitors.
Use benefit-first value-proposition sections to explain why the product’s attributes matter. Insert authentic proof between critical claims rather than isolating reviews in one distant block.
Add a comparison table if shoppers must choose between formats, bundles, or alternatives. Then show a short how-it-works or routine section that clarifies adoption.
Address risk with factual fulfillment, returns, compatibility, ingredient or material, and guarantee information where such a guarantee genuinely exists.

Close with a concise benefit recap, visible product selection or add-to-cart path, real proof, and expectation-setting bullets such as what is included, delivery information, and any valid returns terms.
Build FAQs from recurring pre-purchase questions in support tickets, reviews, on-site search, and customer research.
caveats: The source’s original full-page sequence was designed largely for service lead generation. Ecommerce pages should prioritize product selection, cart mechanics, and purchase objections rather than forms.
Change section order by traffic awareness and product complexity; do not treat this as a mandatory template.
cards.source_name: The Only Landing Page Guide You'll Ever Need.docx

cards.title: Advertorial placement in the funnel
cards.summary: Insert a pre-sell advertorial page between cold prospecting ads and the offer/checkout page to educate and build desire before asking for a sale.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to route paid social or paid search traffic that converts poorly when sent straight to a PDP or offer page.
steps: Place cold prospecting ads that send clicks to an advertorial, then the advertorial CTAs to an offer page, then into cart or checkout.
Diagnose slow-converting traffic: when ad costs rise and competition increases, consumers are less willing to buy immediately, so a straight ad-to-PDP flow may leak money.
Treat the advertorial as a pre-sell layer whose job is education and desire-building, not direct hard-sell.
Do not obsess only over the ad creative and the product page — the source argues the gap between them (the pre-sell page) is where most funnels underperform.
Map the funnel end-to-end so the advertorial's CTA matches the next page (offer page or checkout) rather than competing with it.
caveats: The source's claimed revenue lifts (25%–110% YoY for brands it worked with) are case examples from an agency, not a benchmark you should assume.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: The seven-section advertorial architecture
cards.summary: Sequence advertorials as hook/trust above the fold, skimmable listicle, origin story and unique mechanism, proof story plus social proof, risk reversal, two-options close, and a final CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing or restructuring the section order of an advertorial or long-form pre-sell landing page.
steps: Above the fold: lead with a hook that opens on a pain point, build trust, and introduce the product.
Listicle: give a skimmable '5 reasons why' block so scanners can absorb the value fast.
Origin story and unique mechanism: explain how the product was created, then name and detail the differentiating mechanism plus features.
Proof story and social proof: present a narrative testimonial plus a stack of shorter proof. Introduce features translated into consumer benefits.
Risk reversal: add the money-back guarantee and address purchase risk directly.
Two-options close: present 'keep doing what you do' versus 'try this risk-free,' then a final CTA.
Reinforce with repeated CTAs: at least one mid-page CTA after risk reversal, plus CTAs after social proof and at the end.
caveats: This is one high-performing structure, not a mandatory template; adapt section order to your product's buying cycle.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Hit the pain threshold, not just a pain point
cards.summary: Stack pain points aggressively until the reader's emotional pain threshold is crossed and they are compelled to act.
cards.use_when: Writing advertorial or PDP copy that agitates a problem but still fails to convert readers who acknowledge the issue.
steps: Accept that awareness of a problem is not enough: people tolerate pain (e.g., someone overweight who doesn't diet) until it exceeds their personal threshold.
Identify the reader's specific embarrassments and frustrations (e.g., dreaded slices, mishits, embarrassment on the course, wasting money on training aids that don't work).
Layer these into the copy repeatedly rather than mentioning each once — the source stacks the same handful of pain points throughout the page in different framings.
Alternate pain with a desired state, then position the product as the bridge between current state and desired state.
Recall the selling principle: create separation between where the prospect is and where they want to be, and frame the product as the vehicle.
caveats: The 'pain threshold' framing comes from Tony Robbins as cited by the presenter; over-agitation can damage trust for premium or repeat-purchase audiences.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Name and repeat a unique mechanism
cards.summary: Define a specific, named mechanism explaining why the product works when past solutions failed, and reference it throughout the page.
cards.use_when: Selling a product in a category where buyers have tried several competing solutions and are skeptical they'll work.
steps: Name the differentiating feature or technology as a coined phrase (e.g., 'fear-based feedback' swing trainer).
Use that name consistently in the hook, listicle, feature section, proof, and CTA so it becomes the anchor of the whole page.
Contrast against failed alternatives: traditional training aids 'don't provide instant feedback,' so buyers get repeated slices and hooks.
Explain the mechanism's origin — a story of consulting engineers, coaches and instructors, studying what didn't work, and iterating (e.g., nearly two years to perfect).
Tie the mechanism directly to the buyer's desired outcome (club-face control, flush contact, fewer mishits).
caveats: The mechanism must be substantiated; an invented technology claim can create legal and refund risk.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Map pain points and desires before writing
cards.summary: List the 3–5 dominant customer pains and desires up front, then repeat that same set throughout the page in different formats.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write an advertorial or long-form product page and needing a repeatable messaging spine.
steps: Write down the customer's core pain points (e.g., mishits, embarrassment, complexity) and core desires (e.g., confidence, consistency, enjoyment, fast results).
Keep the list short — the source reuses roughly 3–5 items rather than introducing new themes.
Deliver the same items through multiple formats: a skimmable listicle, a point-of-view customer story, feature descriptions, and social proof.
Cycle the pattern: pain point → desire → unique mechanism, repeated across the page.
Before publishing, count how many times each core pain and desire appears — if one is missing from a section, add it.
caveats: Repetition is deliberate in this format; on short or premium pages the same density can read as pushy.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Order testimonials against specific objections
cards.summary: Structure social proof so each testimonial systematically dismantles one specific buying objection instead of offering generic praise.
cards.use_when: Building the social-proof section of an advertorial, PDP, or offer page where testimonials feel interchangeable and weak.
steps: List the top 3–5 objections buyers raise before purchase (e.g., 'will this fix my hand position?', 'is it comfortable?', 'does it work fast?').
Select or elicit a testimonial that directly answers each objection, one testimonial per objection.
Make the testimonial name the objection implicitly and show the resolution (e.g., 'the square head helped me finally get the correct feel without guessing').
Place the proof stack after the risk-reversal/first CTA where the reader is close to deciding, then follow with another CTA.
Avoid random praise testimonials — the source argues unstructured social proof leaves objections unresolved.
caveats: Do not fabricate or edit testimonials to fit objections; source-stated testimonials should reflect real customer feedback.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Deploy risk reversals to remove purchase friction
cards.summary: State a strong, low-friction guarantee — extended money-back terms, no-hoops, no questions asked — to eliminate the perceived risk of buying.
cards.use_when: Designing the guarantee and risk-reversal section of an advertorial, offer page, or PDP for a considered-purchase product.
steps: State the guarantee plainly: 'you either love it or you get your money back, no questions asked,' with zero hard feelings, no receipts, and no annoying hoops.
Use a long, extended window (the source example offers up to one full year) to reduce buyer hesitation.
Position the guarantee as evidence of the company's confidence in the product rather than a legal disclaimer.
Pair the guarantee with the current promotion terms (e.g., 50% off and free shipping) so the deal and the risk reversal reinforce each other.
Follow the risk reversal with a CTA that leads with scarcity framing (see the availability-framed CTA card).
caveats: Extended, no-questions guarantees increase refund exposure; ensure operations and margins can absorb the returns policy you advertise.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Frame CTAs as checking availability, not 'buy now'
cards.summary: Replace pushy 'buy now' buttons with scarcity-framed CTAs like 'apply discount / check availability' to reduce resistance.
cards.use_when: Writing advertorial or offer-page CTA copy where a hard-sell button would feel too aggressive for the audience.
steps: Write the CTA as an action that implies demand and limited supply — 'apply discount, check availability' style framing.
Place the first CTA immediately after the risk-reversal section, then repeat CTAs after social proof and near the close.
Reinforce the scarcity with a credible mechanism: a special new-customer offer (e.g., 50% off and free shipping) available only to people who act on this page today.
Add a close-side scarcity line: if they leave the page, the deal is only available at the regular full price on the brand's site.
Ensure the CTA's scarcity claim is truthful and consistent with the actual checkout offer.
caveats: Fabricated scarcity or fake deadlines are misleading and erode trust; only use scarcity the brand will honor.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Write the 'two options' close
cards.summary: Close by laying out a stay-the-course option versus a risk-free product option, then let the reader conclude the product is the better choice.
cards.use_when: Finishing the close of an advertorial or long-form offer page after the reader has seen the proof and guarantee.
steps: Give the reader an explicit way out: option one is to leave the page and keep using current methods (e.g., expensive brand-name trainers or cheap alternatives with the same design flaws).
Detail option two: try the product risk-free, as thousands of other buyers already have, backed by the money-back guarantee.
Use the reader's position as evidence — reaching the bottom of the page means they are ready to try something new.
Frame the decision as self-trust and an easy comparison rather than a command to purchase.
Restate the offer and guarantee one final time next to the closing CTA so no relevant detail is left for the reader to remember.
caveats: The close assumes the reader has already absorbed the earlier proof; placing it without that groundwork undermines it.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Use a point-of-view proof story with before/after arc
cards.summary: Run a long narrative customer story that starts with skepticism, records quick early results, and escalates to a transformed outcome.
cards.use_when: Writing the proof-story section of an advertorial where a short testimonial lacks persuasive depth.
steps: Open with the customer's low expectations ('I didn't expect any difference yet, nothing works after one round').
Record specific early results within the first use (e.g., 'saved four to five shots in my first round' — a modest, credible claim rather than an exaggerated one).
Escalate the narrative through time: first session, first round, first month, and sustained use.
Include third-party validation inside the story — compliments from friends, the club pro assuming the customer took lessons.
Anchor the story in a recurring routine so it reads as ongoing (using the trainer every practice session, hitting at home at night).
Keep the story credible by admitting imperfection ('I still had two or three misses') before describing the improvement.
caveats: The source's specific numbers are fictional/illustrative advertorial copy; real customer stories should reflect actual results.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Build a fast proof-of-results claim
cards.summary: Reduce time-to-result claims to the first use or first round and quantify cumulative user volume to imply reliability.
cards.use_when: Writing the results section of an advertorial or PDP for a product whose benefit normally takes weeks.
steps: State that noticeable results appear in the very first use (e.g., first swing, first round) to collapse the perceived time cost.
Quantify the installed base to imply reliability: the source cites over 33,000 golfers who eliminated fat shots and mishits since testing in 2023.
Suggest a concrete tracking behavior so the buyer believes in the result: keep track of fairways and greens and watch the score improve.
State a specific improvement quantity (e.g., saving four to six strokes on the first round) paired with an honest acknowledgment that some misses remain.
Follow the claim with the guarantee to reduce the risk of trying under a 'results or you don't pay' framing.
caveats: Only cite user counts and outcome ranges the brand can substantiate; fabricated volume and results claims carry legal risk.
cards.source_name: The ultimate Advertorial Blueprint to scale past $1m_month.docx

cards.title: Advertorial input-prep: strip the sales page into a clean text PDF once
cards.summary: Convert the sales page or sales letter you want advertorials for into an image-free PDF so it can be attached to AI prompts as the source of truth.
cards.use_when: You are about to produce advertorials (pre-sell articles) for a product page and need a reusable source document of the sales copy.
steps: Open the live landing page or sales letter you want advertorials to feed into.
Copy the main body copy, then paste into a Google Doc using paste-as-plain-text (Command/Ctrl+Shift+V) so styling and images don't come along.
Expand and copy the FAQ accordions — the presenter calls these valuable because objection answers are already written there.
Copy several testimonials (name plus quote) so the model has real social proof to reuse rather than inventing it.
Export the doc as PDF. This becomes the single attachment you re-use for every advertorial on that product.
Store the page URL at the top of the doc for reference.
Note that this prep is a one-time cost per product; all later advertorials reuse the same PDF.
caveats: Pasting without plain-text mode drags in HTML/images that break the AI attachment.
Short ecommerce pages will produce thin input — accept that and let the model fill gaps, then edit those gaps by hand.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Extract the sales-page input set before writing any advertorial
cards.summary: Run a fixed question battery against the sales-page PDF to pull target market, pain points, promises, proof, common failed solutions, real culprit, product facts and ingredients into one reusable doc.
cards.use_when: Product selection and messaging: you are preparing to write advertorials or ad angles and need the raw claims and audience material extracted first.
steps: Attach the image-free sales-page PDF and ask for: target market, market problems/pain points, and primary promises made.
Ask next for credible proof (universities, person's reference) and social proof (X number of people). If the page has none, note 'didn't have it for this page' and continue — don't stop the process.
Ask for common solutions mentioned in the sales letter plus why each isn't the real answer (e.g. strict keto, keto flu, exogenous ketones, fasting, excessive exercise).
Ask what the page names as the real culprit/mechanism, and the product description without naming the product, plus product name, how to consume, price and any exclusive price.
Ask for testimonials and for the ingredient list in a clean format.
Paste every output into one living 'inputs' document. This is what makes later advertorial runs fast and lets you skip re-analysis.
Correct anything the model invents if your brand page actually states the fact (e.g. real pricing).
caveats: On short ecommerce pages the model may say a section doesn't exist — that's expected; move on.
Treat extracted claims as raw material; you still own the accuracy check.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Split one broad product into avatar archetypes for advertorial variants
cards.summary: Ask the model to propose several audience archetypes from the extracted market data so each advertorial speaks to one specific segment instead of everyone.
cards.use_when: Product selection and creative strategy: you want multiple advertorial versions to test against different cold-traffic segments for the same product.
steps: After pulling target market and pain points, tell the model you'll write several advertorials and that speaking to everyone will underperform.

Ask it to propose avatar archetypes grounded only in the data you pulled, and state explicit constraints where you know the market (the presenter added: assume the market skews heavily female because the weight-loss market typically does).

Typical archetypes the model returned for a keto weight-loss product: busy working mom (20s–40s juggling work and family), post-pregnancy weight struggler (new mom 20s–late 30s), peri-menopausal woman (40s–50s, body change/fat gain/energy drop), yo-yo dieter, keto-conscious health enthusiast, post-retirement weight gainer.
Ask for more archetypes if you need more variants (the presenter asked for roughly 10).
For each archetype, write one parallel advertorial with matching demographic and psychographic experience.
Use the archetype list as your test matrix so creative variants differ by audience, not just by headline.
caveats: These archetypes are source-specific examples generated for one supplement, not a validated segmentation — validate against your own customer data.
Implied claims (menopause, post-pregnancy) need compliance review in many categories.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Find live advertorial swipe structures to model
cards.summary: Collect real advertorials from mainstream sites and spy tools to use as structural templates before writing.
cards.use_when: Creative strategy: you need proven advertorial structures to model your ecommerce advertorial on.
steps: Visit mainstream content sites — the presenter uses weather.com — and look in the sponsored content slots for advertorials.
Click a sponsored piece to see whether it leads to a long-form text advertorial or straight to a video sales letter (VSL).
Log which destination each uses; the presenter notes many advertisers go to advertorials, some go straight to VSL.
Also look in spy tools and simply browse sites you already read to spot advertorials in the wild.
Choose a swipe whose spokesperson type matches your brand's credibility (e.g. don't model a doctor-fronted advertorial if your brand has no doctor).
Feed one chosen swipe to the AI with the instruction to analyze its structure before writing anything new.
caveats: Swipe structures are templates for format and flow, not permission to copy claims, names or brand facts.
The presenter explicitly said he would not share one doctor-fronted swipe he used as a teaching example.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Advertorial architecture: the repeating section skeleton
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer the standard advertorial flow — problem story, failed solutions, discovery, mechanism, product reveal, proof, CTA — and reproduce it for your product.
cards.use_when: Landing-page and advertorial writing: you are drafting or reviewing an advertorial draft and need the structural spine it should follow.
steps: Identify the headline plus the subhead that functions as the reader's personal problem statement — the presenter maps 'my dog Daisy was slowing down, I was scared of losing her' to the 'I was drowning in mom guilt and stubborn baby weight' line.
Story: relatable protagonist with the avatar's problem and the daily life that makes it hard.
Failed solutions: list what the person tried (counting calories, intense workouts, hormone replacement therapy, strict keto/macros/meal prep) and why each failed.
Discovery: the article, expert or research that reframed the problem — ideally explains why the old approach was never going to work (e.g. even small amounts of carbs kick you out of ketosis).
Mechanism and product: name the supplement/drink and explain the blend that delivers the result plus how to consume it and the taste experience.
Proof: studies and testimonials, then a risk-free CTA and a link to the offer.
Write the advertorial section by section, telling the model to ask you to continue at each output limit rather than condensing, because effective direct response is usually longer.
caveats: The mechanism explanation is where hallucination risk is highest — verify any ingredient or biological claim before publishing.
Structure example comes from supplement advertorials; adapt section order for other categories.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Prompt pattern: model a new advertorial on a swipe plus your input doc
cards.summary: Combine an unrelated advertorial swipe, the extracted sales-page inputs and a chosen avatar into one prompt that produces a full draft in the swipe's style.
cards.use_when: PDP/landing-page work: you need a complete advertorial draft for a specific avatar written fast, in the style of a proven example.
steps: Attach the swipe advertorial and first ask the model to 'analyze the structure' — the presenter says this deliberate step primes the model on what an advertorial should look like.
Then instruct: write a new advertorial for [your product], follow the example advertorial page and its style and tone, base it on the sales page you reviewed, and match the named avatar archetype.
Add tone notes: match the example's sound, find a good blend of storytelling and news-article reporting.
Add a length note: take your time, go section by section, ask me to continue when you run out of space, and do not condense to conserve output.
If you're running the process a second time later, skip re-analysis and instead paste your saved input document plus the archetype into the prompt.
Review the output and correct placeholder specifics — real testimonials, real price, real flavor details — before it goes live.
caveats: The workflow assumes you keep the inputs document; without it you must re-run the extraction prompts.
Named experts, studies and testimonials produced by the model are often invented — the presenter flagged a doctor name it inserted that wasn't associated with the brand.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Scrub hallucinated spokespeople, studies and prices from AI drafts
cards.summary: Treat every named person, study citation, price and testimonial in an AI advertorial as unverified until checked against the real offer.
cards.use_when: Pre-publish QA on any AI-drafted advertorial or ad before it goes to the offer page.
steps: Flag any named doctor or expert. In the demo the model invented 'Dr Ryan Shelton'; the fix was to tell it to say the article came from 'an expert' or 'a world-renowned expert in holistic medicine and weight loss' without naming anyone.
If the real page has no doctor, tell the model not to use a doctor spokesperson at all and to leverage brand credibility or general experts instead.
Flag study citations — the model produced several 'clinical studies'; the presenter says you would want to look them up and make sure they're legit, and you can remove them entirely if not.
Flag prices and testimonials: the demo output did not match the actual page. If it's your brand you can fill in the true values up front; otherwise replace with real ones from the site.
Where your brand genuinely has studies (the presenter notes nutraceutical brands often do), you can supply them so the model doesn't fabricate.
Keep the advertorial clearly labeled as an advertisement/sponsored content at the top, as real advertorials do.
caveats: The presenter states plainly that hallucinations will occur, especially on short pages with little detail.
Regulatory exposure for health and weight-loss claims is high; this is editing guidance, not a compliance review.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Vary the swipe template as well as the avatar
cards.summary: Produce more advertorial variants by swapping the structural swipe (e.g. a doctor-fronted one) in addition to swapping the avatar.
cards.use_when: Creative testing at scale: you need a larger batch of distinct advertorial variants for one product to feed cold traffic.
steps: Hold the input document constant; change one variable at a time — avatar or swipe template.
For a second batch, attach a different advertorial example and repeat the analyze-structure step before writing.
Keep the same product and avatar to isolate the effect of format, or change avatar while holding format to isolate audience effect.
When the new swipe relies on credibility you don't have (a named doctor), substitute brand credibility or 'leading health and weight-loss experts' in the instructions.
The presenter produced three finished advertorials for one product in roughly 47 minutes including explanation, and estimates 5–10 per hour once the process is known.
Collect 10–20 advertorials produced this way as a test batch rather than shipping a single one.
caveats: Batch size is the presenter's own throughput estimate, not a performance benchmark; results depend on editing quality.
Don't model a format whose required assets (spokesperson type, video) you can't actually produce.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Advertorial as pre-sell between ad and offer
cards.summary: Use an advertorial when the destination page alone can't carry a cold reader, especially for short ecommerce pages or as a bridge to a long-form sales letter.
cards.use_when: Funnel architecture: deciding whether cold traffic should hit your ecommerce page directly or be routed through an advertorial first.
steps: Assess whether your page supplies enough information for a cold reader to buy. The presenter's example: sending a supplement buyer email straight to a short keto product page isn't enough information to sell, so it probably wouldn't convert well.
If the page is short-form ecommerce, slot an advertorial in front of it to do the pre-selling.
If you have a long-form sales letter, use the advertorial as an intermediary between the ad and the letter.
Understand that advertorials are structured as sponsored articles — the presenter calls them 'fake articles' labeled as ads — and have been used in direct response for about a century.
Keep the advertorial's labels and claims consistent with the destination page so the reader isn't surprised at the switch.
Route the advertorial CTA to either the ecommerce page or a video/long-form letter depending on where you intend to close.
caveats: The presenter's converting/not-converting statements are his expectation, not a measured benchmark.
Readers who feel tricked by an ad that reads as editorial can damage brand trust — label sponsorship clearly.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Keep a running outputs doc so later advertorial runs skip re-analysis
cards.summary: Persist the extracted inputs and each finished advertorial in a project document so future runs only need the swipe, the inputs and a new avatar.
cards.use_when: Landing-page production planning: you'll write advertorials for the same product repeatedly over weeks or months.
steps: Create a project doc holding the source page URL, the input-run outputs, and each finished advertorial labeled by number and avatar.
Also store alternative headline lists per advertorial — the presenter asked for extra headline options after each draft.
Save the swipe files you modeled on (or at least links), since each batch may use a different one.
When returning later, paste the inputs you previously pulled into the new prompt instead of re-attaching and re-analyzing the sales page.

Note which model/plan you used; the demo ran out of messages on Claude 3 and the presenter suggests a paid tier (~$20/month at the time) or switching models to keep writing. Verify the current interface and pricing before relying on this.
Format the final drafts for the destination (strip stray heading markers, set CTA links) before publishing.
caveats: Tool names, model versions, message limits and prices change — verify the current interface.
The presenter's paid-plan and pricing details were accurate only as of recording.
cards.source_name: Using Claude to Write 10 Advertorials in An Hou.docx

cards.title: Quiz funnels work by emotionally priming, not just personalizing
cards.summary: The real conversion power of a quiz funnel is putting cold traffic into an emotionally primed, suggestible state through micro-commitments before the offer appears.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to insert a quiz between paid ad traffic and your PDP/sales page, or defending the extra step to stakeholders who think it only adds friction.
steps: Reframe what the quiz is for: the source argues quizzes convert cold traffic mainly because the sequence of small yeses and selections creates an emotionally primed, suggestible state, not merely because it routes users to a 'matching' product.
Contrast architectures: a direct ad-to-PDP flow asks for the purchase immediately, while a quiz spends several interactions warming the visitor before the offer is shown.
Treat the finished quiz as the top of a two-stage funnel: the quiz's job is to prime and capture, and the sales page/PDP's job is to close the already-warmed visitor.
Use the quiz where cold traffic exists and the offer benefits from belief change; the source describes this as a time-limited funnel format, not a permanent universal law.
caveats: The source's $1M+/month figures are his own claim and an example, not a guaranteed result.
The source calls quiz funnels a limited window of opportunity; verify current saturation and platform norms before betting your whole acquisition budget on it.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Every quiz question must commit, seed, or pre-handle
cards.summary: Each question in a quiz funnel should serve one of three jobs: earn a micro-commitment, seed a buying belief, or pre-handle a sales objection.
cards.use_when: Auditing or writing quiz questions before you build the funnel, so you don't pad it with questions that only create drop-off.
steps: Label each planned question with the job it does: micro-commitment (a small yes/selection that moves the visitor toward purchase), seeding (subconsciously installing a belief the buyer needs), or pre-handling an objection (neutralizing a reason not to buy before the offer appears).
Delete or rewrite any question that doesn't clearly do one of the three jobs — the source says questions included just for the sake of it aren't worth the drop-off.
Sequence so questions alternate between the three jobs rather than clustering many pure micro-commitment clicks in a row.

For seeding, identify the beliefs your buyer must hold to purchase (e.g., 'my gut issue hurts every part of my life') and design questions that reinforce those beliefs rather than merely collecting data.
For pre-handling, place the objection-neutralizing question before the offer (e.g., asking how quickly they expect results to defuse 'it takes too long').
caveats: The three-function framework is the source's own heuristic, not an industry-standard rule.
Seeding and pre-handling still require real customer research to know which beliefs and objections matter — guessing can install the wrong belief.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Keep product-quiz steps easy and visibly responsive
cards.summary: Reduce interaction effort while collecting meaningful product preferences.
cards.use_when: Designing the interaction pattern and answer controls for a quiz funnel that feeds a Shopify PDP.
steps: Ask one useful product-selection question at a time.
Use the control appropriate to the answer; the source suggests avoiding more than two or three repeated formats, a heuristic to test.
Give clear visual feedback when an option is selected.
Measure completion and downstream purchase quality; omit questions that only manufacture agreement.
caveats: The 'hypnotic' framing is the source's metaphor; the practical takeaway is lower per-step effort and varied interaction.
Too much visual gimmickry can slow load time, which itself causes drop-off.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Gradualization: start non-invasive, escalate slowly
cards.summary: Open with questions that are easy and non-personal, then gradually build toward more invasive questions to protect completion.
cards.use_when: Ordering quiz questions, especially when targeting demographics where direct personal questions (age, weight, body issues) would feel rude or intrusive.
steps: Attribute the concept: Eugene Schwartz called it 'gradualization' — begin with the least invasive question and climb.
Make question one your least invasive and arguably most important question (often a goal or motivation question) rather than an age, weight, or health-detail question.
Treat questions that break social norms (e.g., asking an older woman her age directly) as high-risk; the source notes these should be avoided or approached obliquely.
Place demographic and personal-detail questions (age, height, weight target) later in the quiz, after the visitor is invested.
If a personal question is genuinely needed, consider whether it can be reframed as a lower-friction selection.
caveats: No fixed rule for how many questions before you escalate; the source only gives the principle, not a threshold.
Escalation is not permission to include invasive questions that don't serve one of the three core jobs.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Seed buying beliefs through reframing questions
cards.summary: Use quiz questions to reframe a symptom as a serious quality-of-life problem, installing the belief that underpins the purchase.
cards.use_when: Writing quiz questions for a health or problem-solving product where the buyer needs to believe the problem is serious before they'll buy.
steps: Treat marketing as a belief-change game: your job is to move the customer's existing beliefs toward the beliefs that make buying rational.
Identify the specific belief required to buy (e.g., 'gut issues affect my mood, focus, and energy' rather than being a minor annoyance).
Build a question that surfaces or reinforces that belief, such as a 1–10 slider measuring how much the symptom affects daily life — the act of answering reframes it as significant.
Use the beliefs doc from customer research to know which belief to seed, rather than picking questions at random or copying a competitor's quiz wholesale.
Ensure the seeded belief connects to your product's mechanism so the eventual PDP feels like the logical next step.
caveats: Seeding by exaggeration risks mismatched expectations and refunds; keep the reframe defensible.
The source's gut-health examples are illustrative — the belief you seed depends on your own product and research.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Pre-handle objections inside the quiz, before the offer
cards.summary: Ask questions that neutralize common objections (like 'results take too long') so the objection is defused before the sales page is ever shown.
cards.use_when: Preparing quiz questions for a product with well-known objections (time-to-results, 'I've tried everything', ingredients).
steps: List your top purchase objections, typically surfaced through customer research.

Convert each into a low-friction quiz question or 'intra-quiz card' placed before the final offer — e.g., 'How quickly do you expect to feel results?' to pre-handle the 'takes too long' objection, or 'What's been your most frustrating experience with products like this?' to pre-handle 'I've tried everything'.
Use interstitial cards inside the quiz to directly overcome beliefs and objections, getting the visitor one step closer to the sale.
Keep the objection-handling content available on the sales page too (e.g., in the FAQ) so it's reinforced, but the source positions the quiz as where it's pre-emptively handled.
Attribute the underlying principle to sales/copywriting: strong copywriters handle objections before the offer appears rather than only after.
caveats: The source says the underlying pre-handling idea comes from a sales mentor and copywriting practice — treat it as a proven-in-context technique, not a guaranteed lift.
Objections you pre-handle must be real customer objections, not assumptions; research first.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Avoid input questions unless deliberately adding friction
cards.summary: Typing answers has far higher perceived effort than tapping choices and causes heavy drop-off, so reserve input questions for deliberate buyer qualification.
cards.use_when: Choosing answer-control types for quiz questions, or deciding whether to keep a free-text question in an existing quiz.
steps: Default to multiple-choice, selector, slider, or yes/no controls for all quiz questions.
Recognize that free-text/input questions carry much higher perceived effort than tapping a button and are a common source of large drop-off, even in an otherwise strong quiz.
The source flags his own 'most frustrating experience' input question as something he would change — use that as an example of the trade-off rather than a model.
If you want to qualify buyers with friction, add input questions intentionally and sparingly; the source advises launching with minimal friction first, then adding qualifying friction later.
Confirm the question's job: if a free-text answer isn't essential to a core function, replace it with a selection control.
caveats: The source does not forbid input questions — he frames them as a deliberate friction tool, not a default.
Perceived-effort claims are the source's observation, not a measured benchmark across niches.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Target a ~30% quiz completion rate and diagnose per-question drop-off
cards.summary: Aim for roughly 30% of starters finishing the quiz, and use per-question drop-off data to find and fix the questions costing you the most.
cards.use_when: Setting performance benchmarks for a quiz funnel and reviewing its analytics after launch to optimize completion.
steps: Set the completion-rate KPI at approximately 30% (starters reaching the sales page); the source treats ~25% as still quite good and admits 30% at scale is difficult.
Expect some drop-off on every question (the source says at least ~1%), so don't panic at low single-digit drop-offs.
Look across per-question drop-off for a spike above the baseline (his illustrative pattern is roughly 1–2% per question with one outlier higher), and lock in on that question.
For the spike question, either find a less invasive way to ask it, or remove it entirely — unless it is deliberately adding qualifying friction.
Launch with minimal friction to prove the quiz works, then add friction that qualifies the buyer once you have data.
Note the format is only a lever: the source claims adding even a three-question quiz before a sales page increased conversion in his experience.
caveats: 30% is the source's heuristics/goal, not a calculated industry benchmark; treat it as a target band, not a pass/fail line.
The 'adding a quiz always increases conversion' claim is his experience — he calls it not an absolute.
Per-question drop-off percentages are illustrative examples, not your data.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Size the quiz: 3–20 questions, sweet spot 8–12
cards.summary: There is a point of diminishing returns on quiz length; keep it roughly 3–20 questions, typically 8–12, and cut any question that doesn't earn its place.
cards.use_when: Deciding how long to make a quiz funnel before writing or building it.
steps: Use the source's range of roughly 3 to 20 total questions, with a typical sweet spot of 8 to 12.
Understand the risk: every question compounds drop-off, and at scale a long quiz can become so small a funnel that too few people reach the PDP to buy.
Keep only questions that serve one of the three functions (micro-commitment, seeding, or pre-handling) — the source says questions added just for the sake of it aren't worth it.
Use the lower end (closer to 3) for a simple pre-PDP priming quiz and the middle of the range for belief-change plays that need more seeding.
Revisit length after launch using per-question drop-off data rather than defending your initial count.
caveats: The 3–20 and 8–12 figures are the source's opinion/heuristic, not measured benchmarks.
The right length depends on how much belief change and objection handling your specific offer needs.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Build a quiz with AI on top of foundational customer docs
cards.summary: Generate quiz questions in AI only after uploading an offer doc, avatar doc, research doc, and beliefs doc — then have it analyze a proven example quiz first.
cards.use_when: Drafting quiz questions and copy for a new funnel when you already have (or need to build) customer research assets.
steps: Produce four foundational documents before prompting: an offer doc, an avatar doc, a research doc, and a beliefs doc. The source frames these as the deepest level of understanding of customer, market, and offer, and as the starting point for any funnel copy.
In the AI chat, first establish a context profile: state the copywriter role and offer, then upload the foundational docs and ask the model to gain context on them, with no action steps.
Second, upload screenshots of a proven example quiz (the source uses a high-traffic weight-loss quiz from a health brand) and ask the model only to analyze it and give thoughts — no action steps yet.
Third, give a prompt that includes the three core quiz principles plus execution guidance, and have the model generate your quiz questions.
Review every generated question against the three-function test and against gradualization before using it; the source says question quality depends on research, not on blind copying of top ads.
caveats: Prompt and 'GPT5' interface details may change — verify the current model/UI before relying on the exact workflow.
AI output is a draft; the source stresses that question selection must be grounded in your own market research, not random or blindly swiped.
The source promotes his foundational-docs SOP and agency services; skip the promotional material.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Capture name and email at the end to unlock remarketing and email sequences
cards.summary: Require name and email to receive the personalized quiz result, then follow with a 5–7 email sequence — ideally branched by quiz answers.
cards.use_when: Planning the post-quiz step of a funnel to grow a list and drive purchase via email retention flows.
steps: At the end of the quiz, gate the personalized result behind collecting name and email; the source frames this as the moment visitors are most bought-in.
Treat the follow-up as a 5–7 email sequence designed to bring them to purchase.

For a more advanced build, branch sequences by quiz answers: e.g., visitors who said they reject non-natural ingredients get a sequence on the natural formula, while those who prioritize speed get a different workflow.
Use the captured list for remarketing, which the source highlights as a key upside of the email gate.
Note this is where personalization genuinely pays off — as personalized result and follow-up, not merely as product routing.
caveats: The 5–7 email count is the source's suggestion, not a tested universal cadence; confirm your own send/reply data.
Branching by answer is more operationally complex; the source calls it the 'psycho maniac' version — start simple if list volume or tooling is limited.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Evaluate health niches for quiz funnel inspiration
cards.summary: Look inside the health niche (and similar problem-aware categories) to study high-traffic quiz funnels as models for structure and question sequencing.
cards.use_when: Sourcing quiz funnel examples and structures to adapt for your own store's product category.
steps: Prioritize health and adjacent niches when hunting for quiz funnel examples — the source says these niches are 'roaring' with quiz funnels and produce the models worth studying.
Study the flow rather than copying the offer: observe the opening male/female or goal question, the progression through habits and symptoms, and where yes/no and slider formats switch in.
Track which questions function as seeding (reframing a symptom as a quality-of-life issue) versus pre-handling (expectation questions) versus pure micro-commitment.
Note example scale (e.g., a weight-loss quiz with millions of monthly visits) as context, then verify the pattern fits your own market rather than assuming the same copy will work.
Use the observed structure to brief your own question-writing, adjusted to your product's beliefs and objections.
caveats: A competitor's high traffic is not proof the quiz converts well or will work for your category.
Copying another brand's questions wholesale risks mismatch with your own offer and research.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Treat quiz funnels as a time-limited opportunity, not a permanent channel
cards.summary: The source frames quiz funnels as the current 'funnel architecture' to exploit with urgency, implying you should test and scale quickly rather than wait.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to prioritize building a quiz funnel now versus other acquisition projects, and planning how long to rely on it.
steps: Recognize the source's claim that funnel architectures cycle (e.g., advertorials, VSLs, now quiz funnels), so an effective format can saturate or decline.
Because of that window, prioritize testing the quiz concept on live paid traffic quickly rather than perfecting it indefinitely.
Build the quiz with minimal friction first to prove it works, then refine using completion-rate and per-question drop-off data.
Plan for the format to lose edge over time: keep the underlying assets (foundational docs, list capture, email sequences) that survive an architecture change.
Balance the urgency claim against your own budget and test capacity — it is the source's opinion, not a measured market forecast.
caveats: The 'limited window' and cycle claim is the source's assertion and a promotional framing used to encourage action; do not treat it as a factual market prediction.
Urgency is not a substitute for validating whether a quiz fits your specific offer and traffic.
cards.source_name: how i build quiz funnels that make $1,073,966_mo with branded dropshipping.docx

cards.title: Landing page success is a two-metric game
cards.summary: Judge landing pages only by conversion rate and average order value, not by visual aesthetics.
cards.use_when: Auditing a store's PDP, advertorial or sales page before redesigning it, or deciding whether to ship an ugly-but-fast page.
steps: Stop evaluating a page by design polish. The presenter's claim: only two quantitative metrics matter - conversion rate and average order value. If both are healthy, he will run the ugliest page he can.
Instrument both metrics per page and per funnel step, not just account-level revenue, so you can tell which step is broken.
If the page converts and AOV is strong, leave the aesthetics alone; redirect redesign budget to copy or to AOV steps instead.
If either metric is weak, diagnose in this order: (1) is the copy clear? (2) is the page fast? (3) only then consider design changes.
Treat the marketing 'ugly landers convert better' framing as a claim about the relative weight of copy clarity versus decoration, not as a rule that ugliness causes conversion.
caveats: This is a direct-response marketer's opinion, not a benchmark study; some markets and premium brands legitimately win on perceived quality and design.
AOV only counts if you know your COGS - profit contribution per funnel step is the number that actually funds ad spend.
Pages that are slow or confusing because of broken layout are not 'ugly but clear'.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Sales page, order page, OTO: route traffic through a response funnel instead of a PDP
cards.summary: Replace the ad-to-PDP-to-checkout flow with a Sales Page, Order Page and sequential post-purchase one-time offers.
cards.use_when: Designing or rebuilding the funnel for a high-AOV direct-to-consumer offer, especially where ad traffic currently lands on a standard product detail page.
steps: Map the current flow. Most stores run ad to PDP to checkout and then stop contact after payment. A PDP is built to sell the product; the presenter argues marketing sells the transformation the product produces.

Insert a dedicated sales page between ad and order form. It should sell the outcome, not just the item, and give the visitor context before the ask - the presenter's analogy is that ad-to-PDP is asking a stranger to go home with you on the first line.
Use an order page (not a generic Shopify checkout) so you control quantity breaks and order bumps on the payment step.
Continue selling after payment with OTO1, then OTO2, and route OTO1 declines to a down-sell page instead of stopping.
Optionally consider a pre-sales page (advertorial, listicle, quiz) before the sales page; the source deliberately excludes that from this framework.
Measure drop-off at every step: the biggest leak is usually sales page to order page.
caveats: Requires copywriting skill; a weak sales page adds a step without converting.
The source gives no back-end tooling, platform or compliance guidance for multi-step OTO flows - verify your platform and payment processor support them.
This is a direct-response opinion aimed at high-AOV offers, not a universal structure for every store.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Post-purchase OTOs exploit peak price elasticity
cards.summary: The moment after payment is the most emotional and most price-elastic point in the customer relationship, so put the biggest upsell there.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to charge for an upsell and where in the funnel to place the highest-ticket offer.
steps: Recognize that immediately after a card is accepted the customer is in an elevated emotional state; the source argues most operators waste this by stopping contact after payment.

Exploit high price elasticity at that step: the presenter's heuristic is that OTO1 can be priced at roughly 10x the front-end price (e.g. $500 after a $50 front end) and still contribute AOV. He notes some operators go to $5,000.

Do not optimize for take rate. Optimize AOV or profit contribution for that step: 10% of buyers taking a $500 upsell = $50 added AOV, which doubled a $50 AOV in his worked example; 5% take = $25 added AOV.
Factor COGS into the calculation so you are measuring profit contribution per funnel step, not gross offer price.
Keep selling after OTO1: send buyers to OTO2 and send declines to a down-sell rather than ending the session.
Run this as a deliberate AOV test with a defined measurement window per funnel step.
caveats: The 10x multiple is a source-specific heuristic, not a validated benchmark, and the presenter states it depends on your ability to write copy.
A lower take rate on a high-ticket OTO may still be the better AOV decision - compare contribution, not conversion.
Upsells must be ethically framed and compliant; the source explicitly flags ethics and disclaims legal advice on urgency elsewhere.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Landing pages are copy plus media plus design - only two carry the sale
cards.summary: Break any landing page into copy, media and design; copy is the main lever and design only matters if it adds friction.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend effort when building or improving a product page, advertorial or sales page.
steps: Decompose the page into three parts: copy (the words), media (images, GIFs, video) and design/aesthetics (call-to-action button colour, theme, animations).
Invest first in copy: the presenter argues design questions like button colour or Shopify theme barely matter if the sales message is right and substantiated by good visual assets.
Make media substantiate the copy claim - it exists to prove what the words say, not to decorate.
Attack confusion deliberately: 'a confused mind doesn't buy'. Treat the work as subtraction of confusing elements rather than addition of features.
Prefer an ugly, fast, clear page over a heavy page with animations, huge images and average copy, on the presenter's stated preference.
Watch for design that creates friction - the one case where aesthetics do matter in this framework is when they slow the page or slow comprehension.
caveats: The source's preference for ugly-but-fast is an opinion from direct-response experience, not a test result; premium and design-led brands may need different standards.
Media quality still matters - the claim is about design embellishment, not about ignoring assets.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Voice of Customer: write copy in the customer's words using a four-document research set
cards.summary: Produce a research doc, offer brief, avatar sheet and necessary-belief doc from forums and reviews, then write copy from customer language rather than marketer bias.
cards.use_when: Starting copy, angles or ad creative for a new product, or diagnosing why existing page copy does not resonate.
steps: Gather raw customer language from Reddit threads, forums, YouTube comments, TikTok comments and reviews - their words, not yours. The presenter's core diagnosis is that bad copy usually comes from bad research, and that writing through your own filters creates a disconnect.
Document 1 - Research document: 20 to 60 pages of sourced verbatim customer language covering pains, phrases and previous solutions tried, with resources cited.

Document 2 - Offer brief: turn the research into the selling construction - product name, level of awareness, stage of sophistication, the big idea and the mechanism. Treat these as the fixed ingredients of a copy recipe.
Document 3 - Avatar sheet: demographics, key challenges and pain points, goals and aspirations, emotional drivers, plus a bank of direct quotes for hooks and headlines.
Document 4 - Necessary beliefs: four to six statements beginning 'I believe that' that the customer must hold to buy, derived from the research with no assumptions.
Use AI prompts to compress this process, but verify that outputs are grounded in real harvested quotes before using them in copy.
Feed the researched phrases into headlines, hooks and OTO copy so objections are pre-handled in the customer's own vocabulary.
caveats: The source promotes a specific SOP behind an Instagram DM; the four-document structure is the transferable part.
AI output that is not grounded in real customer text reintroduces marketer bias even if it reads well.
Length (20-60 pages) is the source's own output range and varies with prompting, not a required standard.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Marketing as belief change: define the limiting beliefs you must shift
cards.summary: List the beliefs a visitor currently holds, then design the page to move them from limiting to empowering beliefs.
cards.use_when: Structuring a sales page or ad angle for a skeptical audience, or when conversion stalls despite clear copy.
steps: Write down the beliefs your target customer currently holds about the world, your product category and your brand, sourced from researched customer language rather than assumptions.
Express each as a short 'I believe that...' statement - the source suggests four to six, e.g. 'I believe this brand is safe and transparent' or 'I believe lasting results are worth waiting for'.
Label each one limiting (blocks purchase) or empowering (supports purchase).
Assign each limiting belief to a page element that shifts it: a headline, an embedded testimonial, a mechanism section, an FAQ answer or a credibility block.
Remove or rewrite page content that reinforces a limiting belief, since a confused or distrustful mind does not buy.
Re-check after edits that every belief in your necessary-belief list is addressed somewhere on the page.
caveats: The source's claim that 'marketing is at its core belief change work' is his framing, not an established law.
Belief lists are only as good as the underlying customer research.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Headline checklist: hit three to four of seven to earn the scroll
cards.summary: Score benefit-driven headlines against seven traits and rewrite until at least three or four are present.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the above-the-fold headline on a sales page, advertorial, PDP or ad landing page.
steps: Accept the premise that the first piece of copy is the most important; the source claims roughly 80% of visitors glance and decide within a split second whether to keep scrolling, so a failed headline invalidates the rest of the page.
Score the headline against seven traits: curiosity, calling out the pain point, promising the solution, specificity, simplicity, credibility and a timeframe for results.
Target at least three or four of the seven; the presenter notes that more is often better but not all seven are required.

Test against his worked example: '7-second brain trick. Scientists stunned... with no effort.' It hits curiosity (multiple times), solution promise, specificity ('7-second'), simplicity (12 words) and credibility ('scientists stunned') but never directly calls out the pain point.
Fix a missing trait surgically rather than rewriting: he suggests adding a small eyebrow or pre-headline to call out the pain point and complete the checklist.
Keep the headline only as long as needed for clarity - the source's rule of thumb from copywriters is never make copy longer than necessary, not that short is always better.
Use a benefit-driven framing rather than a feature list.
caveats: The seven traits and the 'three to four' threshold are the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
The 80% drop-off figure is recalled from his experience, not cited data.
A headline can be strong on checklist traits but still fail on audience-message mismatch.

cards.title: Urgency and scarcity: sell time or sell volume, but do it honestly
cards.summary: Use time-based urgency and supply-based scarcity to prompt action, keeping the claims defensible.
cards.use_when: Designing hero banners, offer sections, shipping cut-offs or promo modules on a sales or order page.
steps: Urgency manipulates the perception of time to prompt a purchase. Examples from the source's review of Primal Queen: a sale countdown timer, and an offer-section message that orders placed within X time ship today.

Scarcity centres on volume instead of time - typically 'we may run out of stock'. The source's example reads 'due to high demand... very high risk of selling out', which he presents as ethical positioning that avoids claiming a specific unit count.
Choose which lever fits your operation: shipping cut-off urgency must match your real fulfilment schedule; stock scarcity must reflect real supply constraints.
Use framing hedges ('risk of selling out') rather than fabricated unit counts or permanent fake countdowns; the presenter states fake urgency timers tread a thin line and disclaims legal advice.
Place urgency at the point of decision - the offer block on the order page - and scarcity near the product explanation where it supports the mechanism.
Rotate or stop claims when they stop being true; trust damage is a retention cost, not just a legal one.
caveats: The source explicitly is not providing legal advice; urgency and scarcity claims are regulated in many jurisdictions - check with counsel.
Fake or evergreen timers are called out by the presenter as risky for both legal exposure and customer relationships.
Fabricated inventory claims can breach advertising standards.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Risk reversal: design a guarantee, don't just lengthen one
cards.summary: Make the guarantee remove risk for the buyer rather than compete on duration alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing the guarantee, returns policy or trial offer shown on a sales page or order page.
steps: Start from the purpose: a guarantee is risk reversal, not a badge. Ask what would make the purchase risk-free even if the product fails completely.
Standard option: a money-back window (the source mentions 30, 90 and 365 days as common defaults).
Creative option he cites from the info space: conditional guarantees such as 'if it doesn't work you don't pay', or adding a cash penalty on top of the refund.
Avoid the escalation trap: competing by extending duration (30 days to a year to lifetime) has nowhere to go - he argues creativity in structure beats length.
Match the structure to your actual cost of goods and return behaviour so the guarantee stays affordable at scale.
State the guarantee plainly in the offer block and, where relevant, repeat a short version near the checkout button to reduce last-step hesitation.
caveats: Aggressive guarantee structures can be exploited; model return rates before adopting one.
The source offers no data on how much guarantees lift conversion - treat as a structural principle, not a benchmark.
Consumer law in many regions sets minimum return rights regardless of your policy.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Unique mechanism: explain why everything else failed and yours works
cards.summary: State the specific reason the product works and why prior attempts did not, to make the promise believable.
cards.use_when: Writing the mechanism section of a sales page or the core angle of an ad for a crowded category.
steps: Split the mechanism into two halves: the unique mechanism of the problem (why the customer's problem exists or persists) and the unique mechanism of the solution (why this product resolves it).
Use the source's weight-loss example: a 'fat burn switch' is presented as the biological reason previous diets failed and this product works.
Test the mechanism by asking: does it logically explain why everything the customer tried before didn't work, and why this is different?
Place it after the headline and problem framing, before proof and offer, so the promise has support when the price appears.
Keep it concrete and specific to the product category; avoid generic 'science-backed' language that does not name a causal mechanism.
Carry the same mechanism language into OTO copy so the upsell feels like a continuation rather than a new pitch.
caveats: Mechanism claims must be substantiated to stay compliant; the source gives no regulatory guidance.
The source's example is an illustrative page he pulled up, not a verified clinical claim.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Embedded testimonials pre-handle objections before the FAQ
cards.summary: Place purposeful social proof throughout the page to overcome objections or install an empowering belief.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to put customer reviews and testimonials across a sales page or order page.
steps: Keep a dedicated testimonial or review section, but add embedded testimonials distributed through the page.
Give every embedded testimonial a job - the source's rule is that each should either overcome a specific objection or install an empowering belief. Do not add proof just to fill space.
Map objections first (quality testing, suitability for a specific customer type, results timing), then write or select quotes that answer them.
Place the testimonial near the claim or price it defends, so the objection is dissolved before the visitor consciously forms it.
Use this to pre-empt FAQ items - he notes that customers often hold objections without being conscious enough of them to scroll to an FAQ, so handling them earlier converts better.
Reserve the FAQ for the objections you cannot naturally place elsewhere, and keep its answers framed as objection handling rather than policy disclosure alone.
caveats: Testimonials must be genuine and compliant with advertising rules - the source does not address disclosure requirements.
The claim that pre-handling objections increases conversion is the presenter's assertion, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Credibility is market-specific, so research who the market trusts
cards.summary: Choose credibility signals based on what the target market actually respects, not default authority figures.
cards.use_when: Selecting expert endorsements, certifications or founder story elements for a sales page or ad.
steps: Do not assume a doctor, lawyer or athlete is the right authority. The source notes that in some health markets the medical establishment is framed as the enemy.
Use your customer research to identify who the market looks up to, who they listen to and which institutions they distrust.

Example from the source: Primal Queen frames modern medicine as keeping people sick and positions a return to organ meat and ancestral eating as the credible alternative - credibility is built by siding with the customer's worldview.
Choose proof assets that fit the frame: third-party testing, sourcing transparency, founder story, practitioner endorsements or community consensus.
Repeat the credibility signal at the point of highest skepticism, typically near the offer and near the payment step.
Re-validate the credibility frame when entering a new market or audience segment, because the same proof can read as untrustworthy elsewhere.
caveats: Anti-establishment framing carries compliance, platform-policy and reputational risk; the source gives no regulatory guidance.
The Primal Queen example is the presenter's illustration, not evidence that the framing caused their results.

cards.title: Order page: minimize friction, then add quantity breaks and order bumps
cards.summary: The order page should be boringly clear, with quantity discounts and cheap checkout bumps doing the AOV work.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the payment step of a funnel, or comparing a custom order page against a default Shopify checkout.
steps: Treat the order page as the highest-leverage split test in the funnel - the source states the biggest drop-off in a funnel is usually sales page to order page, and order page tests are among the most impactful he tests.

Make clarity the goal: the visitor must immediately see where to enter card details, CVV and address. He reports having seen pages where buyers could not find the fields; prefer clarity over cleverness.
Add quantity breaks (buy more units at a discount) to lift units per order.

Add low-price order bumps as checkboxes, such as expedited shipping or shipping insurance - he calls the bump the upsell with the highest take rate, citing roughly 50% opt-in at $10-$20, i.e. about $5 added AOV.
Extend the arithmetic to scale: an extra $5 per customer is about $500 per day at 100 orders per day.
Prefer a controllable order page over a stock checkout so bumps and quantity breaks are possible; he also notes digital products can work as bumps because marginal cost is near zero.
Accept an unstyled look - he states his order pages are ugly and they work because copy is clear and the page is not slowed by design elements.
caveats: The 50% bump take rate and $10-$20 price are his recollections, not benchmarks - test on your own traffic.
Shipping insurance and expedited shipping bumps must reflect real services; misleading fees invite chargebacks and complaints.
Requires platform capability - verify your checkout supports bumps and quantity breaks in your current stack.

cards.title: OTO page formats: VSL or TSL, with two proven product frameworks
cards.summary: Structure post-purchase offers as a short video or text sales letter, and pick the product with 'more of the same' or 'solve one problem, create another'.
cards.use_when: Building the post-purchase upsell step for a supplement, consumable or consumable-adjacent product.
steps: Choose the format: a VSL OTO is an embedded video with almost nothing else on the page while the video sells; a TSL OTO is the same content written on the page. Both use the 'wait, your order is not yet complete' frame to hold the customer before the confirmation.
Keep the page minimal - the offer sits directly beneath the video or copy so there is one decision on screen.
Framework 1 - more of the same: sell the identical product in greater quantity at a discount. This dominates supplements, e.g. adding a 3- or 6-month supply while the order is being packed.

Framework 2 - solve one problem, create another (the presenter's preferred option): the front-end product solves a pain point and inevitably creates an adjacent new problem the OTO fixes. His example is weight loss: the product solves the weight problem, and the created problem is keeping the weight off, which the upsell addresses.
Sell the outcome on the OTO as well; on the sales page he frames the underlying principle as selling transformational outcomes rather than products.
Sequence after the first OTO: send buyers to OTO2, and send OTO1 declines to a down-sell page rather than ending the funnel.
caveats: Both frameworks presume a product with a natural adjacent problem or consumable repeat - they fit poorly for one-off durable goods.
Genuinely solving a problem and then inventing a manufactured problem to sell the fix is the ethical failure mode; the source flags ethics explicitly.
VSL and TSL OTOs need strong copy to convert; the presenter ties results directly to copywriting skill.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Retire misconceptions: clarity over cleverness, subtraction over design
cards.summary: On high-drop-off pages, enforce clarity and remove confusing elements before adding anything new.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a checkout or sales page that has high traffic but poor completion.
steps: Apply the source's rule literally on the payment step: clarity is king, keep it simple, and never let cleverness hide the card fields or CVV entry.
Reframe optimisation as subtraction - the presenter describes conversion as a game of removing confusing elements rather than adding features.
Prefer a fast, plain page to a heavy one with animations and large media, because weight adds friction.
Apply the same standard to every step: copy must be clear before any visual polish is considered.
When a page underperforms, check comprehension first (does a stranger know what to do in five seconds?) before changing colour, theme or layout.
Keep the standard even when it conflicts with brand aesthetics - he states he will take the ugly lander every time, accepting the trade-off rather than pretending it does not exist.
caveats: Directional and opinion-based; the source offers no measured comparison of clear-but-plain versus clear-and-designed pages.
Clarity alone does not fix traffic-message mismatch or an uncompetitive offer.
cards.source_name: how i make $535k_mo with landing pages that look like sh_t.docx

cards.title: Funnel drop-off is a leak map: plug gaps with email and SMS
cards.summary: Every step in the funnel loses people, and owned messaging exists to recover those specific leaks.
cards.use_when: Planning lifecycle email or SMS flows for a store that runs a multi-step sales funnel.
steps: Draw the funnel and mark drop-off between each step: ad to sales page, sales page to order page, order page completion, OTO1 acceptance and OTO1 decline.
Assign an owned-channel flow to each leak rather than one generic abandoned-cart series.
For sales-page exits, use a browse or lead-capture sequence if you collected contact details before the order; otherwise treat this as a creative and landing-page problem first.
For order-page abandonment, run the recovery sequence in the same voice as the order page, restating the guarantee and the quantity-break value.
For OTO declines, follow up with the declined offer or a lighter alternative in email rather than dropping the customer.
Treat post-purchase email and SMS as an extension of the funnel's selling job, since the source frames the channel's role as plugging the leaks shown in the funnel diagram.
Note the boundaries: the source defers email platform setup and deliverability, and paid acquisition scaling, to other material.
caveats: The source mentions email and SMS as a leak-plugging layer but gives no sequence structures, timing or platform specifics in this material.
Do not import deliverability or automation setup advice from here - it is explicitly out of scope.

cards.title: Advertorial Fundamentals and the Don't-Rewrite-a-Swipe Rule
cards.summary: What an advertorial is and why asking AI to rewrite a competitor's ad without foundational research produces low-converting copy.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to produce a long-form advertorial landing page for paid traffic rather than a standard product page.
steps: Understand the format: an advertorial blends an ad with an editorial so the page reads like it was written by a third-party, impartial source, while actually selling the product down the page.
Define the funnel role: the advertorial is typically the landing page that paid traffic hits before the sales page or offer, so it must carry the story and belief-shifting, not just product features.

Reject the common shortcut of finding a successful competitor advertorial and prompting an LLM to 'rewrite this but for my company' — the source calls this a terrible strategy because it skips research on your product, audience and offer.

Accept the sequencing: research first, foundational documents second, swipe third, draft fourth, edit ('chief') fifth. The source states this full process took roughly under an hour to complete an advertorial for the demoed product.
Apply to your store by treating every advertorial as built on your own customer research, not as a text-substitution exercise on someone else's asset.
caveats: The five-step framework, prompts and swipe material are the presenter's opinionated SOP; adapt them rather than treating step order as mandatory.
The 'under an hour' figure is the presenter's own example, not a benchmark for your store.
